Going on v_Enhance's suggestion to show that 1006 is the best possible sized set of permutations: it suffices to show that there always exists a non-intersecting permutation given 1005 permutations; having this fact, if  $m < 1005$  permutations are given, we can just add any other  $1005 - m$  permutations and use a non-intersecting permutation for this new set of  $1005$ .

So for a collection  $\mathcal{P}$  of  $1005$  permutations of  $[2010]$ , form a bipartite graph  $G$  with branches  $A$  and  $B$  having vertices  $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2010}$  and  $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_{2010}$ . Connect  $a_i$  to  $b_j$  if and only if there does not exist  $\pi \in \mathcal{P}$  with  $\pi(i) = j$ . A perfect matching in  $G$  would yield a non-intersecting permutation  $\sigma$  by choosing  $\sigma(i)$  to be  $k$  such that  $\overline{a_i b_k}$  appears in the perfect matching, so it suffices to show that  $G$  contains a perfect matching.

Since any  $j \in [2010]$  only appears in at most  $1005$  positions in the permutations of  $\mathcal{P}$  (i.e. there are at most  $1005$   $i$ 's such that  $\pi(i) = j$  for some  $\pi \in \mathcal{P}$ ), this leaves at least  $1005$  positions for  $j$  not to appear in, i.e.  $|N_G(\{a_i\})| \ge 1005$  for all  $i$ , so  $|N_G(S)| \ge |S|$  for all (non-empty) subsets of  $A$  with size at most  $1005$  (and for  $S = \varnothing$ ,  $|N_G(S)| = 0 = |S|$ ). For  $S \subseteq A$  with  $|S| \ge 1006$ , and any  $j$ , at least one of the  $a_i$ 's in  $S$  is such that  $\pi(i) \neq j$  for all  $\pi \in \mathcal{P}$  since  $|\mathcal{P}|$  is only  $1005$ . So there exists  $a_i \in S$  such that  $\overline{a_i b_j}$  appears in  $G$ , i.e.  $|N_G(S)| = 2010 \ge |S|$ .

So in all cases  $|N(S)| \ge |S|$  so by Hall's Marriage Condition there is a perfect matching of  $G$ .

<details><summary>Solution</summary>The answer is that the only such sequence is  $\boxed{x_i=2i}$ ,  $1\le i\le n-1$ .**Lemma:** For all triples of positive integers  $(i, j, k)$  such that  $i+j=k<n$ ,  $x_i+x_j=x_k$ .
*Proof:* Consider the numbers  $x_1+x_1, x_1+x_2, x_1+x_3, \dots, x_1+x_{n-2}$ . By (c), they must all be part of the sequence. Since there are  $n-2$  numbers here and  $n-1$  numbers in the sequence,  $\{x_1+x_1,x_1+x_2,\dots,x_1+x_{n-2}\}=\{x_2,x_3,\dots,x_{n-1}\}$ . Because the sequence is strictly increasing, we know that  $x_1+x_1=x_2, x_1+x_2=x_3, \dots, x_1+x_{n-2}=x_{n-1}$ . Similarly, consider the numbers  $x_2+x_2, x_2+x_3, \dots, x_2+x_{n-3}$ . Again, by (c) these are all part of our sequence. Since  $x_2+x_2>x_2+x_1=x_3$ , we know that  $x_2+x_2\ge x_4$ . There are  $n-4$  numbers in the sequence greater than or equal to  $x_4$ , and  $n-4$  numbers listed above. Therefore, they must all be the same, so that  $x_2+x_2=x_4, x_2+x_3=x_5, \dots, x_2+x_{n-3}=x_{n-1}$ . Continuing in this fashion, we can see that, for all  $k$  between  $1$  and  $\left\lfloor\frac{n-1}{2}\right\rfloor$  inclusive,  $x_k+x_k, x_k+x_{k+1},\dots, x_k+x_{n-1-k}$  are all in the sequence. Furthermore, from our the only possible values for these sums of pairs are  $x_{2k}, x_{2k+1},\dots,x_{n-1}$  from our previous "mapping" (almost like induction). Since there are  $n-2k$  sums and  $n-2k$  possible values in the sequence they can be, they must be exactly those  $n-2k$  values of the sequence. Since they are strictly increasing, we know that  $x_k+x_k=x_{2k}, x_k+x_{k+1}=x_{2k+1},\dots,x_k+x_{n-1-k}=x_{n-1}$ . Combining all of our results, in every case  $x_1+x_j=x_k$ .  $\blacksquare$ **Lemma:**  $x_i=ix_1$ .
*Proof:* We induct on  $i$ . The base case,  $i=1$ , is trivial. Now, assume that this holds true until  $i=k$ . Then,   $$ x_{k+1}=x_k+x_1=kx_1+x_k=(k+1)x_1, $$  as desired.  $\blacksquare$ We can now rewrite our sequence as  $x_1,2x_1,\dots,(n-1)x_1$ . By (b), we know that  $x_1+x_{n-1}=2n$ , which implies that  $x_1+(n-1)x_1=2n$ , and  $x_1=2$ . Now, our sequence must be  $2, 2(2),3(2),\dots, (n-1)(2)=2, 4, 6, \dots, 2n-2$ . This is the only possible answer.</details>

stem_md: There are  $n$  students standing in a circle, one behind the other. The students have heights  $h_1<h_2<\dots <h_n$ . If a student with height  $h_k$  is standing directly behind a student with height  $h_{k-2}$  or less, the two students are permitted to switch places. Prove that it is not possible to make more than  $\binom{n}{3}$  such switches before reaching a position in which no further switches are possible.
solution_md:
We will prove that the student with height  $h_k$  can swap with a shorter student at most  $\binom{k-1}{2}$  times by induction.
Fix  $k$  and observe that we can basically disregard any students with height  $h_{k+1}$  or more: clearly we can always swap around students with height  $h_{k+2}$  or more, and then note that any students with height less than  $h_{k-1}$  can swap with  $h_{k}$ . So we only consider  $h_1,h_2,\ldots,h_k$ . We will inductively show that  $h_{k-i}$  with  $k-1 \geq i \geq 1$  can swap with  $h_k$  at most  $i-1$  times by using induction on  $i$ .
For our base case, observe that clearly the student with height  $h_{k-1}$  can never swap with  $h_k$ .
Now suppose that  $h_{k-(i-1)}$  can swap at most  $i-2$  times. We will demonstrate that  $h_{k-i}$  will swap at most  $i-1$  times. Observe that  $h_{k-i}$  and  $h_{k-(i-1)}$  can never swap. We can see that after the first time  $h_{k-i}$  swaps with  $h_k$ , we must have  $h_{k-(i-1)}$  swap with  $h_k$  before  $h_{k-i}$  can swap with  $h_k$  again (otherwise, we'd have to get  $h_{k-i}$  get "past"  $h_{k-(i-1)}$ , which is impossible). However by inductive hypothesis,  $h_{k-(i-1)}$  can swap with  $h_k$  at most  $i-2$  times which implies that  $h_k$  can swap with  $h_k$  at most  $i-2+1=i-1$  times as desired. 
This is enough to imply that  $h_k$  can swap at most:  $$ 0+1+2+\cdots+k-2=\frac{(k-2)(k-1)}{2}=\binom{k-1}{2} $$  times, which is what we wanted to prove. To finish, note that summing up all of these upper bounds shows that we can make at most:  $$ \binom{0}{2}+\binom{1}{2}+\binom{2}{2}+\cdots+\binom{n-1}{2}=\binom{n}{3} $$  moves (by Hockey Stick), as desired.  $\blacksquare$

First, note that because the tallest person cannot pass the second tallest person, that person can only move forward as many spaces as the second tallest, plus n-2 if he initially starts in front of the second tallest person. This maximum can be reached by moving around the circle once and then following the second tallest person every time they move. Now, let a(n) be the maximum number of moves before there are no more. The maximum distance moved for the tallest person is a(n)-a(n-1), because the tallest person is adding their moves to the solution for a(n-1). This along with the previous comment gives the recurrence relation a(n)-a(n-1)=n-2+a(n-1)-a(n-2). Along with the base cases of a(1)=a(2)=0, the solution to this recurrence is n chose 3, as can be shown by substituting into the relation.

I didn't actually take the USAMO, but here's a nice solution I found.  I think it's more direct than the solutions posted already, but it's not necessarily easier.

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>WLOG let the heights of the students be the first  $n$  positive integers.  Then for  $i < j$ , define  $d(i,j)$  as follows:

Start at the student with height  $j$ .  Go forward around the circle until we get to the student with height  $j-1$ .  Then continue around the circle until we get to the student with height  $j-2$ .  Repeat until we get to the student with height  $i$ .  Let  $d(i,j)$  be the integer number of complete loops traversed.

Now suppose the student with height  $a$  is directly in front of the student with height  $b$ , and  $b - a > 1$ .  Then the students can be switched, so consider switching them.  Since  $a$  and  $b$  aren't consecutive, the path for  $d(i, j)$  for any  $i,j$  hits the students with heights  $a$  and  $b$  on separate loops - both before and after the switch.  Then the switch doesn't affect the length of the path unless one of the students with height  $a$  or  $b$  is an endpoint of the path, in which case the path becomes shorter by exactly one step for each of the two students that's an endpoint of the path.  The length of the path can never be an exact number of complete loops, since it starts and ends at different students.  Therefore, for  $d(i,j)$  to decrease, the path length must decrease by at least two, which can only happen if  $i=b$  and  $j=a$ .  But if we're looking at  $d(b,a)$ , we see that before the switch, the path is just one step longer than an exact number of complete loops, so the switch decreases  $d(b,a)$  by exactly one.

Therefore, switching students with heights  $a$  and  $b$  decreases  $d(b,a)$  by one and leaves all other  $d(i,j)$  unchanged.  So the sum of all  $d(i,j)$  decreases by exactly one every switch.  This sum is always non-negative, and since  $d(b,a)<b-a$ , the sum is at most  $\sum_{0<i<j\le n}(j-i-1)$ .  Note that each term of this sum corresponds to the triples of distinct integers with smallest element  $i$  and largest element  $j$ , so this sum is actually  $\binom{n}{3}$ .  This gives the desired result.</details>

<details><summary>Another Solution</summary>For any particular arrangement R of  $h_0, h_1... h_{n-1}, h_n$  around a circle and positive integers  $a$  and  $b$ , define  $Q(R, a, b)$  as follows: remove all  $h_i$  with either  $i\le a$  or  $i\ge b$  from R to obtain a new arrangement S. For each  $h_i$  in S, define  $f(h_i)$  to be the number of students between  $h_i$  and  $h_{i-1}$  in the forwards direction, including  $h_{i-1}$  (assume that  $h_a=h_{b-1}$ ). Sum all the  $f(h_i)$  to obtain  $Q(R, a, b)$ . If you switch  $h_{a+1}$  and  $h_{b-1}$ , then Q decreases by exactly  $b-a-1$ . Otherwise, switching two students preserves the value of Q, since one student gets closer to every other student and the other student gets farther from every other student, and the distance between the two students themselves doesn't affect Q. Since it *must* end directly after  $h_{n-1}$ , and cannot switch backwards, the total number of moves  $h_n$  makes, regardless of the order of switches in the circle, will be the number that  $h_{n-1}$  makes plus the number of moves it takes to get to  $h_{n-1}$  in the original configuration. Now note that the maximum number of moves it takes  $h_n$  to go behind  $h_{n-1}$  is achieved when he stands directly in front of  $h_{n-1}$  in the diagram in which case it takes him  $n-2$  moves to get behind  $h_{n-1}$ . Thus the theoretical maximum for the total number of moves is going to be \[n-2+2(n-1-2)+3(n-2-2)+\cdots+(n-2)(3-2)\] since  $h_{n}$  takes a maximum of  $n-2$  moves to get behind  $h_{n-1}$ . Consider  $n$  (the tallest one). We can treat  $n$  like a "ghost" and consider all the switches that can be made with the other  $n-1$  people. We can simply have  $n$  move "out of the way" which will add a few moves in case we need to. We would have  $f(i, n-1) = f(i, n)$  where  $i < n$  since there is no way that  $i$  could move even more with the addition of an extra person. Now let us look at  $f(n, n)$ . The person  $n$  could be  $n-2$  people away from  $n$  in which case he will move  $n-2$  times he hits up against person  $n-1$ . And then we have  $$ f(1, n) + f(2, n) + \cdots + f(n, n) \le \binom{0}{2} + \binom{1}{2} + \cdots + \binom{n-1}{2} = \binom{n}{3} $$  as desired.

First we prove the critical claim: **Claim.** Any $k$ eats $1$ at most $k - 2$ times. **Proof.** We use induction on $k$ , with the base case $k = 2$ being obvious. Clearly the first time $k$ eats $1$ , every next time it must be eaten by $k - 1$ first. By the inductive hypothesis, there are at most $1 + (k - 1 - 2) = k - 2$ swaps, thus the claim is proven. We use induction on $n$ (again!), with the base case being obvious (we can do 2 if we define $\binom{2}{3} = 0$ but still, doing 3 with the 2 cases is the morally correct thing to do), since in the case where the cycle looks like $$ 1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 1 $$ there is clearly only one possible move, that is $3$ eats $1$ , and in the other, $$ 1 \to 3 \to 2 \to 1 $$ there are no possible moves. Now for the inductive step, assume the statement is true for $n - 1$ and consider swaps without $1$ . Clearly we have $$ \#\text{number of moves} \ge \binom{n - 1}{3} + \binom{n - 1}{2} = \binom{n}{3} $$

solution_md: Noting the identity  $\frac{2}{n(n+1)(n+2)}=(\frac1{n}+\frac1{n+1}+\frac1{n+2})-\frac3{n+1}$ , computation yields that \[2S_q-\frac1p+1=\sum_{i=\frac{p+1}2}^{p-1}\frac1i+\sum_{i=p+1}^{\frac{3p-1}2}\frac1i.\] Note that  $i$  is never a multiple of  $p$  in the above summation. In particular, if the right hand side above is expressed as a fraction in lowest terms, the denominator will not be divisible by  $p$  while the numerator is congruent to \[\sum_{i=\frac{p+1}2}^{p-1}\frac1i+\sum_{i=p+1}^{\frac{3p-1}2}\frac1i\equiv\sum_{i=1}^{p=1}\frac1{i}\equiv\frac{p(p-1)}2\equiv0\pmod p.\] Thus if  $2S_q-\frac1p+1=\frac{m'}{n'}$  for integers  $m'$  and  $n'$ , then  $p\mid m'$ . But then  $\frac{m}{n}=\frac1p-2S_q=\frac{n'-m'}{n'}$ , so  $p\mid m-n$ .  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: A blackboard contains 68 pairs of nonzero integers.  Suppose that for each positive integer  $k$  at most one of the pairs  $(k, k)$  and  $(-k, -k)$  is written on the blackboard.  A student erases some of the 136 integers, subject to the condition that no two erased integers may add to 0.  The student then scores one point for each of the 68 pairs in which at least one integer is erased.  Determine, with proof, the largest number  $N$  of points that the student can guarantee to score regardless of which 68 pairs have been written on the board.
solution_md:
We claim the answer is  $\boxed{43}$ . This can be achieved using  $5$  copies of each of  $(1,1)$  through  $(8,8)$ , and one copy of each pair of distinct numbers from  $-1$  to  $-8$ .

We prove  $43$  is always attainable. First, perform the following optimizations until they cannot be done anymore:


- If an integer  $k$  exists in an ordered pair but neither  $(k,k)$  nor  $(-k,-k)$  exist, turn the ordered pair into  $(k,k)$ .
- If the ordered pair  $(k,k)$  exists, and there is another ordered pair  $(k,l)$  with  $l\ne k$ , change this pair into  $(k,k)$ .

Notice that both optimizations make the student's job harder.

The resulting configuration must satisfy the property that for any pair  $(k,l)$  with  $k\ne l$ , the ordered pairs  $(-k,-k)$  and  $(-l,-l)$  exist. Let  $S$  be the set of all numbers  $i$  such that  $(i,i)$  exists. For all  $i\in S$ , choose to erase all copies of  $i$  with probability  $p=\frac12(\sqrt5-1)$ , and otherwise erase all copies of  $-i$ . Notice that pairs of identical numbers are scored with probability  $p$ , and pairs with different numbers are scored with probability  $1-p^2=p$ . Thus, in expectation the amount of points scored is  $68p>42$ , so there must be a way to score  $43$  points.

I think the following is an argument that  $N$  is at least 43.

Let  $p$  be  $\frac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2}$ , the inverse golden ratio.  It satisfies  $1 - p^2 = p$ , and is between  $\frac{1}{2}$  and  $1$ .

By replacing  $k$  with  $-k$  everywhere if necessary, we may assume that the only pairs of the form  $(k, k)$  occur when  $k$  is positive.

Let  $S$  be the set of integers constructed (randomly) in the following way.  For every positive integer  $k$ , place  $k$  in  $S$  with probability  $p$  and otherwise place  $-k$  in  $S$ .  

Now let's erase every integer in  $S$ .  For a pair of the form  $(k, k)$ , its integers will be erased with probability  $p$ .  For a pair of the form  $(k, -k)$ , one of its integers will be erased with probability  $1$ .  For a pair of the form  $(x, y)$ , where  $y \ne \pm x$ , the  $x$  will be erased with probability at least  $1 - p$  and the same for  $y$ ; hence the probability that at least one of them is erased is at least  $1 - p^2$ , which is equal to  $p$ .

So for every pair, at least one of its integers is erased with probability at least  $p$ .  By linearity of expectation, that means the expected number of pairs with an erasure is at least  $68p$ .  Since  $p > \frac{42}{68}$ , that means the expected number of pairs with erasure is more than  $42$ .  Hence there is some way to erase more than  $42$  pairs.  So  $N$  is at least  $43$ .

The total number of pairs you write on the blackboard for this arrangement is:

\[(n-1)+(n-2)+(n-2)(n-3)=n^2-3n+3\]
edges.
The fraction of the pairs which are in the winning set is
\[\frac{n^2-3n+3}{\frac n2(3n+7)}.\]
Magically, this function is minimized at some  $n$  just shy of 8, and minimized along the integers at  $n=8$ .  So for some reason, 68 is the optimal question for which this particular graph is the answer.

One note on where this problem (may have) come from.

In computer science there is a famous problem known as MAXSAT which can be described as follows:  You have a list of  $n$  variables, each of which can be set to either true or false.  You are also given a long list of "OR" clauses, meaning clauses like

" $x_5$  is true OR  $x_3$  is false OR  $x_7$  is true"

" $x_1$  is true OR  $x_8$  is true"

or even

" $x_5$  is false".  

A clause is satisfied if any of the conditions in it hold.  So in the above example an assignment where every variable is false would satisfy the first and third clause, but not the second.  The goal is to find an assignment of the variables satisfying as many of the clauses as possible.  

This is known to be a very hard problem, and I believe it is also even very hard to approximate, in the following sense: An efficient algorithm that always satisfies significantly more than  $7/8$  of the number of clauses satisfied by the best assignment would lead to a solution of the million dollar  $P=NP$  problem.

In the problem appearing on the USAMO, erasing the number  $i$  corresponds to setting variable  $i$  to true, and erasing  $-i$  corresponds to setting variable  $i$  to false.  The pairs  $(j, k)$  with  $j \neq k$  correspond to clauses of length  $2$  (like the second of the three clauses above), and the pairs  $(k,k)$  correspond to clauses of length  $1$  (e.g.  $(-5, -5)$  corresponds to " $x_5$  is false").   The problem asked you to show, in the language of MAXSAT, that if there are no contradictory pairs of clauses of length  $1$  (if " $x_i$  is true" and " $x_i$  is false" never both appear at once), you can always satisfy at least a  $\phi^{-1}$  fraction of the clauses.   In this language I had actually seen this result before, with Ravi B's proof.  

As to why  $68$  was chosen, I think it may have been in part because  $68$  is an integer for which the bound  $68 \phi^{-1}$  is only a tiny bit more than an integer (so the lower bound of  $43$  is in a sense a bit stronger for  $68$  than for surrounding integers, as you gain more from rounding up).

The expected number that will be erased is  $p(a_1+a_2+...+a_n)+(1-p*p)(\sum b_{ij})$ , where  $a_i$  is the number of times  $(i,i)$  appears, and  $b_{ij}$  the number of times  $(-i,-j)$   For  $p=\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$ , those two numbers are equal to  $1/\phi$ , and this gives  $x/\phi$  is the expected value, so this value rounded up must be always attainable, where  $x=\sum a_i+\sum b_{ij}$  is the total number (in our case 68).

A blackboard contains 68 pairs of nonzero integers. Suppose that for each positive integer $k$ at most one of the pairs $(k, k)$ and $(-k, -k)$ is written on the blackboard. A student erases some of the 136 integers, subject to the condition that no two erased integers may add to 0. The student then scores one point for each of the 68 pairs in which at least one integer is erased. Determine, with proof, the largest number $N$ of points that the student can guarantee to score regardless of which 68 pairs have been written on the board.
Here is one possible approach to model this problem as a graph-theoretic problem. ------------ 1.) Without loss of generality, every pair $(x,x)$ with equal coordinates has $x>0$ . Otherwise we replace every occurrence of $x$ on the blackboard by $-x$ , and every occurrence of $-x$ by $x$ . 2.) Consider a pair $(x,y)$ with unequal coordinates $x\ne y$ on the blackboard. The student scores for this pair by erasing $x$ , or $y$ , or both $x$ and $y$ . If we replace the pair by $(x,x)$ , then the only possible way of scoring is by erasing $x$ . Hence, unless $(-x,-x)$ is already on the blackboard, we may perform this replacement and make the student's life more difficult. A symmetric observation holds for replacing the pair by $(y,y)$ . We summarize: Without loss of generality, whenever the blackboard contains a pair $(x,y)$ with $x\ne y$ , then it also contains the two pairs $(-x,-x)$ and $(-y,-y)$ . 3.) Now create a graph. There is a vertex $x$ for every pair $(x,x)$ on the blackboard (note that $x$ is positive). The profit $p(x)$ is defined as the number of times the pair $(x,x)$ occurs on the blackboard. There is an (undirected) edge $[x,y]$ for every pair $(-x,-y)$ on the blackboard (note that $x$ and $y$ are positive). The profit $p[x,y]$ is defined as the number of times the pair $(-x,-y)$ occurs on the blackboard. 4.) Now the student's problems translates into the following optimization problem: Pick a subset $S$ of the vertices. You score the profit $p(x)$ of every vertex $x\in S$ plus the profit of every edge $[x,y]$ for which at least one of its endpoints is not in $S$ . ------------ Up to this point we have just rewritten and reformulated the problem. But the solution is now easier to see. Upper bound: If you pick every vertex (independently) with probability $q$ , then you get every edge (independently) with probability $1-q^2$ . Choose $q$ to make these two probabilities coincide. Then you get at least $q*$ (total profit) in expectation, and there must be some point in the probability space that gives you this profit. Lower bound: Experiment with complete graphs where all vertices have the same integer profit $p_1$ and all edges have the same integer profit $p_2$ . ------------ There was no particular reason for picking 68 for the number of pairs. It just was big enough. The number 39 looked somewhat small, and the students could have tried to settle the problem through long case distinctions.

I think the following is an argument that $N$ is at least 43. Let $p$ be $\frac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2}$ , the inverse golden ratio. It satisfies $1 - p^2 = p$ , and is between $\frac{1}{2}$ and $1$ . By replacing $k$ with $-k$ everywhere if necessary, we may assume that the only pairs of the form $(k, k)$ occur when $k$ is positive. Let $S$ be the set of integers constructed (randomly) in the following way. For every positive integer $k$ , place $k$ in $S$ with probability $p$ and otherwise place $-k$ in $S$ . Now let's erase every integer in $S$ . For a pair of the form $(k, k)$ , its integers will be erased with probability $p$ . For a pair of the form $(k, -k)$ , one of its integers will be erased with probability $1$ . For a pair of the form $(x, y)$ , where $y \ne \pm x$ , the $x$ will be erased with probability at least $1 - p$ and the same for $y$ ; hence the probability that at least one of them is erased is at least $1 - p^2$ , which is equal to $p$ . So for every pair, at least one of its integers is erased with probability at least $p$ . By linearity of expectation, that means the expected number of pairs with an erasure is at least $68p$ . Since $p > \frac{42}{68}$ , that means the expected number of pairs with erasure is more than $42$ . Hence there is some way to erase more than $42$ pairs. So $N$ is at least $43$ . Definitions: Let  $U$  denote the set of ordered pairs. Let  $T = \{k \in \mathbb{Z}\mid \exists u \in U \mbox{ s.t. } k \in u\}$ , that is, the set of integers that appear in the ordered pairs. Let  $S$  be the set of absolute values  $|k|$  of integers  $k \in T$ . For each absolute value  $v \in S$ , let  $S_v = \{k \in T\mid |k| = v\}$ . Let the number of instances of  $v \in S$  in pairs  $u \in U$  be  $T_v$  and the number of instances of  $-v \in S$  in pairs  $u \in U$  be  $T_{-v}$ . Let  $\phi = \displaystyle\frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$ .

Complicated Deletion Decision-maker: Now, for each  $v \in V$ , we either choose with probability  $\frac{1}{\phi}$  to erase all instances of  $v$  if  $T_v \ge T_{-v}$  and neither  $\{v,v\}$  nor  $\{-v,-v\}$  is a subset of  $U$ , probability  $\frac{1}{\phi}$  to erase all instances of  $-v$  if  $T_{-v} > T_v$  and neither  $\{v,v\}$  nor  $\{-v,-v\}$  is a subset of  $U$ , probability  $\frac{1}{\phi}$  to erase all instances of  $v$  if  $\{v,v\} \in U$ , or probability  $\frac{1}{\phi}$  to erase all instances of  $-v$  if  $\{-v,-v\} \in U$ . 

Probabilistic Method: Now, consider a random pair  $u \in U$ . The probability that at least one of the members of  $u$  is erased is in the set \[\left\{\frac{1}{\phi},1-\frac{1}{\phi^2},1-\frac{1}{\phi}\left(1-\frac{1}{\phi}\right), 1-\left(1-\frac{1}{\phi}\right)^2\right\}.\]
We note that  $\displaystyle\frac{1}{\phi} > \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}$ , so the minimum element of this set is clearly one of  $\displaystyle\frac{1}{\phi}$  and  $1-\displaystyle\frac{1}{\phi^2}$ . However, we have the well-known fact that  $1 = \phi - \displaystyle\frac{1}{\phi}$ , so the minimum of this set must be  $\displaystyle\frac{1}{\phi}$ . Since there are  $68$  pairs in  $U$ , we see that the expected value of of the number of pairs with at least one element erased is at least  $\displaystyle\frac{68}{\phi} \approx 42.026$ . Thus, there exists a way of erasing elements that gives at least  $43$  pairs with at least one element missing.

Note that each  $(k, k)$  has a  $p$  chance of being partly erased, each  $(k, -k)$  will definitely be partly erased, and for each other pair: it has  $1-(1-p)^2>p$  chance of being partly erased if both elements are +, a  $1-p^2=p$  chance if both are -, and a  $1-p(p-1)>p$  chance if one is + and one is -. Clearly the first number we erase yields a score of at most $7$ , the second number erased yields a score at most $6$ , and every successive number yields a score at most $5$ .**Bound:** The proof comes in two parts. Assume without loss of generality that all pairs of the form $(a, a)$ are between two negative numbers. First, we have the following claim:**Claim:** It suffices to show the bound for the case where there are no pairs $(a, b)$ for $b < 0 < a$ or vice versa. *Proof:* Replace the pair $(a, b)$ with the pair $(b, b)$ . Then, any selection $S$ of erased numbers for which $(b, b)$ scores $(a, b)$ also scores, therefore the same selection $S'$ with the pair $(a, b)$ yields at least the same score. $\blacksquare$ Now let $p = \frac{\sqrt 5 - 1}2$ . For each positive integer $a$ , we erase $a$ with probability $1-p$ and $b$ with probability $p$ . Then every pair of the form $(b, b)$ is scored with probability $p$ , while every pair of the form $(a, a')$ is scored with probability $1-p^2 = p$ . Hence the expected score is at least $68p>42$ and thus at least $43$ . **Remark:** One of the hardest parts of the problem is figuring out the answer: off the bat, based on the construction, there's no reason why $43$ *should* be optimal. The most natural way to see the solution, in my opinion, is to see the claim first, which reduces the problem to some multigraph on the positive vertices and self-loops on the negative vertices—from here, the construction for $43$ is clearly the most ``balanced". The reduction (and fairly arbitrary value of $43$ ) suggests that the solution should follow some local path of smoothing to that equality case—say, by contracting vertices, replacing edges, expanding vertices, etc. Unfortunately, this doesn't work, although it seems very promising. Once we get past the hurdle of realizing that the problem is purely *global*, the value of $p$ derives itself: we want some kind of probability space that treats self-loops and edges equally because they contribute equally to score.

stem_md: The 2010 positive numbers  $a_1, a_2, \ldots , a_{2010}$  satisfy the inequality  $a_ia_j \le i+j$  for all distinct indices  $i, j$ . Determine, with proof, the largest possible value of the product  $a_1a_2\ldots a_{2010}$ .
solution_md:
Obviously we can write \[a_1a_2 \cdots a_{2010} = (a_1a_2)(a_3a_4)\cdots (a_{2009}a_{2010}) \le (1+2)(3+4)\cdots (2009+2010).\] I claim that this bound is tight; i.e. there exist  $a_i$  such that equality holds.

Let's let  $a_i^2 = b_i$ , so  $b_ib_j \le (i+j)^2$  for all distinct  $i,j$ . Let's make a preliminary choice of  $b_i$  as follows:
\[b_{2k+1} = 4k+2 + \frac{1}{4k+2}\]
\[b_{2k+2} = 4k+4\]

We have  $b_{2k+1}b_{2k+2}> (4k+3)^2$ . If we can show that  $b_ib_j \le (i+j)^2$  for all  $i < j$  not of the form  $(i,j) = (2k+1, 2k+2)$ , we can scale the  $b_i$ 's downwards until  $b_{2k+1}b_{2k+2} = (4k+3)^2$  holds; then  $b_ib_j \le (i+j)^2$  holds for all distinct  $i,j$  and equality holds.

To show that  $b_ib_j \le (i+j)^2$  for all  $i<j$  not of the form  $(i,j) = (2k+1,2k+2)$ , we will do casework on the parity of  $i,j$ .**Case 1.**  $i,j$  are both even

*Proof.* This is the easiest case. Just note that  $b_i = 2i$  and  $b_j = 2j$ , so  $b_ib_j = 4ij \le (i+j)^2$ .**Case 2.**  $i$  is even,  $j$  is odd

*Proof.* We have  $b_i = 2i$  and  $b_j = 2j + \frac{1}{2j}$ , so  $b_ib_j = 4ij + \frac{i}{j}$ . Now we want  $4ij + \frac{i}{j} \le i^2 + 2ij + j^2$ , which rearranges to  $(j-i)^2 \ge \frac{i}{j}$ . But since  $i<j$ , we have  $\frac{i}{j} < 1$ . Furthermore,  $j-i$  is an odd integer and thus  $(j-i)^2 \ge 1$ . It follows that  $(j-i)^2 \ge \frac{i}{j}$ .**Caes 3.**  $i$  is odd,  $j$  is even

*Proof.* We have  $b_i = 2i + \frac{1}{2i}$  and  $b_j = 2j$ , so  $b_ib_j = 4ij + \frac{j}{i}$ . Now we want  $4ij + \frac{j}{i} \le i^2 + 2ij + j^2$ , which rearranges to  $(j-i)^2 \ge \frac{j}{i}$ . If we decrease  $i,j$  each by 2,  $(j-i)^2$  stays constant but  $\frac{j}{i}$  increases. Thus we can decrease  $i$  until  $i = 1$ . We also know that  $(i,j) \not= (2k+1, 2k+2)$ , so  $j-i \ge 3$ . Thus  $j \ge 4$ . We want to prove  $(j-1)^2 \ge \frac{j}{1} = j$ , which is true for  $j \ge 4$ .**Case 4.**  $i,j$  are both odd

*Proof.* We have  $b_i = 2i + \frac{1}{2i}$  and  $b_j = 2j + \frac{1}{2j}$ , so  $b_ib_j = 4ij + \frac{j}{i} + \frac{i}{j} + \frac{1}{4ij}$ . Now we want  $4ij + \frac{j}{i} + \frac{i}{j} + \frac{1}{4ij} \le i^2 + 2ij + j^2$ , which rearranges to  $(j-i)^2 \ge \frac{j}{i} + \frac{i}{j} + \frac{1}{4ij}$ . Similarly to above, we can decrease  $i,j$  each by 2 until  $i = 1$ . Then we want to show that  $(j-1)^2 \ge j + \frac{1}{j} + \frac{1}{4j}$ . We know that  $j \ge 3$ , so  $\frac{1}{j} + \frac{1}{4j} \le \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{12} = \frac{5}{12}$ . We see that this is true for all  $j \ge 3$ , as desired.  $\blacksquare$

What generalizations did you have in mind? Generalizing to all even-length sequences is how one solves the problem. See whether you can use any of the methods in http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Wiki/index.php/2010_USAMO_Problems/Problem_3 to obtain bounds for sequences with an odd length of 3 or more. (A sequence with just one term is not subject to any constraints). For three elements if: \begin{align*} xy &\le 3 yz &\le 5 zx &\le 4 \end{align*} We multiply all the inequalities to give $x^2y^2z^2 \le 60$ , and so $xyz \le \sqrt{60}.$ Since in this case we can make all three inequalities be equalities, the maximum is $\sqrt{60},$ with $x = \sqrt{\frac{12}5}, y = \sqrt{\frac{15}4}, z = \sqrt{\frac{20}3}.$ For longer odd sequences it is probably not possible to make the product of the first and last term equal to $n+1,$ so the bound will be less than $\sqrt{(n+1)(2n-1)!!}.$ What is the bound for $n = 5$ ?

stem_md:
Let a positive integer  $n$ .Consider square table  $3*3$ .One use  $n$ colors to color all cell of table such that

each cell is colored by exactly one color.

Two colored table is same if we can receive them from other by a rotation
through center of  $3*3$  table

How many way to color this square table satifies above conditions.
solution_md:
Actually I don't think it's that hard, only messy.

Sketch:
For each board which has a 4-fold rotational symmetry (every 90-degree turn gives the same board), each board has no "match", so each board is counted toward the solution.
For each board which has a 2-fold rotational symmetry (every 180-degree turn gives the same board), each board has exactly one "match", so each pair of boards is counted toward the solution; in other words, divide the number of boards here by 2.
For each board which has no rotational symmetry, each board has exactly three "matches", so each quartet of boards is counted toward the solution; in other words, divide the number of boards here by 4.

Counting the number of boards for each condition shouldn't be too hard. Like, the first scenario only permutes three (center, edge, corner); the second scenario only permutes five (two pairs of corners, two pairs of edges, center, where the two pairs of corner/edge cannot be the same). The third...it's a little hard, but I think you can easily do it by counting the total number of possible colorings ( $n^9$ ) subtracted by the colorings mentioned above.

stem_md: Prove that for each positive integer n,the equation  $x^{2}+15y^{2}=4^{n}$ has at least  $n$  integer solution  $(x,y)$
solution_md: If  $(x,y)$  is a solution for  $n$ , then  $(2x,2y)$  is a solution for  $n+1$ . So it suffices to find a solution  $(x,y)$  for every  $n$  where  $x,y$  are both odd. First, if one of them is odd while the other is even, then  $x^2+15y^2$  will be odd, a contradiction. Thus if one of them is odd, so is the other. Note that  $(2,0)$  is a solution for  $n=1$  and  $(1,1)$  is a solution for  $n=2$ . Now suppose  $(x,y)$  is an odd solution for  $n$ . Then consider the 2 pairs of solution  $\left(\frac{x+15y}{2},\frac{x-y}{2}\right), \left(\frac{x-15y}{2},\frac{x+y}{2}\right)$ , both of which are easy to show that they are integer solutions for  $n+1$ . But since  $\frac{x-y}{2}+\frac{x+y}{2}=x$  is odd, either  $\frac{x-y}{2}$  or  $\frac{x+y}{2}$  is odd, and so is its partner (example,  $\frac{x-y}{2}$  is odd, then  $\frac{x+15y}{2}$  is also odd). Thus we have an odd solution for  $n+1$ . Thus by induction we have an odd solution for all  $n\geq 2$ , and we also have a solution  $(2,0)$  for  $n=1$ , so we have at least  $n$  solutions for every  $n$ .

stem_md:
Let  $n$  be a positive integer. Let   $T_n$  be a set of positive integers such that:
\[{T_n={ \{11(k+h)+10(n^k+n^h)| (1 \leq k,h \leq 10)}}\}\]
Find all  $n$  for which there don't exist two distinct positive integers  $a, b \in T_n$   such that  $a\equiv b \pmod{110}$
solution_md:
If  $n$  is divisible by  $11$  then take  $k=6,h=4$  and  $k=5,h=5$  to note that they do not satisfy our requirements.

We first consider those  $n$  which are primitive roots of  $11$ .

Note that  $11(k+h)+10(n^k+n^h)$  is never divisible by  $110$ .To see this note that the contrary assumption would imply that  $10|k+h$  and  $11|n^k+n^h$  or  $11|n^{2k}+n^{k+h}$  or  $11|(n^k)^2+1$  which is not possible since  $11 \equiv 3\pmod{4}$ .

We have  $11(k+h)+10(n^k+n^h) \equiv 11j \pmod{110}$  yeilds  $11|n^k+n^h$  or  $11|n^{|k-h|}+1$ .So we may choose  $|k-h|=5$ .Since there are  $10$  such pairs of  $h,k$  and only  $9$  possible values of  $j$ (i.e., $j=1,2,\cdots,9$ ) two of the numbers are congruent modulo  $110$ .So n **cannot** be a primitive root to satisfy the conditions.

For the non primitive roots just take  $k=h=5$  and  $k=h=10$  and see that both of them leave equal remainders.

So there are **no** such  $n$ .
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2010 Contests/2010 Vietnam Team Selection Test/373495.json

Let  $a,b,c$  be positive integers which satisfy the condition:  $16(a+b+c)\geq \frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}$ .

solution_md:
Let $a,b,c$ be positive integers which satisfy the condition: $16(a+b+c)\geq \frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}$ . Prove that \[\sum_{cyc} \left( \frac{1}{a+b+\sqrt{2a+2c}} \right)^{3}\leq \frac{8}{9}\]
*My solution* According to Am-Gm inequality we have $\sum_{cyc} \left( \frac{1}{a+b+\sqrt{2a+2c}} \right)^{3}$ $ =\sum \left(\frac{1}{a+b+\sqrt{\frac{a+c}{2}}+\sqrt{\frac{a+c}{2}}}\right)^3$ $\le \sum \frac{1}{\frac{27(a+b)(\sqrt{a+c})^2}{2}}$ thus it suffices to prove that $\sum \frac{1}{(a+b)(a+c)} \le 12$ which reduces to $6(a+b)(b+c)(c+a) \ge a+b+c$ or equivalently $6abc\left(\sum a\right) \left(\sum ab \right)\ge abc\sum a+6a^2b^2c^2$ but due to The Am-Gm inequality and the given condition we have $16abc\sum a\left(\sum ab \right) \ge \left(\sum ab \right)^2 \ge 3abc\sum a$ and $2abc\sum a \sum ab\ge 18a^2b^2c^2$ Summing up the last inequalities and dividing by $3$ we get the desired result The proof is completed equality occurs when $a=b=c=\frac{1}{4}$

stem_md:
We have  $n$  countries. Each country have  $m$  persons who live in that country ( $n>m>1$ ). We divide  $m \cdot n$  persons into  $n$  groups each with  $m$  members such that there don't exist two persons in any groups who come from one country.
Prove that one can choose  $n$  people into one class such that  they come from different groups and different countries.
solution_md:
Ohh... I literally forgot  $\text{HALL MARRIAGE THEOREM}$  , Anyways here's my solution using Turan's Theorem..

First we will count number of pairs of people  $(P_i , P_j)$  such that both the country and the group of  $P_i$  and  $P_j$  are different.
This is exactly   $$  \binom{mn}{2} - 2n \binom{m}{2} $$   from  $\text{PIE}$  ..

Now construct a graph  $\mathcal{G}$  in which there are  $mn$  vertices , each representing a  $Person$  and Join  $2$  vertices if and only if the corresponding persons neither share a group nor a country.  And total number of edges in   $\mathcal{G}$  is   $$  \binom{mn}{2} - 2n \binom{m}{2} $$  Now note that we have to prove that  $\mathcal{G}$  contains a  $K_n$  , which is equivalently to prove from Turan's Theorem that   $$  \binom{mn}{2} - 2n  \binom{m}{2} > \frac{(n-2)(mn)^2}{2(n-1)} $$   , which boils down to prove that  $mn+1 > 3m$  which is true as  $n>m>1$ . 

And we are done.       $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Let  $S_n $  be sum of squares of the coefficient of the polynomial  $(1+x)^n$ . Prove that  $S_{2n} +1$  is not divisible by  $3.$
solution_md: Clearly $S_{2n} +1 = \binom{4n}{2n} +1$ $\textbf{Lemma :}$ If $\binom{2x}{x}$ is not divisible by $p$ . and $x=(a_0,\dots,a_t)_p$ then $0 \leq a_i \leq \frac{p-1}{2} $ and $2x=(2a_0 ,\dots , 2a_t)_p$ Proof: obvious by either Lucas or Kummer. ____________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ So by the lemma $2n=(a_0,\dots ,a_t)_3$ s.t $a_i \in \{0,1\} $ So FSoC $-1 = \binom{4n}{2n} = \sum_{i=0}^{t} \binom{2a_i}{a_i} $ $\text{mod} (3)$ Notice each term of RHS becomes $-1$ if $a_i = 1$ and otherwise $1$ . so we should have odd number of them equal to $1$ . But $2n = a_0 + a_1 3+ \dots + a_t 3^t$ ( $\spadesuit$ ) odd number of $a_i$ 's are $1$ so RHS of ( $\spadesuit$ ) is odd but LHS of it is even. Contradiction $\blacksquare$

$\binom{4n}{2n} \equiv 0, 1 \; (mod\ \;3) $ .
why?
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Use Lucas theorem,the proof is very straight forward</details>

Obviously we will have to show that  $\binom{4n}{2n}+1$  is never divisible by  $3$ .

We now convert the numbers into ternary form.
Let  $4n=(i_1i_2 \cdots i_m)_3$  $2n=(j_1j_2 \cdots j_m)_3$ Then by Lucas' theorem $\binom{4n}{2n}=\binom{i_1}{i_2}\binom{i_2}{j_2}\cdots\binom{i_m}{j_m} \pmod{3}$ If for any  $k$  we have  $i_k<j_k$  then LHS would be divisible by  $3$  and the problem statement would be true.So we assume  $i_k \ge j_k \forall k$ .If  $j_x$  equals  $0$  then  $\binom{i_x}{j_x} \equiv 1\pmod{3}$ .If  $i_x,j_x$  both equals  $1$  or  $2$  then  $\binom{i_x}{j_x} \equiv 1\pmod{3}$ .

Now let's consider those cases when  $i_x=2,j_x=1$ .I claim that number of such pairs is even.To see this note that since  $(j_1j_2 \cdots j_m)_3$  is even in base 10,there are an even number of  $1$ 's among the  $j_k$ 's.Analogously we see that there are an even number of  $1$ 's among the  $i_k$ 's.For those  $j_k$ 's which are equal to  $1$ ,the corresponding  $i_k$ 's are either  $1$  or  $2$ .Consider the RHS of the equality $2n=\sum_{k=1}^{m}{(i_k-j_k)3^{m-k}}$ .

If the corresponding  $i_k$ 's are  $1$  then this does not affect the parity of the RHS.If the  $i_k$ 's are  $2$  then  $(i_k-j_k)3^{m-k}=3^{m-k}$ ,an odd number.Since the LHS is even there should be an even number of odd numbers,i.e., even number of  $2$ 's among corresponding  $j_k$ 's and consequently even number of indices  $k$  with  $i_k=2,j_k=1$ .My claim is proven.

Thus we see that when  $\dbinom{4n}{2n}$  is not divisible by  $3$  it should be  $1$  modulo  $3$  and in this case the problem statement is also true.

We need to show that $3 \nmid \binom{4n}{2n}+1$ **Lemma:** If $\binom{2x}{x}$ is not divisible by $p$ . and $x=(a_0,\dots,a_t)_p$ then $0 \leq a_i \leq \frac{p-1}{2} $ with $2x=(2a_0 \dots 2a_t)_p$ For the sake of contradiction assume not and suppose that $2n=a_0+3a_1+........+3^d a_d$ in base $3$ and $4n=2a_0+6a_1+........+3^d \cdot 2 a_d$ in base $3$ By Lucas Theorem, $-1 \equiv \binom{4n}{2n} =\prod_{j=0}^d \binom{2a_j}{a_j} \pmod 3$ The RHS becomes $-1$ if $a_i = 1$ and otherwise $1$ so we should have odd number of them equal to $1$ ,which isn't possible so we are done

stem_md: A 16-step path is to go from  $ ( \minus{} 4, \minus{}4)$  to  $ (4,4)$  with each step increasing either the  $x$ -coordinate or the  $y$ -coordinate by 1. How many such paths stay outside or on the boundary of the square  $ \minus{} 2 \le x \le 2$ ,  $ \minus{} 2 \le y \le 2$  at each step? $ \textbf{(A)}\ 92 \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ 144 \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ 1568 \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ 1698 \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ 12,\!800$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Block-walking</summary>As a lemma, we claim that the number of unrestricted paths only going up and right through an  $ m\times n$  grid is  $ \binom{m \plus{} n}{n}$ . Consider the sequence of moves; written out as urrruru..., with u representing an up move and r representing a right move, it will consist of  $ m \plus{} n$  letters of which we choose  $ n$  to be right moves.

For the main problem, we consider only the paths that go below the square and double at the end by symmetry. Every such path must pass through exactly one of  $ (2, \minus{} 2)$ ,  $ (3, \minus{} 3)$ , and  $ (4, \minus{} 4)$ , as if it passed through two it would have to go down or left at some point. The number of ways to go from  $ ( \minus{} 4, \minus{} 4)$  to  $ (2, \minus{} 2)$  is  $ \binom{8}{2}$  by the lemma, and the number of ways to go from  $ (2, \minus{} 2)$  to  $ (4,4)$  is also  $ \binom{8}{2}$ . Thus, the number of paths which pass through  $ (2, \minus{} 2)$  is  $ \binom{8}{2}^2$ . Similarly, the numbers which pass through  $ (3, \minus{} 3)$  and  $ (4, \minus{} 4)$ , respectively, are  $ \binom{8}{1}^2$  and  $ \binom{8}{0}^2$ . This makes a total of
\[ 2\left[\binom{8}{2}^2 \plus{} \binom{8}{1}^2 \plus{} \binom{8}{0}^2\right] \equal{} 2(784 \plus{} 64 \plus{} 1) \equal{} 1698\Rightarrow\boxed{\textbf{(D)}}.\]</details>

The number of ways of rearranging the letters of the 16-letter "word" $ \texttt{RRRRRRRRUUUUUUUU}$ is $ {16\choose 8} \equal{} 12870.$ However, some of those paths pass through the banned center square. All paths through the center square will pass through one of $ ( \minus{} 1, \plus{} 1),$ $ (0,0),$ or $ ( \plus{} 1, \minus{} 1).$ The number of paths through the point $ (0,0)$ is the number of paths from the lower-left to the origin times the number of paths from the origin to the upper-right. The number of paths from $ ( \minus{} 4, \minus{} 4)$ to $ (0,0)$ is the number of ways of rearranging the letters of the 8-letter word $ \texttt{RRRRUUUU}$ , which is $ {8\choose 4}.$ The number of paths from $ (0,0)$ to $ ( \plus{} 4, \plus{} 4)$ is also the number of ways of rearranging the letters of the 8-letter word $ \texttt{RRRRUUUU}$ . So, we exclude $ {8\choose 4}^2 \equal{} 70^2 \equal{} 4900$ paths. The number of paths from $ ( \minus{} 4, \minus{} 4)$ to $ ( \minus{} 1, \plus{} 1)$ is the number of ways of rearranging the letters of the 8-letter word $ \texttt{RRRUUUUU}$ , which is $ {8\choose 3}.$ The number of paths from $ ( \minus{} 1, \plus{} 1)$ to $ ( \plus{} 4, \plus{} 4)$ is the number of ways or rearranging the letters of the 8-letter word $ \texttt{RRRRRUUU}$ , which is $ {8\choose 3}.$ So, we exclude $ {8\choose 3}^2 \equal{} 56^2 \equal{} 3136$ paths. Finally, the number of paths passing through $ ( \plus{} 1, \minus{} 1)$ is the same as shown in the previous paragraph. So, we exclude another $ {8\choose 3}^2 \equal{} 56^2 \equal{} 3136$ paths. The final number of paths that don't pass through the center square is: $ {16\choose 8} \minus{} {8\choose 4}^2 \minus{} 2{8\choose 3}^2 \equal{} 1698.$

stem_md:
A coin is altered so that the probability that it lands on heads is less than  $ \frac {1}{2}$  and when the coin is flipped four times, the probability of an equal number of heads and tails is  $ \frac {1}{6}$ . What is the probability that the coin lands on heads?
 $ \textbf{(A)}\ \frac {\sqrt {15} \minus{} 3}{6}\qquad
\textbf{(B)}\ \frac {6 \minus{} \sqrt {6\sqrt {6} \plus{} 2}}{12}\qquad
\textbf{(C)}\ \frac {\sqrt {2} \minus{} 1}{2}\qquad
\textbf{(D)}\ \frac {3 \minus{} \sqrt {3}}{6}\qquad
\textbf{(E)}\ \frac {\sqrt {3} \minus{} 1}{2}$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>There are  $ \binom{4}{2} \equal{} 6$  ways of flipping two heads and two tails.

Let  $ x$  be the probability of flipping a head, so  $ 1\minus{}x$  is the probability of flipping a tail. Thus,  $ 6x^2(1\minus{}x)^2 \equal{} \frac{1}{6}$ , so  $ (x(1\minus{}x))^2 \equal{} \frac{1}{36}$ , so  $ x(1\minus{}x) \equal{} \frac{1}{6}$ . We disregard the minus sign here because probabilities must be positive, so they will never multiply to be negative.

Therefore, we must solve  $ x \minus{} x^2 \equal{} \frac{1}{6}$ , or  $ 6x^2 \minus{} 6x \plus{} 1 \equal{} 0$ . By the quadratic formula, this is  $ \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{12}}{12} \equal{} \frac{6 \pm 2\sqrt{3}}{12} \equal{} \frac{3 \pm \sqrt{3}}{6}$ . Now, we must subtract here since we desire the probability that is less than one half, so our solution is  $ \boxed{\frac{3\minus{}\sqrt{3}}{6}}$ , or  $ \boxed{D}$ .</details>

Arithmetic sequences  $ (a_n)$  and  $ (b_n)$  have integer terms with  $ a_1 \equal{} b_1 \equal{} 1 < a_2 \le b_2$  and  $ a_nb_n \equal{} 2010$  for some  $ n$ . What is the largest possible value of  $ n$ ?
 $ \textbf{(A)}\ 2 \qquad
\textbf{(B)}\ 3 \qquad
\textbf{(C)}\ 8 \qquad
\textbf{(D)}\ 288 \qquad
\textbf{(E)}\ 2009$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let the common differences of  ${a_n}$  and  ${b_n}$  be  $a$  and  $b$  respectively.
The condition  $1 < a_2 \le b_2$  implies  $1 < a \le b$ . $a_n = 1 + a(n-1)$  $b_n = 1 + b(n-1)$   $$ 2010 = a_n \cdot b_n \equiv 1 \pmod{n-1} $$   $2009 \equiv 0 \pmod{n-1} \Rightarrow n - 1 \mid 2009 = 7^2 \cdot 41$ .
As we have determine the possible candidates for  $n$ , divisors of  $2009$ , the rest is to setup a diophatine equation in terms of  $a$  and  $b$  for the given  $n$ , to determine whether that possible value of  $n$  is valid.  $$ 2010 = a_n \cdot b_n = [1 + a(n-1)][1 + b(n-1)] $$     $$  = 1 + (a+b)(n-1) + ab(n-1)^2 $$    $$ 2009 = (n-1)[a+b + ab(n-1)] $$  The divisors of  $2009$ ,  $n - 1 < a+b + ab(n-1)$  implies that  $n - 1$  must be the smaller of the divisors of  $2009$ .
This limits the search of  $n - 1$  to the lower half of the divisors of  $2009$ ,  ${1, 7, 41}$  (which each correspond to a larger divisor)
Rearrange the equation to be easier for casework of  $n-1$ ,  $$ \frac{2009}{n-1} = [a+b + ab(n-1)] $$  The objective is to determine the maximum possible of  $n$ , hence we work from the largest value down.
*Case*  $n - 1 = 41$   $$ 49 = a + b + 41ab $$  However from  $1 < a \le b$ , the minimum values of  $ab = 2 \cdot 2 = 4$ , but  $2 + 2 + 41 \cdot 4$  is already larger, therefore there are no solutions.
*Case*  $n - 1 = 7$   $$ a + b + 7ab = 7 \cdot 41 $$   $\left(a + \frac{1}{7}\right)(7b + 1) = 7 \cdot 41 + \frac{1}{7}$  $(7a + 1)(7b + 1) = 7^2 \cdot 41 + 1 = 2010 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 67$ We see that  $3 \cdot 5$  and  $2 \cdot 67$  work for  $7a + 1$  and  $7b + 1$ Having found the maximum value of  $n = \boxed{8}$</details>

stem_md:
What is the minimum value of  $ f(x) \equal{} |x \minus{} 1| \plus{} |2x \minus{} 1| \plus{} |3x \minus{} 1| \plus{} \cdots \plus{} |119x \minus{} 1|$ ?
 $ \textbf{(A)}\ 49 \qquad
\textbf{(B)}\ 50 \qquad
\textbf{(C)}\ 51 \qquad
\textbf{(D)}\ 52 \qquad
\textbf{(E)}\ 53$
solution_md:
SolutionWe begin with the following**Claim.** $f$ is continuous. *Proof.* This is trivial; at every point where $f$ 's piecewise definition changes, there is a real number $x$ that is the same result of two portions. Therefore $f$ is continuous. $\blacksquare$ Henceforth it suffices to find the slope of $f$ at each point. Observe that there exists a positive integer $x$ such that for all $x<\dfrac 1k$ , $f$ is strictly decreasing, and for all $x > \dfrac 1k$ , $f$ is strictly increasing. The minimum of $f$ is simply $f\left(\frac 1k\right)$ . Furthermore, the slope of $f$ in the given interval $\left[\dfrac 1{k+1}, \dfrac 1k\right]$ is given by $$ (k+1)+(k+2)+(k+3)+\cdots+119 - (1+2+3+\cdots+k) = \frac{(119-k)(k+120)}2 - \frac {k(k+1)}2, $$ where we assume that we take the positive slope of the $|kx-1|$ term (taking the negative slope, aka letting $|kx-1| = 1-kx$ , yields a different constant $\dfrac 1k$ , but it turns out the minimum outputted by those two values is the same). We just need to find the root of this quadratic. The positive root of this quadratic is $k=84$ ; therefore, the minimum is attained when $x=\dfrac 1{84}$ . It remains to compute this value. When we write the expression out in full, assuming $x=\dfrac 1{84}$ , it is known the slope term is $0x=0$ , and exactly $84$ constant terms (we take the positive of $|84x-1|$ in our original calculations) are positive ( $|-1| = 1$ ), while the other $35$ terms are negative. Hence, the answer equals $84-35 = \boxed{49} \implies \textbf{(A)}$ is the minimum.
**Question:** Is there a rigorous proof of continuity of any combination of absolute value functions? Or does it require calculus? My start was a bit sketchy...

The first four terms of an arithmetic sequence are  $ p,9,3p\minus{}q,$  and  $ 3p\plus{}q$ . What is the  $ 2010^{\text{th}}$  term of the sequence?
 $ \textbf{(A)}\ 8041\qquad \textbf{(B)}\ 8043\qquad \textbf{(C)}\ 8045\qquad \textbf{(D)}\ 8047\qquad \textbf{(E)}\ 8049$
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>We can form the equations  $$ 9-p=3p-q-9=3p+q-3p+q $$  So,  $$ 18+q=4p \text{ and } 9=p+2q $$  From the second equation,   $$ p=9-2q $$  Thus,  $$ 18+q=36-8q \implies 9q=18 \implies q=2 \implies p=5 $$  So, we have a sequence with first term  $5$  and common difference  $4,$  so  $$ a+(n-1)d=5+(2009) \cdot 4=\boxed{8041} $$</details>

Two quadrilaterals are considered the same if one can be obtained from the other by a rotation and a translation. How many different convex cyclic quadrilaterals are there with integer sides and perimeter equal to  $ 32$ ?
 $ \textbf{(A)}\ 560 \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ 564 \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ 568 \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ 1498 \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ 2255$
solution_md:
This is honestly a pretty bad solution as it is very similar to the AoPS wiki solution, and I was too lazy to outline my specific casework. I don't think there's a reliable, rigorous proof of the key lemma yet, and I don't really think my solution did it really well either. If anyone has a rigorous proof it would be nice if they could post it. :)
SolutionThe crux of the problem is the following**Lemma.** For four integers $a, b, c, d$ , there exists a cyclic quadrilateral with side lengths $a, b, c, d$ in that order if and only if $a+b+c>d$ and cyclic permutations. *Proof.* Let our given quadrilateral $ABCD$ have $AB=a, BC=b, CD=c, DA=d$ . Then, we just need the opposite angles to sum to $180^{\circ}$ . It suffices to construct such a quadrilateral. However, this is trivial; by the Intermediate Value Theorem, there exists a solution $R$ to the equation \[\arcsin\frac{a}{2R} + \arcsin\frac{b}{2R} + \arcsin\frac{c}{2R} + \arcsin \frac{d}{2R} = 180^\circ\] for predetermined integers $a, b, c, d$ that we are already given. This finishes the proof. (The case $a+b+c \leq d$ cannot exist by the Triangle Inequality.) $\blacksquare$ The problem becomes counting the number of quadruplets $(a, b, c, d)$ such that $a+b+c+d=32$ and $a+b+c>d$ . WLOG let $a \leq b \leq c \leq d$ , then the condition becomes equivalent to $a, b, c, d < 16$ . We consider cases. [list=1] [*] $a=b=c=d$ . Trivially there is only one cyclic quadrilateral, $(a, b, c, d)=(8, 8, 8, 8)$ . [*]Three side lengths are equal. The triple-repeated side can be 6, 7, 9 or 10 (the case 8 is already counted), and each quadrilateral formed by the side lengths is unique. There are therefore 4 quadrilaterals in this case. [*]Two pairs of side lengths are equal. Then we just have to choose $a, b$ such that $a+b=16$ , which has $15-1=14$ solutions (Remember we cannot have $a=b=8$ ). However, we can permute the side lengths once chosen in two ways each, for $14 \cdot 2 = 28$ total quadrilaterals. [*]Two side lengths are equal. We do *very careful casework* on the value of equal side length: We find that $a=1$ can only create two pairs of 15 by our restriction, which is impossible. For $a=2$ , there is one pair; for $a=3$ , there are 2 pairs with no double overlap, and so on. Adding all the cases, we get $1+2+3+4+4+5+7+5+4+4+3+2+1 = 45$ total tuplets of side lengths. Therefore, since there are 3 ways to permute the side lengths, there are $45 \cdot 3 = 135$ quadrilaterals in this case. [*]No side lengths are equal. It suffices to casework the largest side from $9$ to $15$ , eventually reaching $69$ quadruplets that satisfy this condition. There are $3!=6$ ways to permute the sides, since rotations are not distinct, giving us $69 \cdot 6 = 414$ quadrilaterals in this case. [/list] Adding the cases gives us $414+135+14+4+1 = \boxed{568} \implies \textbf{(C)}$ is the answer.

So we're counting the number of valid quadruples  $ (a,b,c,d)$  which are different under any cyclic rotation. Burnside's lemma says that this is the average of the number of valid quadruples that are fixed by each rotation. There are  $ 2255$  fixed by the identity,  $ 1$  fixed by each of the two single rotations, and  $ 15$  fixed by the rotation by two spaces. The average of these four numbers is the answer.

Just to enumerate, note that the problem reduces to counting all quadruples  $(a,b,c,d)$  of positive integers  $\mid a+b+c+d=32$  and  $max(a,b,c,d)\le15$ .  Biject the initial condition with a stars and bars argument, in which case there are  $\binom{n-1}{k-1}=\binom{31}{3}$  potential quadruples.  For the second condition, WLOG assume  $a \ge b\ge c\ge d$  (we will multiply by four later for each side being max).  Now assume  $a\ge16$  and thus  $b+c+d\le16$ .  Add a filler variable e to get a more manageable equation,  $b+c+d+e=16$ .  The number of solutions in positive integers is obviously  $\binom{15}{3}$ , but this is insufficient because e is essentially a dummy variable (i.e., not a sidelength) and can take on a value of 0.  Taking this into account yields  $b+c+d=16$ , in which case there are  $\binom{15}{2}$  solutions.  Remembering to multiply by four, our grand total becomes  $[\binom{15}{3}+\binom{15}{2}]\times4=2240$  solutions  $\mid$  one of  $(a,b,c,d)\ge16$ .  What we want is the opposite, which is  $\binom{31}{3}-2240=2255$  valid quadruples.  Now we are ready to apply the rotational group  $G$  to our set  $X$  of non-rotationally distinct quadrilaterals.  Burnside's lemma states that the resulting number of orbits (rotationally distinct quadrilaterals) is the average number of points that remain fixed after rotation.  Rotation by one and three spaces require  $(a,a,a,a)=(8,8,8,8)$ , two spaces require quadruples of form  $(a,b,a,b)$  where  $a+b=16$  ( $\binom{15}{1}$  solutions), and four spaces fix all  $2255$  quadruples.  The solution is thus  $\frac{1+15+15+2255}{4}=568\Longrightarrow C$ .

The graph of  $ y \equal{} x^6 \minus{} 10x^5 \plus{} 29x^4 \minus{} 4x^3 \plus{} ax^2$  lies above the line  $ y \equal{} bx \plus{} c$  except at three values of  $ x$ , where the graph and the line intersect. What is the largest of those values?
 $ \textbf{(A)}\ 4 \qquad
\textbf{(B)}\ 5 \qquad
\textbf{(C)}\ 6 \qquad
\textbf{(D)}\ 7 \qquad
\textbf{(E)}\ 8$
solution_md: If we were to translate  $x^6 - 10x^5 + 29x^4 - 4x^3 + ax^2$  down by  $bx + c$  to get:  $f(x) = x^6 - 10x^5 + 29x^4 - 4x^3 + ax^2 - bx - c$ , then the problem statement becomes: find the largest root of  $f(x)$  given that  $f$  is always positive and has three roots. This is a considerably easier task. Note that this means for some  $m,n,p$ :  $f(x) = (x-m)^{e_1}(x-n)^{e_2}(x-p)^{e_3}$ . Clearly,  $e_1,e_2,e_3$  are all even because  $f(x)$  is never negative. This means that  $f(x) = (x-m)^2(x-n)^2(x-p)^2$ . From here, the task is a lot simpler. We can write  $g(x) = x^3 + a_2x^2 + a_1x+a_0$ . We define  $(g(x))^2 = f(x)$ . We have:  $$ (x^3 + a_2x^2 + a_1x+a_0)(x^3 + a_2x^2 + a_1x+a_0) = x^6 + x^5(2a_2) + x^4(2a_1+a_2^2) + x^3 (2a_0+ 2a_1a_2) + cx^2 + dx + e $$  for some constants  $c,d,e$ . From here, we get:  $a_2 = -5$ ,  $a_1 = 2$ ,  $a_0 = 8$ . Therefore,  $g(x) = x^3 -5x^2 + 2x + 8 = (x-4)(x-2)(x+1)$ . Thus, our answer is  $\boxed{4}$ .

Let  $ f(x) \equal{} \log_{10} (\sin (\pi x)\cdot\sin (2\pi x)\cdot\sin (3\pi x) \cdots \sin (8\pi x))$ . The intersection of the domain of  $ f(x)$  with the interval  $ [0,1]$  is a union of  $ n$  disjoint open intervals. What is  $ n$ ?
 $ \textbf{(A)}\ 2 \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ 12 \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ 18 \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ 22 \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ 36$
solution_md: SolutionThe $\log$ function is defined only when the input $$ \sin(\pi x) \cdot \sin(2\pi x) \cdot \sin(3\pi x) \cdots \sin(8\pi x) > 0. $$ First, we analyze the behavior of the function $\sin(n\pi x)$ . It suffices to observe that the range for which $\sin(n \pi x) > 0$ in the interval $[0, 1]$ is the union of intervals $$ \left[0, \frac 1n\right] \cup \left[\frac 2n, \frac 3n \right]\cdots \cup \begin{cases} \left[\frac {n-1}n, 1\right] & \text{if $n$ is odd} \left[\frac{n-2}n, \frac{n-1}n\right] & \text{if $n$ is even.} \end{cases} $$ Now, we find the number of zeroes of $f(x)$ in the interval $[0, 1]$ . Notice that at every zero, either $f(x)$ is tangent to the $x$ -axis, or $f(x)$ crosses the $x$ -axis. Since there are not many terms, we can simply list out the unique places where each term equals 0: \begin{tabular}{c|c} $\sin(\pi x)$ & None \hline $\sin(2\pi x)$ & $\frac 12$ \hline $\sin(3\pi x)$ & $\frac 13, \frac 23$ \hline $\sin(4\pi x)$ & $\frac 14$ , $\frac 34$ \hline $\sin(5\pi x)$ & $\frac 15, \frac 25, \frac 35, \frac 45$ \hline $\sin(6\pi x)$ & $\frac 16, \frac 56$ \hline $\sin(7\pi x)$ & $\frac 17, \frac 27, \frac 37, \frac 47, \frac 57, \frac 67$ \hline $\sin(8\pi x)$ & $\frac 18, \frac 38, \frac 58, \frac 78$ \end{tabular}**Remark.** A faster shortcut might just to be to compute $\phi(1)+\phi(2)+\cdots+\phi(7)$ , but listing out all the zeros gives us a standing point for the next step. This gives us 22 zeroes in total. Providing that we start with a positive value and alternate at every zero, there would be 11 disjoint positive intervals. However, this is not the case! At many points, like $\frac 14$ , two terms meet 0 and slope to negativity. However, two negatives make a positive, so at those points, the graph will be tangent to the $x$ -axis. Let us closely analyze each of these tangencies. We list out all the tangencies: [center] \begin{tabular}{c|c} Tangent Point & Terms that equal $0$ \hline $x=\frac 14$ & $4x$ and $8x$ terms \hline $x=\frac 13$ & $3x$ and $6x$ terms \hline $x=\frac 12$ & $2x, 4x, 6x, 8x$ terms \hline $x=\frac 23$ & $3x$ and $6x$ terms \hline $x = \frac 34$ & $4x$ and $8x$ terms \end{tabular} [/center] Finally, it suffices to find whether each tangency is a positive or negative tangency. [list=1] [*]Tangency at $\frac 14$ : This is a positive tangency, since right before this point, the function is positive. [*]Tangency at $\frac 13$ : This is a negative tangency, since right before this point, the function is negative. Similarly, [*]Tangency at $\frac 12$ : This is a positive tangency. [*]Tangency at $\frac 23$ : This is is a negative tangency. [*]Tangency at $\frac 34$ : This is a positive tangency. [/list] Observe that for every negative tangency, an interval that we predicted to be positive becomes negative, while the alternating nature of the function is retained. Therefore, it will give us one more negative interval and one less positive interval. Similarly, for every positive tangency, the tangency gives us one more positive interval and one less negative interval. We assumed there were $11$ positive intervals without tangencies, so in total there are $11+3-2 = \boxed{12} \implies \textbf{(B)}$ total positive intervals.

The number of such distinct fractions is given by  $ \minus{}1\plus{}\sum_{n \equal{} 1}^8 \varphi(n) \equal{} 21$ , and the answer has to be near half of that, so the answer must be  $ \mathbf{(B)}$ . The reason why its larger comes from the fractions  $ 1/4,3/4,1/2,1/3,2/3$ , where the  $ \sin$  product does not change sign, and counting, we see that the first three are surrounded by open positive intervals. <details><summary>Solution</summary>We're aiming to calculate on how many intervals the argument of  $ \log$  is positive, because when the argument's negative,  $ \log$  is undefined. The best way to do this is to calculate the number of sign changes as we move from 0 to 1. At any fraction  $ \frac{p}{q}$ , with  $ q\le 8$ , at least one multiplicative term  $ \sin(q\pi x)$  changes sign, as  $ \sin$  changes sign at integer multiples of  $ \pi$ . There is 1 fraction with  $ q\equal{}2$ , 2 with  $ q\equal{}3$ , etc., up through 7 with  $ q\equal{}8$ , for a total of 28 flips. However, we are counting  $ \frac12\equal{}\frac24\equal{}\frac36\equal{}\frac48$ ,  $ \frac23\equal{}\frac46$ ,  $ \frac13\equal{}\frac26$ ,  $ \frac14\equal{}\frac28$ , and  $ \frac34\equal{}\frac68$  multiple times, as we count the ones which are not in lowest terms. Four  $ \sin$  terms change sign at  $ \frac12$ , and two at each of the others. Any fraction where an even number of multiplicative terms change sign is irrelevant - then the overall product does not change sign, although it still splits whatever interval it is in into two open intervals. So there are  $ 28\minus{}12\equal{}16$  total sign changes. Since the product is positive on the interval starting at 0, there are  $ 16/2\equal{}8$  full flips from positive to negative to positive, or 9 regions where the product is positive, with possible holes. At this point we can look at the answers and see that 12 is the only one between 9 and 14, but we can also solve the problem rigorously. We now need to find which of the repeated fractions fall in regions where the product is positive, which can be done by evaluating the nonzero multiplicative terms at a point. Around  $ \frac12$ , the product is positive, as well as around  $ \frac13$  and  $ \frac23$ . This makes 3 new regions, for a total of  $ 12\Rightarrow\boxed{\textbf{(B)}}$ .</details>

<details><summary>Eliminate the impossible</summary>Quick thinking should reveal that  $ \log_{10} {z}$  is defined for  $ z > 0.$   So it is logical to find the zeros of  $ z \equal{} \sin(\pi x)\times \sin(2\pi x)\times \cdots \times\sin(8\pi x).$ If you were asked to multiply a polynomial with 3 zeros by a polynomial with 4 zeros, you would expect the result to be a polynomial with 7 zeros.  Similar reasoning applies here... $ \sin(\pi x)$  has no zeros on the open interval  $ (0,1).$  $ \sin(2\pi x)$  has one zero on the open interval  $ (0,1).$  $ \sin(3\pi x)$  has two zeros on the open interval  $ (0,1).$  $ \cdots$  $ \sin(8\pi x)$  has seven zeros on the open interval  $ (0,1).$ So the total number of zeros (including repeated zeros) is  $ 1 \plus{} 2 \plus{} 3 \plus{} \cdots \plus{} 7 \equal{} 28.$   The maximum number of subintervals occurs if each zero is distinct ( $ z$  crosses the  $ x \minus{}$ axis with each zero).  In this case, the maximum number of subintervals where  $ z > 0$  is 15.  We can rule out answers C, D, and E.

As explained in another post, the number of distinct zeros is 21.  (The sum of the totient functions from 2 through 8.)  So, we know there are a total of  $ 28 \minus{} 21 \equal{} 7$  repeated roots.

Without considering exactly where these repeated zeros lie, it is possible that each repeated root would be a double-root, with  $ z$  tangent to the  $ x \minus{}$ axis from below the  $ x \minus{}$ axis.  For counting the number of subintervals the problem requires, this is as if these roots didn't exist at all.  So  $ 21 \minus{} 7 \equal{} 14$  is the minimum number of axis-crossing zeros  $ z$  could possibly have.

But this would result in at least 7 subintervals for which  $ z > 0.$   So we can rule out answer A.</details>

solution_md:
The solution of the equation $ 7^{x\plus{}7}\equal{}8^x$ can be expressed in the form $ x\equal{}\log_b 7^7$ . What is $ b$ ? $ \textbf{(A)}\ \frac{7}{15} \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ \frac{7}{8} \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ \frac{8}{7} \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ \frac{15}{8} \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ \frac{15}{7}$
SolutionWe have $$ 7^x \cdot 7^7=8^x $$ $$ 7^7=\left (\frac{8}{7}\right )^x $$ $$ x=\log_{\frac{8}{7}} 7^7 $$ $$ b=\frac{8}{7} \implies \boxed{\textbf{(C) }\frac{8}{7}} $$

stem_md: A frog makes  $ 3$  jumps, each exactly  $ 1$  meter long. The directions of the jumps are chosen independently and at random. What is the probability the frog's final position is no more than  $ 1$  meter from its starting position? $ \textbf{(A)}\ \frac {1}{6} \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ \frac {1}{5} \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ \frac {1}{4} \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ \frac {1}{3} \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ \frac {1}{2}$
solution_md:
We will let the moves be complex numbers $ a$ , $ b$ , and $ c$ , each of magnitude one. The frog starts on the origin. It is relatively easy to show that exactly one element in the set \[ \{|a + b + c|, |a + b - c|, |a - b + c|, |a - b - c|\}\] has magnitude less than or equal to $ 1$ . Hence, the probability is $ \boxed{\frac {1}{4}}$ .
This is totally non-obvious to me, but here's a proof. [asy]size(6cm); draw(unitcircle); pair a = Drawing(dir(42)); pair b = Drawing(dir(133)); pair c = Drawing(dir(256)); pointpen=blue; draw(a--Drawing("\pm a", -a, -a), dashed); draw(b--Drawing("\pm b", -b, -b), dashed); draw(c--Drawing("\pm c", -c, -c), dashed); draw(a--b--c--cycle, red); draw((-a)--(-b)--(-c)--cycle, blue); [/asy] So consider three complex numbers $x$ , $y$ , $z$ on the unit circle. Recall that $x+y+z$ represents the orthocenter of said triangle. (If you don't know this you can prove it by using the fact that $HO = 3GO$ , where $O$ , $G$ , $H$ are the circumcenter, centroid, and orthocenter.) We claim $\left\lvert x+y+z \right\rvert \le 1$ if and only if $x$ , $y$ , $z$ are the vertices of an acute triangle. One direction is clear -- if $\triangle XYZ$ is acute then the orthocenter lies inside the triangle. Now suppose it's obtuse at $\angle X$ . If $D$ is the foot of $X$ on $\overline{YZ}$ , then it the orthocenter must lie on ray $DX$ . It doesn't lie in the triangle though, and hence must be outside. So consider $\pm a \pm b \pm c$ . Looking at the pretty picture I have above, it's not hard to see that there are only two ways to get an acute triangle, the red/blue triangles: that is, when you get the alternating vertices. This is because the diameters mark out $180^{\circ}$ arcs, so if you ever have three red points in a row you have an obtuse angle at the middle point. So you can group all triples of jumps $(a,b,c)$ in sets of eight like this, and exactly two will work. Hence the answer is $\frac 14$ .

This is a wrong argument even though it luckily leads to the right answer. You do not get a uniformly distributed point in the circle of radius 2 after two jumps of size 1. If there is an angle of $\theta$ between the two jumps, where doubling back is an angle of 0, the distance is $2 \sin \theta/2$ . The angle $\theta$ is uniformly distributed on $[0,\pi]$ so the probability is $\theta/\pi$ that the distance is under $2 \sin \theta/2$ . In general, $\theta/\pi \ne \sin^2 \theta/2$ , the probability of a distance under $2 \sin \theta/2$ for a point uniformly distributed in the disk of radius 2, although they are equal if $\theta = \pi/2$ . If $\theta = \pi/3,$ the probability the distance is under $1$ is $1/3$ , not $1/4$ . If $\theta = 2 \pi/3$ , the probability that the distance is under $\sqrt{3}$ is $2/3$ , not $3/4$ . If $\theta = \pi/100,$ the probability the distance is under $0.0314$ is $1/100$ , not $\sin^2 \pi/200 = 0.000247$ . This incorrect argument should not be in the wiki of solutions for this problem, which currently does not contain any complete and correct solution, though there are some correct arguments above.

<details><summary>Official Solution</summary>Let  $A$  denote the frog's starting point, and let  $P$ ,  $Q$ , and  $B$  denote its positions after the first, second, and third jumps, respectively.  Introduce a coordinate system with  $P$  at  $(0,0)$ ,  $Q$  at  $(1,0)$ ,  $A$  at  $(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)$ , and  $B$  at  $(1+\cos\beta,\sin\beta)$ .  It may be assumed that  $0\leq\alpha\leq\pi$  and  $0\leq\beta\leq 2\pi$ .  For  $\alpha = 0$ , the require condition is met for all values of  $\beta$ .  For  $\alpha = \pi$ , the required condition is met only if  $\beta=\pi$ .  For  $0 < \alpha<\pi$ ,  $AB = 1$  if and only if  $\beta = \alpha$  or  $\beta=\pi$ , and the required condition is met if and only if  $\alpha\leq\beta\leq\pi$ .  In the  $\alpha\beta$ -plane, the rectangle  $0\leq\alpha\leq\pi$ ,  $0\leq\beta\leq2\pi$  has area  $2\pi^2$ .  The triangle  $0\leq\alpha\leq\pi$ ,  $\alpha\leq\beta\leq\pi$  has area  $\tfrac{\pi^2}2$ , so the requested probability is  $\tfrac14$ .</details>

<details><summary>solution</summary>We may substitute  $ y \equal{} x \minus{} 2010$  for convenience. This will not change the lengths of the intervals, only the positions.
We now have  $ \frac {1}{y \plus{} 1} \plus{} \frac {1}{y} \plus{} \frac {1}{y \minus{} 1}\ge 1$ *
Combining denominators, we have  $ \frac {3y^2 \minus{} 1}{y^3 \minus{} y}\ge 1$ .
Note that if  $ y < \minus{} 1$ ,  $ \minus{} \frac {1}{\sqrt {3}} < y < 0$  or  $ \frac {1}{\sqrt {3}} < y < 1$ , then the left-hand side will be negative, so we will assume that  $ y$  does not lie in these intervals.
If  $ 0 < y < \frac {1}{\sqrt {3}}$ , then  $ y^3 \minus{} y$  is negative. The inequality is satisfied iff $ 3y^2 \minus{} 1\le y^3 \minus{} y \iff y^3 \minus{} 3y^2 \minus{} y \plus{} 1\ge 0$ .

If  $ y > 1$  or  $ \minus{} 1 < y < \minus{} \frac {1}{\sqrt {3}}$ , then we have that the inequality is satisfied iff $ 3y^2 \minus{} 1\ge y^3 \minus{} y \iff y^3 \minus{} 3y^2 \minus{} y \plus{} 1\le 0$ .

Let the roots of  $ f(y) \equal{} y^3 \minus{} 3y^2 \minus{} y \plus{} 1$  be  $ a, b,$  and  $ c$ , with  $ a > b > c$  It is easy to check that  $ a > 1$ ,  $ \frac {1}{\sqrt {3}} > b > 0$ , and  $ \minus{} \frac {1}{\sqrt {3}} > c > \minus{} 1$ . Also,  $ f(y)$  alternates signs at  $ a, b,$  and  $ c$ , so if  $ y < c$ ,  $ f(y) < 0$ , if  $ c < y < b$ ,  $ f(y) > 0$ , etc.
From the bounds above, we can check that:
The intersection of  $ 0 < y < \frac {1}{\sqrt {3}}$  and  $ f(y) > 0$  is  $ 0 < y < b$ .
The intersection of  $ y > 1$  and  $ f(y) < 0$  is  $ 1 < y < a$ .
The intersection of  $ \minus{} 1 < y < \minus{} \frac {1}{\sqrt {3}}$  and  $ f(y) < 0$  is  $ \minus{} 1 < y < c$ Each of these intervals work and are the only possible intervals, so the total length of these intervals is  $ (b \minus{} 0) \plus{} (a \minus{} 1) \plus{} (c \minus{} ( \minus{} 1)) \equal{} a \plus{} b \plus{} c$ . Monic quadratic polynomials  $ P(x)$  and  $ Q(x)$  have the property that  $ P(Q(x))$  has zeroes at  $ x\equal{}\minus{}23,\minus{}21,\minus{}17, \text{and} \minus{}15$ , and  $ Q(P(x))$  has zeroes at  $ x\equal{}\minus{}59, \minus{}57, \minus{}51, \text{and} \minus{}49$ . What is the sum of the minimum values of  $ P(x)$  and  $ Q(x)$ ?
 $ \textbf{(A)}\ \text{\minus{}100} \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ \text{\minus{}82} \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ \text{\minus{}73} \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ \text{\minus{}64} \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ 0$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Let  $ P(x) \equal{} (x \minus{} a)^2 \minus{} b, Q(x) \equal{} (x \minus{} c)^2 \minus{} d$ . Notice that  $ P(x)$  has roots  $ a\pm \sqrt {b}$ , so that the roots of  $ P(Q(x))$  are the roots of  $ Q(x) \equal{} a \plus{} \sqrt {b}, a \minus{} \sqrt {b}$ . For each individual equation, the sum of the roots will be  $ 2c$  (symmetry or Vieta's). Thus, we have  $ 4c \equal{} \minus{} 23 \minus{} 21 \minus{} 17 \minus{} 15$ , or  $ c \equal{} \minus{} 19$ . Doing something similar for  $ Q(P(x))$  gives us  $ a \equal{} \minus{} 54$ .
We now have  $ P(x) \equal{} (x \plus{} 35)^2 \minus{} b, Q(x) \equal{} (x \plus{} 19)^2 \minus{} d$ . Since  $ Q$  is monic, the roots of  $ Q(x) \equal{} a \plus{} \sqrt {b}$  are "farther" from the axis of symmetry than the roots of  $ Q(x) \equal{} a \minus{} \sqrt {b}$ . Thus, we have  $ Q( \minus{} 23) \equal{} \minus{} 54 \plus{} \sqrt {b}, Q( \minus{} 21) \equal{} \minus{} 54 \minus{} \sqrt {b}$ , or  $ 16 \minus{} d \equal{} \minus{} 54 \plus{} \sqrt {b}, 4 \minus{} d \equal{} \minus{} 54 \minus{} \sqrt {b}$ . Adding these gives us  $ 20 \minus{} 2d \equal{} \minus{} 108$ , or  $ d \equal{} 64$ . Plugging this into  $ 16 \minus{} d \equal{} \minus{} 54 \plus{} \sqrt {b}$ , we get  $ b \equal{} 36$ .
The minimum value of  $ P(x)$  is  $ \minus{} b$ , and the minimum value of  $ Q(x)$  is  $ \minus{} d$ . Thus, our answer is  $ \minus{} (b \plus{} d) \equal{} \minus{} 100$ , or answer  $ \boxed{\textbf{(A)}}$ .</details>

solution_md:
Solution OutlineHere is a really quick outline: BC=6, CD=14, AB=12, DA=7 use law of cosines with BD as your unknown side and you get D.

Click to expandLet $ AB \equal{} a,BC \equal{} b,CD \equal{} c,DA \equal{} d$ . We have $ ad \equal{} bc \equal{} P$ . Since $ ABCD$ is cyclic, $ \angle BAD \equal{} 180 \minus{} \angle BCD$ . Let $ \angle BAD \equal{} \theta$ . Then by the law of cosines, we have $ BD^2 \equal{} a^2 \plus{} d^2 \minus{} 2P \cos \theta \equal{} b^2 \plus{} c^2 \plus{} 2P\cos \theta$ . Adding the two and dividing by two, we have $ BD^2 \equal{} (a^2 \plus{} b^2 \plus{} c^2 \plus{} d^2)/2$ . Now it becomes a problem of maximizing this sum of squares. It's easy to show that we can maximize this with $ a \equal{} 14,b \equal{} 6,c \equal{} 7,d \equal{} 12$ . This gives us $ BD^2 \equal{} \frac {425}{2}$ , so our answer is $ \textbf{(D)}$ . Alternatively, you can overkill this with the 4 number theorem. Let $ a \equal{} wx, d \equal{} yz, b \equal{} wy, c \equal{} xz$ . Then $ a^2 \plus{} b^2 \plus{} c^2 \plus{} d^2 \equal{} (w^2 \plus{} z^2)(x^2 \plus{} y^2)$ . We've shown that $ a^2 \plus{} b^2 \plus{} c^2 \plus{} d^2$ is possible, so we only need to show that $ a^2 \plus{} b^2 \plus{} c^2 \plus{} d^2 \equal{} 533$ is impossible. But $ 533 \equal{} 13\cdot41$ , so we must have $ (3^2 \plus{} 2^2)(5^2 \plus{} 4^2)$ . This will give the numbers $ a,b,c,d$ equal to $ 15,12,10,8$ in some order, which isn't allowed. Thus, our answer must be D.

For how many ordered triples  $ (x,y,z)$  of nonnegative integers less than  $ 20$  are there exactly two distinct elements in the set  $ \{i^x,(1 \plus{} i)^y,z\}$ , where  $ i \equal{} \sqrt { \minus{} 1}$ ?
 $ \textbf{(A)}\ 149 \qquad
\textbf{(B)}\ 205 \qquad
\textbf{(C)}\ 215 \qquad
\textbf{(D)}\ 225 \qquad
\textbf{(E)}\ 235$
solution_md:
<details><summary>casework bash!</summary>Case 1:  $ i^x \equal{} (1 \plus{} i)^y$ .
Note that the magnitude of  $ 1 \plus{} i$  is  $ \sqrt {2}$ , so if  $ y > 0$ , then the magnitude of  $ (1 \plus{} i)^y$  will be greater than that of  $ i^x$ , so we must have  $ y \equal{} 0$ , and  $ (1 \plus{} i)^y \equal{} i^x \equal{} 1$ . Then, we must have  $ x \equal{} 0, 4, 8, 12,$  or  $ 16$ , and finally,  $ z$  can be any of the 19 integers besides  $ 1$ . Total:  $ 5\cdot 19 \equal{} 95$ .

Case 2:  $ i^x \equal{} z$  $ i^x$  can only equal  $ 1, \minus{} 1, i,$  or  $ \minus{} i$ . The only non-negative integer here is  $ 1$ , so we must have  $ z \equal{} 1$  and  $ x \equal{} 0, 4, 8, 12,$  or  $ 16$ . By the same reasoning as in case 1,  $ (1 \plus{} i)^y$  will not equal  $ 1$  iff  $ y > 0$ , so  $ y$  can equal any of the 19 integers besides  $ 0$ . Total:  $ 5\cdot 19 \equal{} 95$ .

Case 3:  $ (1 \plus{} i)^y \equal{} z$ .
Note that the magnitude of  $ (1 \plus{} i)^y$  needs to be an integer, so  $ y$  must be even (because the magnitude of  $ 1 \plus{} i$  is  $ \sqrt {2}$ ). If we let  $ y \equal{} 2a$ , then we have  $ (1 \plus{} i)^{2a} \equal{} z \iff ((1 \plus{} i)^2)^a \equal{} z \iff (2i)^a \equal{} z \iff 2^a\cdot i^a \equal{} z$ . 
Therefore,  $ a$  needs to be a multiple of 4, because otherwise,  $ z$  would equal a positive integer multiplied by either  $ i, \minus{} i,$  or  $ \minus{} 1$ , none of which are a non-negative integer. Setting  $ a \equal{} 4b$  gives  $ 2^{4b} \equal{} z\iff 16^b \equal{} z$ . Therefore,  $ b$  can only equal 0 or 1 (otherwise,  $ z$  would be greater than  $ 20$ ).
Case 3a:  $ b \equal{} 0$ We have  $ y \equal{} 8b \equal{} 0$ , and  $ z \equal{} 1$ . Now,  $ x$  can be any integer except for  $ 0, 4, 8, 12,$  or  $ 16$ , so there are a total of  $ 20 \minus{} 5 \equal{} 15$  triples in this case.
Case 3b:  $ b \equal{} 1$ We have  $ y \equal{} 8$  and  $ z \equal{} 16$ . In this case, any value of  $ x$  works, so there are  $ 20$  triples here.

Total for case 3:  $ 15 \plus{} 20 \equal{} 35$ .

Final answer:  $ 95 \plus{} 95 \plus{} 35 \equal{} 225$ .  $ \boxed{\textbf{(D)}}$ .</details>
