stem_md:
There are 999 scientists. Every 2 scientists are both interested in exactly 1 topic and for each topic there are exactly 3 scientists that are interested in that topic. Prove that it is possible to choose 250 topics such that every scientist is interested in at most 1 theme.

*A. Magazinov*
solution_md:
Here's a solution, since I don't see one above. I'll rephrase it into graph theory, so I can explain easier:
Decompose a  $K_{999}$  into edge disjoint triangles. Prove that we can find  $250$  vertex disjoint triangles.

We use extremal principle, i.e. take a configuration with maximal triangles who are vertex disjoint (I'll use a * every time I reference maximal triangles). Let us have  $t$  triangles, where  $t = 249$ . Let the sets of vertices of our triangles be  $T_i = \{a_i, b_i, c_i\}$  for  $1 \le i \le t$ . Let  $X$  be the union of the  $T_i$ , and let  $Y$  be the other  $999-3t$  vertices not part of a  $T_i$ . Note that we cannot have any triangles with vertices solely in  $Y$  (*). Consequently, for every edge between 2 vertices in  $Y$ , the third vertex completing the triangle must lie in  $X$ . Now for each point in  $X$  we look at how it forms triangles with 2 other vertices in  $Y$ .

Now look at the set  $T_i$ . Assume that  $a_i, b_i$  form triangles with the edges  $ef, gh$  (all in  $Y$ ) Then we can form more triangles, by deleting  $T_i$  and forming the triangles  $\{a_i, e, f\}$  and  $\{b_i, g, h\}$  contradiction, by maximality (*). We'll call this result  (**). We now show that form each  $T_i$ , the total number of edges in  $Y$  that vertices in  $T_i$  can form is  $|Y|/2$ . Assume WLOG firstly that both  $a_i$ ,  $b_i$  make triangles, otherwise its trivial. Note that  $a_i$  can form at most  $|Y|/2$  triangles with an edge in  $Y$ , and that those are edge disjoint, and therefore share no vertices in  $Y$ . Assume that for  $a_i$ , it forms triangles with the edges  $ef, gh, ij$ . Then all triangles formed by  $b_i$  must touch both of these edges (**), impossible. Now say  $a_i$  makes triangles with only 2 of these edges, but all triangles formed by  $b_i$  must touch both of these edges, so that's only 4 more triangles. Same for  $c_i$ . So in total, we can get at most  $2 + 4 = 6$  triangles. Similarly, we can now assume that for all vertices  $a_i. b_i, c_i$  they form only one triangle, so at most 3. So we can now assume that only  $a_i$  forms triangles, giving at most  $|Y|/2$ . To finish, we just count edges. We must use up all the edges, so looking at all  $t$  groups,  $t(|Y|/2) > \binom{|Y|}{2} \implies 249 = t >  |Y|-1 = 251$ , contradiction. So we still have edges left, so we can add more triangles.

Number the vertices.  Say we have picked (1,2,3),... (3k-2,3k-1,3k) where k<250.  We got 999-3k vertices remaining.  Call the set S={1,...3k}.  Let C be the number of remaining triangles with exactly one vertex in S, assuming for contradiction none of the remaining triangles are completely outside of S.  We have C=(999-3k)(998-3k)/2 by double counting the edges outside of S.  Let's look at the triangles in C, and our given k triangles.

If we have two triangles that C counts who are vertex disjoint but each share a vertex with one of the initial k triangles, we can scrap that initial triangle and replace it by two triangles C counts, which contradicts the maximality of k.

Note that (999-3k)(998-3k)/2 triangles of C each share a vertex with one of the k initial triangles, so at least (999-3k)(998-3k)/2k triangles of C share a vertex with a particular one of the initial k triangles, call it XYZ.  The other two vertices of such triangles are going to come from a set of size 999-3k which is a set less than twice as large (using k<250 here).

The wonderful thing is that if one triangle shares vertex X with C and one shares vertex Y, and their other vertices are disjoint, we are immediately done because we contradict maximality.

Let's look at the 999-3k vertices and construct some graphs.  Construct the "X-graph" which is look at the triangles in C hooked to X and draw their edges in C.  Construct the Y and Z graphs similarly.  Color X graph red, Y green, and Z blue.  In total the number of edges in this graph is going to be more than half the number of vertices.  Also, if we have two disjoint edges differently colored, we're done by what I said before.  Furthermore, you can't have degree >1 in each of the X,Y,Z graphs for pretty obvious reasons (triangles are supposed to have disjoint edges). But because the total degree in this graph exceeds the vertex number, some vertex must have degree at least 2.  Name one of the remaining 999-3k vertices U, and UV is red WLOG though UW is green.  Every blue edge must attach to one of U,V, and to one of U,W.  Every red edge must attach to one of U,W and every green edge to one of U,V.  So every remaining edge must attach to one of U,V,W.  But then there are at least (999-3k)/2 edges, so there are at the very least 100 edges in the graph.  So the sum of the degrees of U,V,W in the graph is clearly at least 100 so one vertex has degree at least 34 in the graph, and thus has 12 incident edges of some color, contradiction.

So we get a contradiction from k<250, and the maximal size of a bunch of independent triangles is at least 250.  We're done.

stem_md:
Ten cars are moving at the road. There are some cities at the road. Each car is moving with some constant speed through cities and with some different constant speed outside the cities (different cars may move with different speed). There are 2011 points at the road. Cars don't overtake at the points. Prove that there are 2 points such that cars pass through these points in the same order.

*S. Berlov*
solution_md:
Rephrase the problem as follows:
The number line is colored red and blue. Points $A_1,\ldots,A_{10}$ are picked on the positive number line and $10$ cars $\mathcal{C}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{10}$ start at their corresponding point. Choose $a_1,b_1,\ldots,a_{10},b_{10}>0$ , and suppose that $\mathcal{C}_i$ travels with speed $a_i$ on red and $b_i$ on blue for $i=1,\ldots,10$ . Prove that there are less than $2011$ possible orders in which the cars can pass through any set of points, given that no two cars pass through any point at the same time.
Let $t_i$ be the time it takes for $\mathcal{C}_i$ to travel to $0$ , assuming that it travels forward and backward at the same speed. Notice that if there are $x$ units of red and $y$ units of blue between $0$ and a point on the positive number line, then it takes $\tfrac{x}{a_i}+\tfrac{y}{b_i}-t_i$ units of time for $\mathcal{C}_i$ to travel to the point. Notice that for any pair of cars $\mathcal{C}_i$ and $\mathcal{C}_j$ , there exists a line (possibly at infinity) such that $C_i$ passes through a point before $C_j$ if and only if the corresponding $(x,y)$ for that point is on one side of the line. Draw all $\tbinom{10}{2}=45$ lines corresponding to each pair of cars, and notice that these lines divide the plane into at most $\tbinom{46}{2}+1=1036$ regions. Each of these regions corresponds to a single total ordering of the cars, so there are at most $1036<2011$ total orderings of the cars, as desired. $\square$

stem_md:
The graph  $G$  is not  $3$ -coloured. Prove that  $G$  can be divided into two graphs  $M$  and  $N$  such that  $M$  is not  $2$ -coloured and  $N$  is not  $1$ -coloured.

*V. Dolnikov*
solution_md:
We use the correct formulation with the  $K_4$ . We are essentially asked to prove that if a graph  $G$  is not  $3$ -colorable, we can pick some two adjacent vertices, delete them, and get a graph that is not  $2$ -colorable (i.e. not bipartite). Suppose that this was not possible.

Pick the smallest odd cycle in  $G$ , call it  $C$ , and suppose it is on the vertices  $v_1,\ldots,v_n$  in that order. If there exists some edge disjoint from  $C$ , then we can delete it and the resulting graph is not  $2$ -colorable: contradiction. Now suppose that  $C$  is not a triangle. If no vertex not in  $C$  has degree more than  $2$  (equivalently, is adjacent to more than  $3$  vertices in  $C$ ), then we can simply  $3$ -color  $C$ , and then we have enough colors to color the remaining vertices. Thus pick some vertex  $w \not \in C$  with three edges  $\overline{wv_i},\overline{wv_j},\overline{wv_k}$ , with  $i<j<k$ . Divide the cycle into "arcs" from  $v_i$  to  $v_j$ ,  $v_j$  to  $v_k$ , and  $v_k$  to  $v_i$ . Clearly at least one of these must be odd, WLOG the one from  $v_i$  to  $v_j$ . Then the odd cycle formed from adding  $w$  to this arc should be shorter than  $C$ , unless this arc has "length"  $n-2$  (i.e. contains  $n-1$  vertices), but this means that  $v_jv_kw$  is a triangle and hence a smaller odd cycle: contradiction.

Therefore, the minimal odd cycle is a triangle. Since  $G$  is  $K_4$ -free, no vertex is adjacent to  $v_1$ ,  $v_2$ , and  $v_3$ , hence this graph is clearly  $3$ -colorable.  $\blacksquare$

Let  $P(a)$  be the largest prime positive divisor of  $a^2 + 1$ . Prove that exist infinitely many positive integers  $a, b, c$  such that  $P(a)=P(b)=P(c)$ .

*A. Golovanov*
solution_md: We can pick  $P((x+1)^2+1)>P(x^2+1)$  since otherwise we would have  $P((x+1)^2+1)\leq P(x^2+1)$  for sufficiently large  $x$  but for a large prime  $q\equiv 1(mod \ 4)$  we can find  $q|x^2+1$ . Let  $p$  be the largest prime divisor of  $(x+1)^2+1$ . Pick the numbers as  $\{(x+1)^2+1,(p-x-1)^2+1,(x^2+x+1)^2+1\}$ . We see that  $(x^2+x+1)^2+1=(x^2+1)((x+1)^2+1)$  and  $p^2>(x+1)^2+1,(p-x-1)^2+1$  as desired. $\blacksquare$

stem_md:
A  $2010\times 2010$  board is divided into corner-shaped figures of three cells. Prove that it is possible to mark one cell in each figure such that each row and each column will have the same number of marked cells.

*I. Bogdanov & O. Podlipsky*
solution_md:
For some marking of the trominos let  $r_i$  and  $c_j$  denote the number of marked cells in the  $i^{\text{th}}$  row and  $j^{\text{th}}$  column respectively. Then let  $R_i = \textstyle\sum_{k=1}^i r_k$  and  $C_j = \textstyle\sum_{k=1}^j c_j$ . First mark the corner cell of each tromino on the board. 

Now suppose for some  $i$  we have  $R_i > 670\cdot i$  then there must be at least  $3R_i - 2010i$  trominos with a marked cell in row  $i$  and a free cell in row  $i+1$ . Otherwise, the first  $i$  rows would contain less than  $\frac{2010i - 2(3R_i-2010i)}{3} + (3R_i-2010i) = R_i$  marked cells, which is absurd because that is the definition of  $R_i$ . By a similar argument, if  $R_i < 670\cdot i$  then there are at least  $2010i-3R_i$  trominos with a marked cell in row  $i+1$  and a free cell in row  $i$ . 

For each row  $i$  with  $R_i>670i$  we want to take  $R_i-670i$  of the  $\ge 3(R_i - 670i)$  *potential* trominos with marked cells in row  $i$  and shift them to neighbouring cells row  $i+1$ . And for rows with  $R_i < 670$  we take  $670i-R_i$  cells from row  $i+1$  and shift them to row  $i$ . If we do the same with columns then all rows and columns will end up with the same number of marked cells. It is left to show that we can select the correct number of cells for both rows and columns without choosing a tetromino for both a row and column (i.e. needing to shift the marked cell in two directions). 

So define a bipartite graph  $G$  with  $V=A\cup B$ . Vertices in  $A$  represent all the *potential* tominos whose marked cells could be shifted to equalise the  $R_i$ s and  $C_j$ s. Vertices in  $B$  represent the 4020 rows and columns. Then a vertex in  $A$  is connected to its row or column in which it is to be shifted. All we must show is that there exists a subgraph  $H$  such that no two vertices in  $B$  share a common neighbour and for all  $v\in B, \,\,\, d_H(v)\ge \textstyle\frac{1}{3}d_G(v)$ . But this is simple, because vertices in  $A$  have  $d(v)\le 2$  so let all vertices of degree  $1$  go to their neighbours in  $B$ , and the remaining graph decomposes into even cycles or paths (where each vertex in  $B$  is the end of at most one path). discarding every other edge of each cycle or path we end up with subgraph such that each vertex  $v\in B$  is connected to at least  $\textstyle\frac{1}{2}d_G(v)$  vertices, which is more than we needed. This completes the proof  $\square$

We will prove by induction that:**Claim:** For $k < 670$ , if we have marked one cell in each of $2010k$ trominoes such that every row and every column has exactly $k$ marks, then we can add another set of $2010$ marks to unmarked trominoes so that every row and every column has exactly $k+1$ marks. We consider this as a problem of matching rows to columns and appeal to Hall's marriage lemma. Each row $R$ is to be consider to be compatible with those columns $C$ for which $R \cap C$ is part of an unmarked tromino. We contend that Hall's condition holds. *Proof.* [Proof that Hall's condition holds, implying claim] Select any subset of $n$ rows. There are at most $k \cdot n$ trominoes with some cell in a selected row; this means that the total area of unmarked cells among these $n$ rows is at least $2010n - 3kn = n \cdot (2010-3k) \ge 3n$ . So, since there are at least $3n$ cells unmarked among the selected rows it follows there are at least $n$ unmarked trominoes having at least one cell in the selected rows. End proof. $\blacksquare$

Let  $N$  be the midpoint of arc  $ABC$  of the circumcircle of triangle  $ABC$ , let  $M$  be the midpoint of  $AC$  and let  $I_1, I_2$  be the incentres of triangles  $ABM$  and  $CBM$ . Prove that points  $I_1, I_2, B, N$  lie on a circle.

*M. Kungojin*
solution_md:
Consider an inversion with pole  $B$  and arbitrary power. Let  $X'$  be the image of  $X$  under the inversion. The image of  $AC$  is circle  $\odot BA'C'$ , and the image of  $\odot ABC$  is line  $A'C'$ . The image of  $N$  is the foot of the external bisector of  $\angle A'BC'$ , and the image of line  $MN$  is the  $B$ -Apollonius circle of  $\triangle BA'C'$ , thus the image of  $M$  is the intersection of the  $B$ -Apollonius circle with  $\odot BA'C'$ . 

Let  $(I_1)$  be tangent to  $BM$ ,  $MA$ ,  $AB$ , at  $D$ ,  $E$ ,  $F$  respectively. Then  $\angle BDI_1=\angle BFI_1=90$ , so  $\angle BI_1'D'=\angle BI_1'F'=90$ , and  $BD=BF$ , hence  $I_1'$  is the intersection of the internal bisector of  $\angle ABM$  and  $D'F'$ .  $(I_1)'$  is tangent to  $\odot BA'M'$  at  $E'$ . Let  $E'D'$  and  $E'F'$  intersect  $\odot BA'M'$  again at  $Y'$ ,  $Z'$  respectively. The dilation with center  $E'$  taking  $(I_1)'$  to  $\odot BA'M'$  takes  $D'$ ,  $F'$  to  $Y'$ ,  $Z'$  respectively, hence the tangents to  $\odot BA'M'$  at  $Y'$ ,  $Z'$  are parallel to  $BA'$ ,  $BM'$  respectively, so  $Y'$ ,  $Z'$  are the midpoints of arcs  $BM'A'$  and  $BA'M'$  respectively. It follows that  $Y'M'$  and  $Z'A'$  meet at the  $B$ -excenter  $I_3'$  of  $\triangle ABM$ , which lies on the internal bisector of  $\angle A'BM'$ .  Pascal's theorem on  $Z'A'BM'Y'E'$  then gives that  $D'$ ,  $F'$ , and  $I_3'$  are collinear, so  $I_1'=I_3'$ . Similarly  $I_2'$  is the  $B$ -excenter of  $\triangle C'BM'$ .

We need to show  $N'$ ,  $I_1'$ ,  $I_2'$  are collinear. Since  $M'$  lies on the  $B$ -Apollonius circle of  $\triangle BA'C'$ ,  $\frac{M'A'}{M'C'}=\frac{BA'}{BC'} \Longleftrightarrow \frac{A'M'}{A'B}=\frac{M'C'}{C'B}$ . Let  $A'I_1' \cap BM' = P'$ ,  $C'I_2' \cap BM'=Q'$ . Then  $P'$ ,  $Q'$  are the feet of the external bisectors of  $\angle BA'M'$ ,  $\angle BC'M'$ , so  $\frac{M'P'}{P'B}=\frac{A'M'}{A'B}=\frac{M'C'}{C'B}=\frac{M'Q'}{Q'B} \Longrightarrow P'=Q'$ .  $M'I_1'$  and  $M'I_2'$  are internal bisectors of  $\angle A'M'P'$  and  $\angle C'M'P'$  hence   $\frac{A'I_1'}{I_1'P'}=\frac{A'M'}{M'P'}$  and  $\frac{P'I_2'}{I_2'C'}=\frac{P'M'}{M'C'}$ .  We have  $\frac{A'I_1'}{I_1'P'} \cdot \frac{P'I_2'}{I_2'C'} \cdot \frac{C'N'}{N'A'} = \frac{A'M'}{M'P'} \cdot \frac{P'M'}{M'C'} \cdot \frac{BC'}{BA'} =\frac{M'A'}{M'C'} \cdot \frac{BC'}{BA'} =1$ , and since  $I_1'$ ,  $I_2'$  are interior on segments  $A'P'$  and  $C'P'$ , and  $N'$  is on line  $A'C'$  but not segment  $A'C'$ , this implies  $N'$ ,  $I_1'$ ,  $I_2'$  are collinear by Menelaus' theorem so we are done.

solution_md: Official solution.**Lemma**. For every square  $X$  there exists a set of squares  $S$  that contains  $X$ , consists of even number of squares and such that any each square from the entire board has even number of neighbors that are in  $S$ . $\blacktriangledown$  Let's color the board black and white as the chess board. Without loss of generality, we can assume that  $X$  is black. Consider one of the diagonals passing through  $X$ . Let  $A$  and  $B$  be the terminal squares of that diagonal. FTSOC, assume there's only 1 nice cell. Consider a checkerboard coloring with the main diagonal being black, and only consider the black squares. WLOG, let the nice cell be white. Put  $1$ s in squares with checkers,  $0$ s without. Define a black square as "same" if the reflection of it across the main diagonal has the same parity, and "diff" otherwise. Clearly all cells on the main diagonal are same. Furthermore, if there existed a white cell with an odd number of diff neighbors, then either that white cell or its reflection is nice.

Define the ith minor diagonal as the diagonal with slope  $-1$  going through the ith square (call this square ith main) on the main diagonal from the top. Let the first diff cell  $D$  appear on the ith minor diagonal, and wlog let it be under the main diagonal, which means no diff cells appear in the jth minor diagonal for  $j < i$ , and every cell between  $D$  and ith main are same. Let there be  $j$  squares between  $D$  and ith main. Clearly, the white square above  $D$  has odd number of diff neighbors, so either it or its reflection is nice. Thus, every other white square must have an even amount of diff neighbors.

Now, define the ith major diagonal as the diagonal with slope  $1$  that has  $i-1$  cells between it and the major diagonal. Then, the 1st, 2nd,  $\ldots$  jth major diagonals must only contain same cells (we can just induct down). Next, the  $j+1$ th main diagonal must only contain diff cells (we can again induct down). Consider the cell on the  $j+1$  main diagonal and on the bottom most row. This cell is diff. Now, the white cell to the left of it will only have  $1$  diff neighbor, since the other two cells adjacent to it are on the  $j$ th main diagonal. We have two nice cells, a contradiction.

We conclude that there can't be exactly one nice cell.

solution_md:
For positive integers $a>b>1$ , define \[x_n = \frac {a^n-1}{b^n-1}\] Find the least $d$ such that for any $a,b$ , the sequence $x_n$ does not contain $d$ consecutive prime numbers. *V. Senderov*
Cute :P We claim that the least $d$ is $3$ . To prove that it is necessary, consider $(a,b) = (4,2)$ , which gives $x_n = 2^n + 1$ , and notice that $x_1 = 2^1 + 1 = 3, x_2 = 2^2 + 1 = 5$ are both primes. It suffices to prove that it is impossible to have $x_n, x_{n + 1}, x_{n + 2}$ all being primes. **Claim 01.** The sequence is increasing. *Proof.* It suffices to prove that $x_n < x_{n + 1}$ , which is easy by bashing. --------**Claim 02.** If $x_n, x_{n + 1} \in \mathbb{N}$ , then $b - 1 \mid a - 1$ . *Proof.* We have $b^n - 1 \mid a^n - 1$ and $b^{n + 1} - 1 \mid a^{n + 1} - 1$ . Take $p \mid b - 1$ , we then have \[ p \mid b - 1 \mid b^n - 1 \mid a^n - 1 \ \text{and} \ p \mid b - 1 \mid b^{n + 1} - 1 \mid a^{n + 1} - 1 \Rightarrow p \mid a^{\gcd(n,n+1)} - 1 = a - 1 \] Furthermore, by LTE, we have $\nu_p(b - 1) + \nu_p(n) = \nu_p(b^n - 1) \le \nu_p(a^n - 1) = \nu_p(a - 1) + \nu_p(n)$ for all $p \mid b - 1$ , we hence get $\nu_p(b - 1) \le \nu_p(a - 1)$ for all such primes $p$ , forcing $b - 1 \mid a - 1$ . ---------- Now, let $k = \frac{a - 1}{b - 1}$ be a fixed constant. For convenience, define $a_n = a^{n - 1} + a^{n - 2} + \dots + 1$ for all $n \ge 2$ and define $b_n$ similarly. Now, notice that $a_n > b_n$ for all $n \ge 2$ . Suppose for the sake of contradiction, that there exists $x_n, x_{n + 1}, x_{n + 2}$ are all primes. Notice that \[ \frac{a_{n + 1}}{b_{n + 1}} = \frac{x_{n + 1}}{k} \ \text{and} \ \frac{a_{n + 2}}{b_{n + 2}} = \frac{x_{n + 2}}{k} \] Since $a_{n + 1} > b_{n + 1}$ and $a_{n + 2} > b_{n + 2}$ , then $\gcd(x_{n + 1}, k) = \gcd(x_{n + 2}, k) = 1$ , and hence $k \mid b_{n + 1} \mid b^{n + 1} - 1$ and $k \mid b_{n + 2} - b_{n + 1} = b^{n + 1}$ . This is enough to force $k = 1$ , which gives us $\boxed{a = b}$ , a contradiction.

stem_md:
There are more than  $n^2$  stones on the table. Peter and Vasya play a game, Peter starts. Each turn, a player can take any prime number less than  $n$  stones, or any multiple of  $n$  stones, or  $1$  stone. Prove that Peter always can take the last stone (regardless of Vasya's strategy).

*S Berlov*
solution_md:
Call a number of stones *winning* if Peter can win if he starts with that many stones and *losing* otherwise. Let  $S$  be the set containing of all primes less than  $n$  as well as  $1$ .

We claim that for all remainders  $r$  modulo  $n$  there exists some  $\ell \equiv r \pmod{n}$  such that  $\ell$  is losing and that  $\ell < n^2$ . Assume for the sake of contradiction that this is not true. Clearly  $\ell \ne 0$ .

Now for all  $k=an+r$  for  $0 \leq a < n$  to be winning, there must be some  $s \in S$  such that  $k - s$  is losing for each  $k$  since Peter must take some stones and then Vasya, who must now be on a losing number, will move (and taking a multiple of  $n$  will, by the assumption, not get to a losing number). Now since all such  $k$  differ by  $n$  and  $s < n$  for all  $s \in S$ , we have that all such losing numbers we need are distinct. But there are only at most  $n-1$  other remainders modulo  $n$  and  $n$  losing numbers, thus there must be two losing numbers  $\ell_1, \ell_2$  congruent modulo  $n$ . But this is absurd, since from the larger one we can take a multiple of  $n$  rocks to get to the other, hence the larger one cannot possibly be losing, so we are done.  $\square$ Now if there are  $N$  stones on the table at the beginning, Peter can simply take a multiple of  $n$  stones such that there are  $\ell \equiv N \pmod{n}$  stones left and  $\ell$  is losing. Thus Vasya is at a losing position, and Peter is guaranteed to win.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: A quadratic trinomial  $P(x)$  with the  $x^2$  coefficient of one is such, that  $P(x)$  and  $P(P(P(x)))$  share a root. Prove that  $P(0)*P(1)=0$ .
solution_md:
Let  $r_1$  and  $r_2$  be the roots of  $P(x)$  and WLOG,  $r_1$  is the root it shares with  $P(P(P(x)))$ . Then, 
\[ 0 = P(r_1) = P(P(P(r_1))) = P(P(0)), \]
so  $P(0)\in \{r_1, r_2\}$ . If  $P(0) = r_1$ , then  $P(P(P(0))) = P(P(P(r_1)))$ , so  $P(0)=0$ . If  $P(0) = r_2$ , then from Vieta,  $r_1\cdot r_2 = r_2$ , so  $r_2\cdot(r_1-1) = 0$  which implies either  $P(0)=0$  or  $P(1)=0$ . In either case, we have  $P(0)\cdot P(1) = 0$ .  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Given is an acute angled triangle  $ABC$ . A circle going through  $B$  and the triangle's circumcenter,  $O$ , intersects  $BC$  and  $BA$  at points  $P$  and  $Q$  respectively. Prove that the intersection of the heights of the triangle  $POQ$  lies on line  $AC$ .
solution_md:
Here's a strange solution.

Let  $H$  be the orthocenter of  $\triangle ABC$ , and denote by  $H'$  and  $A'$  the reflections of  $H$  and  $A$  respectively about the midpoint of  $BC$ .  Note that  $\angle OPQ = \angle OAB = \angle HBC$ , and similarly  $\angle OQP=\angle HCB$ , so  $\triangle OQP\sim\triangle HBC$ .

Let  $B'$  be the reflection of  $B$  over  $P$  and let  $C'$  be the reflection of  $C$  over  $Q$ .  Note that  $O$  is the midpoint of  $AH'$ , so by standard spiral similarity arguments (e.g. MGT) we know that  $\triangle B'AC'\sim\triangle POQ\sim\triangle BH'C$ .  Furthermore, remark that \[\angle AB'C' = \angle HCB = \angle BAH\quad\implies\quad B'C'\perp BC.\] This means that the orthocenter  $H''$  of  $\triangle AB'C'$  satisfies  $d(H'',BC) = d(A,BC) = d(A',BC)$ , where  $d(P,\ell)$  denotes the distance from  $P$  to  $\ell$ .

Finally, note that the orthocenter of  $\triangle POQ$  must be the midpoint of  $A'H''$  - by the above argument, this must lie on  $BC$ .   $\blacksquare$

stem_md: A convex 2011-gon is drawn on the board. Peter keeps drawing its diagonals in such a way, that each newly drawn diagonal intersected no more than one of the already drawn diagonals. What is the greatest number of diagonals that Peter can draw?
solution_md: I claim that the greatest number of diagonals that Peter can draw is $\boxed{4016}.$ For the construction, let us number the vertices $A_1, \ldots, A_{2011}$ in that order. Then, Peter can first draw the diagonals $\overline{A_1A_3}, \overline{A_2A_4}, \ldots, \overline{A_{2009}A_{2011}}, \overline{A_{2010}A_1}.$ Afterwards, he can draw the diagonals $\overline{A_1A_4}, \overline{A_1A_5}, \ldots, \overline{A_1A_{2009}}.$ Then, he will have drawn a total of $$ 2010 + 2006 = 4016 $$ diagonals, as claimed. It remains to prove that the bound holds. I prove the following lemma: **Claim:** The greatest number of diagonals that Peter can draw in a convex $n$ -gon for any $n \ge 3$ is $2n-6.$ *Proof.* I proceed by strong induction. Since a triangle has no diagonals and $$ 2 \cdot 3 - 6 = 0, $$ the base case holds. Now, suppose that the desired result holds for all $n=3$ through $n=k$ for some positive integer $k \ge 3.$ Then, let us consider the last diagonal drawn when Peter performs his drawing process on a $(k+1)$ -gon. Clearly, it splits the $(k+1)$ -gon into an $m_1$ -gon and an $m_2$ -gon, where $$ m_1+m_2=(k+1)+2=k+3. $$ (We add $2$ because each of the polygons contains the endpoints of the last diagonal in their set of vertices.) Then, by the inductive hypothesis, the maximum number of diagonals strictly within the $m_1$ -gon that Peter could have drawn is $2m_1-6,$ and the maximum number of diagonals strictly within the $m_2$ -gon that Peter could have drawn is $2m_2-6.$ Also, since every newly drawn diagonal can intersect no more than one already-drawn diagonal, we know that there are $2$ extra diagonals that Peter can draw in the whole $(k+1)$ -gon: the final diagonal and a diagonal intersecting it, connecting the $m_1$ -gon and the $m_2$ -gon. Hence, the maximum number of diagonals that Peter can draw is: \begin{align*} (2m_1-6)+(2m_2-6)+2 &= 2(m_1+m_2)-10 &= 2(k+3)-10 &= 2k-4 &= 2(k+1)-6, \end{align*} concluding the inductive step. Hence, by the Principle of Mathematical Induction, I have proven the claimed result. $\blacksquare$ Taking $n=2011,$ we get the desired bound, so we are done. $\square$

stem_md: Do there exist any three relatively prime natural numbers so that the square of each of them is divisible by the sum of the two remaining numbers?
solution_md:
Let the numbers be  $a,b,c$ . We claim that it is impossible to have   $$ a+b|c^2 $$    $$ b+c|a^2 $$    $$ c+a|b^2 $$  simlutaneously.
Note that  $(a+b,b+c)=(a+c,c+b)=(a+b,a+c)=1$  since they are factors of three relatively prime integers  $a^2,b^2$  and  $c^2$ .
Meanwhile, we have  $a+b|(a+b+c)^2$ , hence  $$ (a+b)(b+c)(c+a)|(a+b+c)^2 $$  Let  $x=a+b,y=b+c,z=c+a$ , WLOG assume  $x\leq y\leq z$ , from triangular inequality we have  $x+y\geq z+1$ , meanwhile from the divisibility we have   $$ 4xyz\leq (x+y+z)^2 $$  Hence   $$ 4xy^2\leq 4xyz\leq (x+y+z)^2\leq (2(x+y)-1)^2< (4y)^2=16y^2 $$  which implies  $x\leq 3$ , since  $a>b$  we must have  $(a,b)=(2,1)$ , this implies   $$ c+a|1 $$  this contradiction completes the proof.

first row 1+2, 2+3, ...
2nd row 1+3, 2+4, ...
...
last row 1+2011.

If this triangle taken modulo 3, thus filled with 0's, 1's and 2's, is rotated 120° clockwise by its center, we find  $0\to 1\to 2\to 0$  so there is an equal number of them.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Take 670 0's, 670 1's, and 671 2's.

Then, we get  $335 \cdot 669 + 670 \cdot 671$  with sum  $0$ ,  $335 \cdot 669 + 670 \cdot 671$  with sum  $1$ , and  $671 \cdot 335 + 670 \cdot 670$  with sum  $2$ . 

As  $335 \cdot 669 + 670 \cdot 671=335 \cdot (669+2 \cdot 671)= 335 \cdot 2011$ , each of these is one-third of the total.</details>

Out of the  $2011$  numbers, consider them mod 3 and let there be  $x$  0's,  $y$  1's, and  $z$  2's.

stem_md: In the notebooks of Peter and Nick, two numbers are written. Initially, these two numbers are 1 and 2 for Peter and 3 and 4 for Nick. Once a minute, Peter writes a quadratic trinomial  $f(x)$ , the roots of which are the two numbers in his notebook, while Nick writes a quadratic trinomial  $g(x)$  the roots of which are the numbers in *his* notebook. If the equation  $f(x)=g(x)$  has two distinct roots, one of the two boys replaces the numbers in his notebook by those two roots. Otherwise, nothing happens. If Peter once made one of his numbers 5, what did the other one of his numbers become?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let the roots written in someone's notebook at any given time be  $a,b$ . We claim that they satisfy the invariant  $2ab-5a-5b=-11$ Proof:

We induct. Clearly it is true at the beginning. 

Now, assume it is true after a few turns. Then, let Peter have  $a,b$  written, and Nick have  $c,d$ , both satisfying the constraint  $2ab-5a-5b=2cd-5c-5d=-11$ Consider the new equation; it is of the form  $m(x-a)(x-b)=(x-c)(x-d)$  (we can divide the leading coefficients to get just that  $m$ ).

Now, this rearranges to  $(m-1)x^2-[m(a+b)-(c+d)]x+(mab-cd)=0$ Let the roots of this be  $p,q$ .

By Vieta's,  $p+q=\frac{m(a+b)-(c+d)}{m-1}$  and  $pq=\frac{mab-cd}{m-1}$ .

Thus,  $2pq-5(p+q)=\frac{-5m(a+b)+5(c+d)+2mab-2cd}{m-1}=\frac{m(2ab-5a-5b)-(2cd-5c-5d)}{m-1}$ .

But, recalling the induction hypothesis, this is just  $\frac{m(-11)-(-11)}{m-1}=-11$  as desired.

Thus, our induction is complete, and the numbers always satisfy this invariant.

So, when  $a=5$  we have that  $10b-25-5b=-11 \implies 5b=14 \implies b=\boxed{\frac{14}{5}}$</details>

Therefore the equation  $f_{n+1}(x)=g_{n+1}(x)$  is of the form  $f_n(x)=kg_n(x)$  for some real  $k$  ( $k=\frac{a+b}a$ ). Inductively any equation of the form  $f_n(x)=g_n(x)$  can be written in the form  $f_1(x)=kg_1(x)$ . But  $f_1(x)=a(x-1)(x-2)$  and  $g_1(x)=b(x-3)(x-4)$  hence  $f_n(x)-g_n(x)=0$  becomes  $ kx^2-3kx+2k-x^2+7x-12=0$   $\Rightarrow (k-1)x^2+(7-3k)x+2k-12=0$ . 
If for some  $n$ ,  $x=5$  is a solution of the last quadratic, then  $25(k-1)+5(7-3k)+2k-12=0 \Rightarrow k=\frac16$ . Hence to find the other solution we may plug  $k=\frac16$  back to the quadratic and find  $-\frac56x^2+\frac{13}2x-\frac{35}3=0$   whose roots are  $5$  (already known) and  $\frac{14}5$  which is the requested.

stem_md: Nine quadratics,  $x^2+a_1x+b_1, x^2+a_2x+b_2,...,x^2+a_9x+b_9$  are written on the board. The sequences  $a_1, a_2,...,a_9$  and  $b_1, b_2,...,b_9$  are arithmetic. The sum of all nine quadratics has at least one real root. What is the the greatest possible number of original quadratics that can have no real roots?
solution_md:
<details><summary>solution</summary>Let  $a_1=a_5-4k$ ,  $a_2=a_5-3k$ , ...,  $a_5=a_5$ , ...,  $a_9=a_5+4k$ .
Similarly, let  $b_1=b_5-4l$ , ...,  $b_9=b_5+4l$ .

Note that for some r,  $1\le r\le 9$ ,  $x^2+a_rx+b_r$  has a real root if and only if  $a_r^2-4b_r\ge 0$ .

From the condition that adding all 9 quadratics gives a real root, we have that  $9x^2+9a_5x+9b_5$  has a real root, which means  $x^2+a_5x+b_5$  must also have a real root and  $a_5^2-4b_5\ge 0$ .

We now claim that for each n such that  $1\le n\le 4$ , at most one of the quadratics  $x^2+a_{5-n}x+b_{5-n}$  and  $x^2+a_{5+n}x+b_{5+n}$  can have no real roots. Assume for contradiction that both quadratics have no real roots. 
This implies  $a_{5-n}^2-4b_{5-n}<0$  $\iff (a_5-nk)^2-4(b_5-nl)<0$  $\iff a_5^2-2a_5nk+n^2k^2-4b_5+4nl<0$ and  $a_{5+n}^2-4b_{5+n}<0$  $\iff (a_5+nk)^2-4(b_5+nl)<0$  $\iff a_5^2+2a_5nk+n^2k^2-4b_5-4nl<0$ .
Adding these two equations gives  $2a_5^2+2n^2k^2-8b_5<0$ , or  $a_5^2+n^2k^2-4b_5<0$ . This is a contradiction, because we already know that  $a_5^2-4b_5\ge 0 \implies a_5^2+n^2k^2-4b_5\ge 0$ . Therefore, at most one of these two quadratics can have no real roots.

This means that at most one of  $x^2+a_1x+b_1$  and  $x^2+a_9x+b_9$  can have no real roots, at most one of  $x^2+a_2x+b_2$  and  $x^2+a_8x+b_8$  can have no real roots, at most one of  $x^2+a_3x+b_3$  and  $x^2+a_7x+b_7$  can have no real roots, and at most one of  $x^2+a_4x+b_4$  and  $x^2+a_6x+b_6$  can have no real roots. Therefore, the maximum number of quadratics that can have no real roots is 4.

This is achievable by letting  $a_n=9-n$  and  $b_n=-1+n$ . For  $n=6, 7, 8, 9$  we have  $a_n^2-4b_n=(9-n)^2-4(-1+n)<0$ , so indeed, 4 quadratics have no real roots. So the answer is  $\boxed{4}$ .</details>

stem_md: Given are  $10$  distinct real numbers. Kyle wrote down the square of the difference for each pair of those numbers in his notebook, while Peter wrote in his notebook the absolute value of the differences of the squares of these numbers. Is it possible for the two boys to have the same set of  $45$  numbers in their notebooks?
solution_md:
<details><summary>solution</summary>If one of the  $a_i$  is equal to zero, we can safely delete it an work with the remaining. In what follows,  $n \in \{9, 10\}$  and  $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$  are nonzero distinct reals satisfying the conditions of the problem. We'll show this is impossible. 

Order them as  $a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_n$ . If the  $a_i$  work, so do the  $-a_i$ , hence we may assume  $a_n > 0$ .  Let us assume that  $a_1 < 0$  for now. The largest number that Kyle writes down is  $(a_n-a_1)^2 > \max(a_n^2, a_1^2) \geq a_i^2$  for all  $1 \leq i \leq n$ . In particular, each number that Peter writes down is strictly smaller than this number, a contradiction. Therefore  $a_1 > 0$ .

Thus all the  $a_i$  are positive. The product of all numbers in Kyle's notebook is  $\prod \limits_{1 \leq i < j \leq n} (a_j-a_i)^2$ , whereas the product of all numbers in Peter's notebook is  $\prod \limits_{1 \leq i < j \leq n} (a_j^2-a_i^2)$ . Equating the two and dividing we obtain that \[1 = \prod \limits_{1 \leq i < j \leq n} \left(\frac{a_j+a_i}{a_j-a_i}\right) > 1\] a contradiction.</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2011 Contests/2011 All-Russian Olympiad/406962.json

Let K(a,b) = (a-b)^2 be Kyle's applied function and P(a,b)=abs(a^2 - b^2) be Peter's function. We prove that the numbers in the notebooks can't be all the same for any set of n>=3 distinct initial numbers. 

Assume the contrary and let the n numbers be a_1 < a_2 ... < a_n.

If we multiply all given numbers by -1, the values of Kyle's and Peter's functions don't change, so we can without loss of generality assume that abs(a_n) >= abs(a_1).

The highest number in Kyle's notbook is obviously K(a_n,a_1) = (a_n-a_1)^2. The highest number in Peter's notebook is [(highest absolute value of (a_1,...,a_n)]^2 - [(smallest absolute value of (a_1,...,a_n)]^2. The highest absolute value of (a_1,...,a_n) is a_n (see above), the smallest absolute value shall be a_m for some 1<=m<n. So the highest value in Peter's notebook is a_n^2 - a_m^2.

If 0 <= a_1, then m=1 and 

P(a_n, a_1) = K (a_n, a_1)

must hold, because on both sides there are the highest values in each notebook. The general equation K(x,y) = P(x,y) has only the following solutions:

1) x=0, and
2) y=0, and
3) x=y.

Case 3) cannot be, as all numbers a_i must be different, so we get a_1=0.

If a_1 < 0, then we have

K(a_n,a_1) = (a_n - a_1)^2  > a_n^2 >= a_n^2 - a_m^2,

which is a contradiction, as the highest number in Kyle's notebook is bigger than the highest number in Peter's notebook.

So we get the result that Kyle's and Peter's highest number in the notebook can only be equal if a_1, the smallest of the original n numbers, is zero. But it holds K(0,x) = P (0,x) = x^2 for all x, so the values in the notebooks obtained from pairing up a_1(=0)  with all the other a_j (j=2,...n) and calculating P(0,a_j) and K(0,a_j), resp., are the same. So if the multisets of values K(a_i,a_j) in Kyle's notebook and values P(a_i,a_j) in Peter's notebook are the same for all 1<=i<j<=n (that was our initial assumption) then they are also the same for all 2 <=i < j <=n.

In other words, the n-1 values a_2, a_3, ... , a_n also must form a set of numbers that would fullfil the condition presented in the problem.

If n=3, then this represents only 2 numbers (a_2 and a_3), so there is only one number in each notebook and it must hold

P(a_2,a_3) = K(a_2,a_3)

which (see above) would imply a_2=0, a_3=0 or a_2=a_3. However, since a_1=0 as proven above, either option would imply two of the three a_i being equal, which cannot be.

If n=4, then a_2, a_3 and a_4 would have to form 3 numbers fullfilling the initial condition, which we have just seen cannot be. By induction, for no number n>=3 (including n=10) the initial condition can be true.

stem_md: Two natural numbers  $d$  and  $d'$ , where  $d'>d$ , are both divisors of  $n$ . Prove that  $d'>d+\frac{d^2}{n}$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Sol.</summary>Let  $x=\frac{n}{d}$ ,  $y=\frac{n}{d'}$  and  $\alpha=d'-d$ .
If  $d\leq\sqrt{n}$  it is obvious so  $d'>d>x>y$ , otherwise write  $n$  as  $$ dx=n=d'y=(d+\alpha)y \Rightarrow d(x-y)=\alpha y \Rightarrow \alpha\geq \frac{d}{y} $$  now we want to prove that  $d+\alpha>d+\frac{d^2}{n}$  which gradually becomes   $$  \frac{d}{y}>\frac{d}{x}\Rightarrow x>y \, \, \square $$</details>

An extension: Instead of $d$ and $d'$ being divisors of $n$ , we have $n|d$ and $n|d'$
Solution Subtract $d$ from both sides of the equation, to result in $d^{'}-d>\frac{d^2}{n}$ . If we can prove that the minimum of the LHS is greater than the RHS, then we will know that the LHS is always greater than the RHS, because all other values would result in a higher value of the LHS, and we have already proved it works for the minimum of the LHS. **Lemma 1:** $\min(d'-d)=n$ .**Proof:** We know $d'>d$ , and that $n|d$ , and $n|d'$ . The minimum difference between two divisors of $n$ is going to be $n$ , and because $d'>d$ , we get the desired minimum result of $n$ . $\Box$ From here, we desire to prove $n>\frac{d^2}{n}$ , because we found the minimum of the left hand side after subtract $d$ , and wish to prove the inequality works for this. **Lemma 2:** $n>0$ **Proof:** We are given that $d$ and $d^{'}$ are natural numbers, hence from $\min(d^{'}-d)=n$ . From $d^{'}>d$ , and $d^{'}$ and $d$ are $>0$ from them being natural numbers, hence we have $d^{'}-d>0\implies d^{'}>d$ , which is true, hence we get $\min(\text{Positive Number})=n>0$ $\Box$ Now note that because $n>0$ , we can multiply both sides of the inequality to give us $n^2>d^2\implies (n+d)(n-d)>0$ . If we can prove that $n>d$ , we will get this to be true, because we know that $n$ and $d$ are $>0$ , hence $(n+d)>0$ , and we now desire $(n-d)>0$ to make this true. To prove $n>d$ , start by remembering that $d^{'}|n$ , hence $n\ge d^{'}$ . We also know that $d^{'}>d$ , hence we get $n\ge d^{'}> d$ , which implies that $n>d$ , and hence we are done $\Box$

stem_md: Given are two distinct monic cubics  $F(x)$  and  $G(x)$ . All roots of the equations  $F(x)=0$ ,  $G(x)=0$  and  $F(x)=G(x)$  are written down. There are eight numbers written. Prove that the greatest of them and the least of them cannot be both roots of the polynomial  $F(x)$ .
solution_md:
Let  $F(x)=x^3+ax^2+...$  and   $G(x)=x^3+bx^2+...$ .Since there are exactly two intersection points (call them  $x_1$  and  $x_2$ ), we have  $a\ne b$ , wlog  $a>b$ .

So  $F(x)>G(x)$  for all  $x<x_1$  and for all  $x>x_2$ . 
So if the smallest of the eight numbers is one of the zeros of  $F$  or  $G$ , it must be the least zero of  $F$ . 
And if the largest of the eight numbers is one of the zeros of  $F$  or  $G$ , it must be the biggest zero of  $G$ . :)

stem_md: In every cell of a table with  $n$  rows and ten columns, a digit is written. It is known that for every row  $A$  and any two columns, you can always find a row that has different digits from  $A$  only when it intersects with two columns. Prove that  $n\geq512$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>One possible approach</summary>Denote the set of columns by  $C=\{C_1,\ldots,C_{10}\}$  and consider the first row  $R$ . Each nonempty, *even* subset of  $C$  (by *even* I mean a subset with an even number of elements), gives rise to a distinct row different from  $R$  (a rough argument for this is below). Assuming this for the moment, since there are  $\frac{2^{10}}{2}-1=511$  nonempty even subsets of  $C$ , the result follows.

As for the claim made above, here's an example of the basic idea. An even subset of  $C$ , say,  $\{C_1,C_2, C_4, C_6,C_7,C_8\}$ , gives rise to a row that differs from  $R$  in columns  $1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8$ . After all, by the given condition, there is a row  $R_1$  differing from  $R$  in columns  $1$  and  $2$ . Again by the given condition, there is a row  $R_2$  differing from  $R_1$  is columns  $4$  and  $6$ . And again by the given condition, there is a row  $R_3$  differing from  $R_2$  is columns  $7$  and  $8$ . Thus  $R_3$  differs from  $R$  in columns  $1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8$ .</details>

Follow-up problem: Show that  $512$  is the best possible.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2011 Contests/2011 All-Russian Olympiad/419046.json

Consider the first row  $R_1$  and two columns  $C_1,C_2$  then there exists  $R_2$  such that  $R_2,R_1$  are good pairs wrt  $C_1,C_2$ .

Consider two columns  $C_1,C_3$  then there exist *good pairs*  $(R_1,R_3),(R_2,R_4)$  wrt these two columns. We can see that the rows in each pair are different from each other, and a row in any pair is different from a row in any other pair (because these two rows have different numbers that are in  $C_2$ ). There are  $2^2=4$  rows after this consideration.

Similarly, consider  $C_1,C_4$  then there exist pairwise distinct *good pairs*  $(R_1,R_5),(R_2,R_6),(R_3,R_7),(R_4,R_8)$  wrt to these two columns. The distinction can be proven similarly. There are  $2^3=8$  rows after in consideration.

Thus, after we consider two columns  $C_1,C_{10}$ , the number of rows is at least  $2^9=512$ . We are done.</details>

<details><summary>solution</summary>We generalise the entries to be any real numbers (not necessarily digits). For a  $n \times m$  table we show a lower bound of  $n \geq 2^{m-1}$ . In our problem,  $m = 10$ . Consider all the reals in the first column. These cannot all be equal, for then picking any row and column along with the first column would yield a contradiction. So there are at least two distinct entries, say  $a, b$ . Consider all rows starting with  $a$  and observe that if we delete this column the hypotheses holds on the columns left. So there are at least  $2^{m-2}$  rows starting with  $a$ , similarily for  $b$ . It follows that the total number of rows is at least  $2 \cdot 2^{m-2} = 2^{m-1}$ . Finally we need to check the base case  $m = 2$ , which is clear since  $n \geq 2$  due to the two distinct entries  $a, b$ .</details>

x\ge 6(80)-385
x\ge 480-385

The key is that you have to use geometry to solve this problem:  when you have an infinite number of choices, you have to use the axiom that if you have a region of (volume/area/length)  $A$ , and you pick a smaller subregion of (volume/area/length)  $B$ , then the probability that a point that is in  $A$  is also in  $B$  is  $\frac{B}{A}$ .

Not true. The probability of choosing any point on a line, or any line on a plane, etc., is $0$ , but that doesn't mean it's not possible to choose that point, as you seem to be suggesting. It means that the event will *almost surely* not occur. But clearly the point you just picked, say, on the dartboard, is just as likely to be hit as any other point, and if all points were impossible to hit, you wouldn't hit the dartboard. So the probability of a selected point being hit is positive, and yet it's "zero". [See this wikipedia article.](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_surely) So, in your tetrahedron example, we can say that *any fixed positive probability is greater than the probability of picking a point (uniformly at random) exactly $1$ unit from one face*, but it is still possible, though almost completely unlikely. This whole issue stems from the phenomenon that $\lim_{x \to \infty}\dfrac{1}{x}=0$ , and yet $\infty\cdot 0 \ne 1$ As for the original problem, refer to Jogo's explanation. solution_md: <details><summary>Alternative Solution</summary>Let  $\angle AMD=\theta$ . This is our unknown. Also, let the length of segment  $\overline{DM}$  be  $x$ . From the given, it also is the case that  $\angle CMD=\theta$ . Then,  $ \angle DCM = 180^\circ - 2 \theta $ , and from the Law of Sines, we have: \[ \dfrac {\sin (180^{\circ} - 2 \theta)}{x} = \dfrac {\sin \theta}{6} \] From  $ \triangle AMD $ , we see that  $ \sin \theta = \tfrac {3}{x} $ . Substituting this into the Law of Sines equation we got above, we have: \[ \begin {eqnarray*} \dfrac {\sin (180^{\circ} - 2\theta)}{\cancel{x}} &=& \dfrac {1}{2\cancel{x}}  \sin (180^{\circ} - 2 \theta) &=& \dfrac {1}{2}  180^{\circ} - 2\theta &=& 30^{\circ}  2\theta &=& 150^{\circ}  \theta &=& 75^{\circ}, \] and we have our answer: \[ \boxed {\textbf {(E) } 75} \] \[ \blacksquare \]</details>

Brian writes down four integers  $w > x > y > z$  whose sum is  $44$ . The pairwise positive differences of these numbers are  $1,3,4,5,6,$  and  $9$ . What is the sum of the possible values for  $w$ ? $ \textbf{(A)}\  16 \qquad
\textbf{(B)}\ 31  \qquad
\textbf{(C)}\ 48  \qquad
\textbf{(D)}\ 62  \qquad
\textbf{(E)}\  93 $
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>$w + x + y + z = 44$  $w - z = 9$  because that's the largest difference.
The smallest difference is either  $w-x = 1$ ,  $x-y = 1$ , or  $y-z = 1$ .  That's because the smallest difference must be two of the closest numbers.

Take the first case: $w-z = 9$  and  $w-x=1$ .  That means  $(w-z) - (w-x) = 8$ , which means that  $x-z = 8$ .  That's a difference of two numbers, but it's not on the list.  Fail.

Take the second case: $w-z = 9$  and  $x-y = 1$ .  That means  $(w-z) + (x-y) = 10$ .  Combine that with  $w+x+y+z = 44$  to get  $(10 + y + z) + y + z = 44$ , or  $y + z = 17$ .  We also know that  $y-z \in \{3, 4, 5, 6\}$ .  Since the sum of two integers is odd, their difference must be odd, too, so  $y-z = 3$  or  $y-z = 5$ .  That gives  $(y,z) = (10, 7)$  or  $(y,z) = (11, 6)$ .  In turn, using the first two equations, that gives  $(w,x,y,z) = (16, 11, 10, 7)$  or  $(w,x,y,z) = (15,12 , 11, 6)$ .  Both work.

Take the third case: $w-z = 9$  and  $y-z = 1$ .  That gives  $(w-z) - (y-z) = 8$ , which means that  $w-y = 8$ .  Again, that's not on the list, so there are no solutions.

Thus, the sum of the possible values of  $w$  is  $\boxed{31}$ .</details>

\textbf{(C)}\ \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}   \qquad

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Answer:  $\boxed{\textbf{(C) } \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}}$  

Draw the perpendicular bisectors of  $BD$ ,  $BC$ , and  $AB$ . The area we want is the intersection of the areas closer to  $B$  from each perpendicular bisector. This area is funky so let's subtract the areas we don't want which are the triangles made by the perpendicular bisectors. We can make this easier by noting that  $R$  is contained entirely in one half of the rhombus, the part closer to  $B$  made by the perpendicular bisector of  $AB$ . The area of the rhombus is  $2\sqrt{3}$  so this area is  $\sqrt{3}$ . Now we got to subtract the areas of the remaining two triangles. Note that these triangles are 30-60-90 right triangles with side length  $1$  opposite the 60 degree angle. Both are congruent and their legs are  $1$  and  $\sqrt{3}{3}$ . The areas of these triangles together is  $2(1)(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$ . $R$  is thus  $\sqrt{3}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}=\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}$</details>

Let  $T_1$  be a triangle with sides  $2011, 2012,$  and  $2013$ . For  $n \ge 1$ , if  $T_n=\triangle ABC$  and  $D,E,$  and  $F$  are the points of tangency of the incircle of  $\triangle ABC$  to the sides  $AB,BC$  and  $AC$ , respectively, then  $T_{n+1}$  is a triangle with side lengths  $AD,BE,$  and  $CF$ , if it exists. What is the perimeter of the last triangle in the sequence  $(T_n)$ ? $ \textbf{(A)}\  \frac{1509}{8} \qquad
\textbf{(B)}\ \frac{1509}{32}  \qquad
\textbf{(C)}\ \frac{1509}{64}  \qquad
\textbf{(D)}\ \frac{1509}{128}  \qquad
\textbf{(E)}\ \frac{1509}{256}  $
solution_md:
I really liked this problem because of the integrated algebra along with the geometry.
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Answer:  $\boxed{\textbf{(D)} \frac{1509}{128}}$ Note that the perimeter of the next triangle in the sequence is the semi-perimeter of the previous triangle and the side lengths are determined by subtracting each side of the previous triangle from the semi perimeter. This can be shown by adding the tangents together while using the theorem that states tangents to a circle from a point are congruent.
Let's list out the first few side lengths of the triangles in the sequence  $(T_n)$ : $T_1=2011, 2012, 2013$  $T_2=\frac{6036}{2}-\{2011, 2012, 2013\}$  $T_3=\frac{6036}{4}-(\frac{6036}{2}-\{2011, 2012, 2013\})$  $T_4=\frac{6036}{8}-(\frac{6036}{4}-(\frac{6036}{2}-\{2011, 2012, 2013\}))$ ...
We see a pattern which is $T_n=\frac{6036}{2^{n-1}}-(\frac{6036}{2^{n-2}}-...(\frac{6036}{2}-\{2011, 2012, 2013\}))...$  
If we took care of the parentheses we get $T_n=\frac{6036}{2^{n-1}}-\frac{6036}{2^{n-2}}+\frac{6036}{2^{n-3}}-...\pm \{2011, 2012, 2013\}$ where the  $\pm$  is  $+$  when  $n$  is odd and  $ - $  when  $n$  is even.
Notice that the expression before the  $\pm$  is a geometric series! The common ratio is  $-2$ . There are  $n-1$  terms and the first term is  $\frac{6036}{2^{n-1}}$ . I will substitute  $y=n-1$  to work with slightly nicer terms.
So using the formula for the sum of geometric series the expression turns into: $\frac{\frac{6036}{2^{y}}\cdot ((-2)^y-1)}{-3}$ If  $y$  is even ( $n$  is odd), we get  $\frac{\frac{6036}{2^{y}}\cdot (2^y-1)}{-3}=-2012+\frac{2012}{2^y}$ If  $y$  is odd ( $n$  is even), we get $\frac{\frac{6036}{2^{y}}\cdot (-2^y-1)}{-3}=2012+\frac{2012}{2^y}$ So now let's rewrite the sequences:
For  $n$  odd:  $T_n: -2012+\frac{2012}{2^y}+\{2011, 2012, 2013\}$ For  $n$  even:  $T_n: 2012+\frac{2012}{2^y}-\{2011, 2012, 2013\}$ Now we got to use the triangle inequality for both cases.
Case 1:  $n$  odd/ $y$  even
* $-2012+\frac{2012}{2^y}+2011+-2012+\frac{2012}{2^y}+2012>-2012+\frac{2012}{2^y}+2013$  $\frac{2012}{2^y}>2$  $2^y<1006$  $y\le9$  
* $\frac{2012}{2^y}>-2$  Always true $\frac{2012}{2^y}>0$  Always true $\max y=8$ Case 2:  $n$  even/ $y$  odd 
* $2012+\frac{2012}{2^y}-2011+2012+\frac{2012}{2^y}-2013>2012+\frac{2012}{2^y}-2012$  $\frac{2012}{2^y}>0$  Always true
* $\frac{2012}{2^y}>-2$  Always true $\frac{2012}{2^y}>2$  $y\le 9$  $\max y=9$ Our maximum  $y$  is thus  $9$ . The perimeter of this triangle is  $\frac{6036}{2^9}=\frac{1509}{2^7}=\frac{1509}{128}$</details>

Consider the set of numbers  $\{1,10,10^2,10^3, ... 10^{10} \}$ . The ratio of the largest element of the set to the sum of the other ten elements of the set is closest to which integer? $ \textbf{(A)}\  1 \qquad

solution_md: <details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Let  $S=1+10+10^2+ \cdots +10^9$ . Multiplying this equation by 10 gives  $10S=10+10^2+ \cdots +10^{10}$ . A rectangular parking lot has a diagonal of  $25$  meters and an area of  $168$  square meters. In meters, what is the perimeter of the parking lot?  $ \textbf{(A)}\  52 \qquad
\textbf{(B)}\  58 \qquad
\textbf{(C)}\ 62  \qquad
\textbf{(D)}\  68 \qquad
\textbf{(E)}\ 70  $
solution_md:
<details><summary>Number Theory Solution</summary>Find pairs of factors of  $168$  and find the length of the diagonal. Use pairs where both numbers are less than  $25$ : $24$  and  $7$ : By the Pythagorean Theorem, $24^2 + 7^2 = h^2 \Rightarrow
\sqrt{576 + 49} = h \Rightarrow
\sqrt{625} = h \Rightarrow
h = 25$ So the sides of the rectangle are of lengths  $24$  and  $7$ , so the perimeter is  $2(24 + 7) = 2(31)= \boxed{62}$  meters, or  $\boxed{C}$ .  $\square$</details>

Let @ denote the "averaged with" operation:  $a$  @  $b$  =  $\frac{a+b}{2}$ . Which of the following distributive laws hold for all numbers  $x,y$  and  $z$ ?

I. x @ (y+z) = (x @ y) + (x @ z)
II. x + (y @ z) = (x + y) @ (x + z)
III. x @ (y @ z) = (x @ y) @ (x @ z) $ \textbf{(A)}\  \text{I only} \qquad
\textbf{(B)}\ \text{II only}   \qquad
\textbf{(C)}\  \text{III only}  \qquad
\textbf{(D)}\  \text{I and III only}  \qquad
\textbf{(E)}\ \text{II and III only}   $
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>I.  $x@(y+z)=\frac{x+y+z}{2}$  and  $(x@y)+(x@z)=\frac{x+y}{2}+\frac{x+z}{2}=\frac{2x+y+z}{2}$  so I is not necessarily true.

II.  $x+(y@z)=x+\frac{y+z}{2}=\frac{2x+y+z}{2}$  and  $(x+y)@(x+z)=\frac{x+y}{2}+\frac{x+z}{2}=\frac{2x+y+z}{2}$  so II is always true.

III.  $x@(y@z)=x@\left(\frac{y+z}{2}\right)=\frac{2x+y+z}{4}$  and  $(x@y)@(x@z)=\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right)@\left(\frac{x+z}{2}\right)=\frac{2x+y+z}{4}$  so III is always true.

Therefore, the answer is **E**.</details>

What is the product of all the roots of the equation \[\sqrt{5|x|+8} = \sqrt{x^2-16}. \] $ \textbf{(A)}\  -64 \qquad
\textbf{(B)}\ -24  \qquad
\textbf{(C)}\  -9  \qquad
\textbf{(D)}\  24  \qquad
\textbf{(E)}\ 576  $
solution_md:
A more "rigorous" solution:

<details><summary>awesometoad is awesome</summary>We have  $ \sqrt{5|x|+8}=\sqrt{x^{2}-16}. $ Squaring both sides gives us  $5|x| + 8 = x^{2} - 16.$ Now we have an absolute value equation. We can split this into two cases.

Case  $1$ :  $x$  is positive.
If  $x$  is positive, we have  $5x + 8 = x^{2} - 16$  or  $x^2 - 5x - 24 = 0$ . Factoring, we get  $(x-8)(x+3) = 0$ . Noting that x must be positive, we have  $x=8$ .

Case  $2$ :  $x$  is negative.
If  $x$  is negative, we have  $5(-x) + 8 = x^{2} - 16$  or  $x^2 + 5x - 24 = 0$ . Factoring, we get  $(x+8)(x-3) = 0$ . Noting that x must be negative, we have  $x=-8$ .

Actually the Charmichael function, which I'll denote $\lambda (n)$ , is strictly better than $\phi(n)$ , in the sense that $\lambda(n) \mid \phi(n)$ holds for all $n$ and the two are in general not equal. For example, $\lambda(1000) = 100$ . So the Charmichael function will tell you immediately that $2011^{100} \equiv 1 \pmod{1000}$ , whereas the $\phi$ function doesn't give you any information. Fortunately, it's not hard using the Chinese Remainder Theorem that \[ \lambda(p_1^{e_1} p_2^{e_2} \dots p_n^{e_n}) = \operatorname{lcm} \left( \lambda(p_1^{e_1}), \lambda(p_2^{e_2}), \dots, \lambda(p_n^{e_n}) \right). \] The theorem on primitive roots states that $\lambda(p^e) = \phi(p^e)$ whenever $p > 2$ . That means that the Charmiachel function is just slightly "smarter" than the $\phi$ function because it takes the LCM of each of the $\phi(p^e)$ ; in contrast, $\phi$ just multiplies them all together. That's how you remember how the Charmiachel function works. There's one caveat: in general $\lambda(2^n) \neq 2^{n-1}$ . It equals $1,2$ for $n=1,2$ and $2^{n-2}$ for $n=3,4,\dots$ . So the Charmiachel function gives you a little more precision there. So to furnish the example earlier, \[ \lambda{1000} = \operatorname{lcm} \left( \lambda(8), \lambda(125) \right) = \operatorname{lcm} \left( 2, 100 \right) = 100. \] So next time you need to compute $m^n \pmod{1000}$ (where $\gcd(m,1000) = 1$ ), take $n$ mod $\lambda(1000) = 100$ , not mod $\phi(1000) = 400$ .

A majority of the 30 students in Ms. Deameanor's class bought pencils at the school bookstore.  Each of these students bought the same number of pencils, and this number was greater than 1.  The cost of a pencil in cents was greater than the number of pencils each student bought, and the total cost of all the pencils was  $\$ 17.71 $.  What was the cost of a pencil in cents?

$ \textbf{(A)}\,7 \qquad\textbf{(B)}\,11 \qquad\textbf{(C)}\,17 \qquad\textbf{(D)}\,23 \qquad\textbf{(E)}\,77$
solution_md:
Let  $x>15$  be the number of students at the bookstore,  $p>1$  be the number of pencils each student bought, and  $c>p$  be the price of one pencil. We see that  $xcp = 1771 = 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 23$ . Then we must have  $x=23, c=11, p=7$  by the original conditions and the answer is  $c=\boxed{11 \ \mathbf{(B)}}$ .

stem_md: Square  $EFGH$  has one vertex on each side of square  $ABCD$ .  Point  $E$  is on  $\overline{AB}$  with  $AE=7\cdot EB$ .  What is the ratio of the area of  $EFGH$  to the area of  $ABCD$ ? $\textbf{(A)}\,\frac{49}{64}     \qquad\textbf{(B)}\,\frac{25}{32}     \qquad\textbf{(C)}\,\frac78 \qquad\textbf{(D)}\,\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{8}   \qquad\textbf{(E)}\,\frac{\sqrt{14}}{4} $
solution_md:
Let  $8s$  be the length of the sides of square  $ABCD$ , then the length of one of the sides of square  $EFGH$  is  $\sqrt{(7s)^2+s^2}=\sqrt{50s^2}$ , and hence the ratio in the areas is  $\frac{\sqrt{50s^2}^2}{(8s)^2}=\frac{50}{64} = \boxed{\frac{25}{32} \ \mathbf{(B)}}$ .

see http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Wiki/index.php/2011_AMC_10A_Problems/Problem_11

stem_md: How many even integers are there between 200 and 700 whose digits are all different and come from the set {1,2,5,7,8,9}? $\textbf{(A)}\,12 \qquad\textbf{(B)}\,20 \qquad\textbf{(C)}\,72 \qquad\textbf{(D)}\,120 \qquad\textbf{(E)}\,200$
solution_md:
We split up into cases of the hundreds digits being  $2$  or  $5$ . If the hundred digits is  $2$ , then the units digits must be  $8$  in order for the number to be even and then there are  $4$  remaining choices ( $1,5,7,9$ ) for the tens digit, giving  $1 \times 1 \times 4=4$  possibilities. Similarly, there are  $1 \times 2 \times 4=8$  possibilities for the  $5$  case, giving a total of  $\boxed{4+8=12 \ \mathbf{(A)}}$  possibilities.

see http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Wiki/index.php/2011_AMC_10A_Problems/Problem_13

stem_md: A pair of standard 6-sided fair dice is rolled once.  The sum of the numbers rolled determines the diameter of a circle.  What is the probability that the numerical value of the area of the circle is less than the numerical value of the circle's circumference? $\textbf{(A)}\,\frac{1}{36} \qquad\textbf{(B)}\,\frac{1}{12} \qquad\textbf{(C)}\,\frac{1}{6} \qquad\textbf{(D)}\,\frac{1}{4} \qquad\textbf{(E)}\,\frac{5}{18}$
solution_md:
We want the area,  $\pi r^2$ , to be less than the circumference,  $2 \pi r$ :

\begin{align*}
\pi r^2 &< 2 \pi r 
r &< 2
\end{align*}

If  $r<2$  then the dice must show  $(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)$  which are  $3$  choices out of a total possible of  $6 \times 6 =36$ , so the probability is  $\frac{3}{36}=\boxed{\frac{1}{12} \ \mathbf{(B)}}$ .

see http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Wiki/index.php/2011_AMC_10A_Problems/Problem_14

stem_md: Roy bought a new battery-gasoline hybrid car. On a trip the car ran exclusively on its battery for the first 40 miles, then ran exclusively on gasoline for the rest of the trip, using gasoline at a rate of 0.02 gallons per mile. On the whole trip he averaged 55 miles per gallon. How long was the trip in miles? $\textbf{(A)}\,140 \qquad\textbf{(B)}\,240 \qquad\textbf{(C)}\,440 \qquad\textbf{(D)}\,640 \qquad\textbf{(E)}\,840$
solution_md:
We know that  $\frac{\text{total miles}}{\text{total gas}}=55$ . Let  $x$  be the distance the car traveled during the time it ran on gasoline, then the amount of gas used is  $0.02x$ . The total distance traveled is  $40+x$ , so we get  $\frac{40+x}{0.02x}=55$ . Solving this equation, we get  $x=400$ , so the total distance is  $400 + 40 = \boxed{440 \ \mathbf{(C)}}$ .

see http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Wiki/index.php/2011_AMC_10A_Problems/Problem_15

stem_md: In the eight-term sequence  $A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H$ , the value of  $C$  is 5 and the sum of any three consecutive terms is 30.  What is  $A+H$ ? $\textbf{(A)}\,17 \qquad\textbf{(B)}\,18 \qquad\textbf{(C)}\,25 \qquad\textbf{(D)}\,26 \qquad\textbf{(E)}\,43$
solution_md:
We consider the sum  $A+B+C+D+E+F+G+H$  and use the fact that  $C=5$ , and hence  $A+B=25$ .

\begin{align*}
&A+B+C+D+E+F+G+H=A+(B+C+D)+(E+F+G)+H=A+30+30+H=A+H+60
&A+B+C+D+E+F+G+H=(A+B)+(C+D+E)+(F+G+H)=25+30+30=85
\end{align*}

Equating the two values we get for the sum, we get the answer  $A+H+60=85$   $\Longrightarrow$   $A+H=\boxed{25 \ \mathbf{(C)}}$ .

see http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Wiki/index.php/2011_AMC_10A_Problems/Problem_17

stem_md: In  $1991$  the population of a town was a perfect square. Ten years later, after an increase of  $150$  people, the population was  $9$  more than a perfect square. Now, in  $2011$ , with an increase of another  $150$  people, the population is once again a perfect square. Which of the following is closest to the percent growth of the town's population during this twenty-year period? $ \textbf{(A)}\ 42 \qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 47 \qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 52\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ 57\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 62 $
solution_md:
Let the population of the town in  $1991$  be  $p^2$ . Let the population in  $2001$  be  $q^2+9$ . Let the population in 2011 be  $r^2$ . It follows that  $p^2+150=q^2+9$ . Rearrange this equation to get  $141=q^2-p^2=(q-p)(q+p)$ . Since  $q$  and  $p$  are both positive integers with  $q>p$ ,  $(q-p)$  and  $(q+p)$  also must be, and thus, they are both factors of  $141$ . We have two choices for pairs of factors of  $141$ :  $1$  and  $141$ , and  $3$  and  $47$ . Assuming the former pair, since  $(q-p)$  must be less than  $(q+p)$ ,  $q-p=1$  and  $q+p=141$ . Solve to get  $p=70, q=71$ . Since  $p^2+300$  is not a perfect square, this is not the correct pair. Solve for the other pair to get  $p=22, q=25$ . This time,  $p^2+300=22^2+300=784=28^2$ . This is the correct pair. Now, we find the percent increase from  $22^2=484$  to  $28^2=784$ . Since the increase is  $300$ , the percent increase is  $\frac{300}{484}\times100\%\approx\boxed{\textbf{(E)}\ 62\%}$ .


see http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Wiki/index.php/2011_AMC_10A_Problems/Problem_19
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2011 Contests/2011 AMC 10/414408.json

stem_md: Two points on the circumference of a circle of radius r are selected independently and at random. From each point a chord of length r is drawn in a clockwise direction. What is the probability that the two chords intersect? $ \textbf{(A)}\ \frac{1}{6}\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ \frac{1}{5}\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ \frac{1}{4}\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ \frac{1}{3}\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ \frac{1}{2} $
solution_md: <details><summary>storage</summary>We first fix a chord of length  $r$  somewhere around the circle. The chords intersect when  $B$  is another chord away from  $A$  (length of  $r$ ) or when  $B$  is on the far endpoint of the chord with  $A$ , and these two chords of radius  $r$  encompass all of the possible spots of  $B$ . Each chord forms a 60 degree angle, so  $\frac{120^\circ}{360^\circ}=\boxed{\frac{1}{3}}$</details>

stem_md: Two counterfeit coins of equal weight are mixed with 8 identical genuine coins. The weight of each of the counterfeit coins is different from the weight of each of the genuine coins. A pair of coins is selected at random without replacement from the 10 coins. A second pair is selected at random without replacement from the remaining 8 coins. The combined weight of the first pair is equal to the combined weight of the second pair. What is the probability that all 4 selected coins are genuine? $ \textbf{(A)}\ \frac{7}{11}\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ \frac{9}{13}\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ \frac{11}{15}\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ \frac{15}{19}\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ \frac{15}{16} $
solution_md:
<details><summary>Alternate Solution</summary>Let  $g$  represent one of the **identical** gold coins and  $c_1$  and  $c_2$  represent the counterfeit coins. We have three cases. \[\begin{cases}\underline{c_1}~\underline{g}=\underline{c_2}~\underline{g}  \underline{c_2}~\underline{g}=\underline{c_1}~\underline{g}  \underline{g}~\underline{g}=\underline{g}~\underline{g}\end{cases}\] Note that we can switch the order that the pairs were picked for the counterfeit coin cases. 

Lets deal with the  $\underline{g}~\underline{g}=\underline{g}~\underline{g}$  case first.

We have  $\binom{8}{2}$  ways to choose the first pair of gold coins and  $\binom{6}{2}$  choices to pick the second pair of gold coins without replacement. We just place all four coins onto the scale. There is only  $1$  way to do this because all of the gold coins are identical. So this gives us  $28\times 15=420$  ways for this case.

Second, we deal with the  $\underline{c_1}~\underline{g}=\underline{c_2}~\underline{g}$  case.

Just place  $c_1$  and  $c_2$  on the opposite sides of the scale, \[\underline{c_1}~\underline{~}=\underline{c_2}~\underline{~}.\] There are  $8$  ways to pick the gold coin for the second slot on the first pair and  $7$  ways to pick the other gold coin for the second slot on the second pair. So there are  $56$  ways for this case.

Similarly, we have  $56$  ways for the  $\underline{c_2}~\underline{g}=\underline{c_1}~\underline{g}$  case.

In total, we have  $420+56+56=532$  total ways. We want the probability that all four coins are gold. So our probability is \[\frac{420}{532}=\frac{105}{133}=\boxed{\frac{15}{19}}.\]</details>

stem_md: Each vertex of convex pentagon  $ABCDE$  is to be assigned a color. There are  $6$  colors to choose from, and the ends of each diagonal must have different colors. How many different colorings are possible? $ \textbf{(A)}\ 2520\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 2880\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 3120\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ 3250\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 3750 $
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let vertex  $A$  be any vertex, then vertex  $B$  be one of the diagonal vertices to  $A$ ,  $C$  be one of the diagonal vertices to  $B$ , and so on. We consider cases for this problem.

In the case that  $C$  has the same color as  $A$ ,  $D$  has a different color from  $A$  and so  $E$  has a different color from  $A$  and  $D$ . In this case,  $A$  has  $6$  choices,  $B$  has  $5$  choices (any color but the color of  $A$ ),  $C$  has  $1$  choice,  $D$  has  $5$  choices, and  $E$  has  $4$  choices, resulting in a possible of  $6 \cdot 5 \cdot 1 \cdot 5 \cdot 4 = 600$  combinations.

In the case that  $C$  has a different color from  $A$  and  $D$  has a different color from  $A$ ,  $A$  has  $6$  choices,  $B$  has  $5$  choices,  $C$  has  $4$  choices (since  $A$  and  $B$  necessarily have different colors),  $D$  has  $4$  choices, and  $E$  has  $4$  choices, resulting in a possible of  $6 \cdot 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 = 1920$  combinations.
 
In the case that  $C$  has a different color from  $A$  and  $D$  has the same color as  $A$ ,  $A$  has  $6$  choices,  $B$  has  $5$  choices,  $C$  has  $4$  choices,  $D$  has  $1$  choice, and  $E$  has  $5$  choices, resulting in a possible of  $6 \cdot 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 1 \cdot 5 = 600$  combinations.

Adding all those combinations up, we get  $600+1920+600=\boxed{3120 \ \mathbf{(C)}}$ .

see http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Wiki/index.php/2011_AMC_10A_Problems/Problem_22</details>

We assign one side of  $ABCDE$  to be the side that contains the pair of vertices colored the same. There are 5 ways to do this. Then we color the pair of vertices 6 ways, the next vertex 5 ways, etc. We have  $5 \cdot 6 \cdot 5\cdot 4\cdot 3=1800$  ways.**Case 3: 2 pairs of vertices share the same color**
We color one pair of vertices  $a$ . The next pair (colored  $b$ ) has no choice but to be adjacent to the first pair. Finally, the last vertex is colored  $c$ . We have the diagram below,
[asy]

label(" $a$ ",(0,1),N);
label(" $b$ ",(1,.4),E);

label(" $c$ ",(-.7,-1),N);
[/asy]
We assign the lonely vertex first to the pentagon  $ABCDE$ . On either side of this point is a pair of vertices colored the same. By symmetry, there is no need to multiply by 2 which side of  $c$  will contain the  $a\textendash\textendash\textendash a$  side. Thus, we continue by coloring each vertex. For one pair of vertices, we have 6 ways. Then we have 5 ways for the next pair and finally 4 ways for the lonely vertex. Overall, we have  $5\cdot 6\cdot 5\cdot 4=600$  ways.

Adding each case gives us  $720+1800+600=\boxed{3120}$  ways total.</details>

<details><summary>Recursion</summary>We can first fix the color of the first vertex as Color 1; it is trivial to just multiply by  $6$  afterward.

Now we present a recursion since each vertex is only previously linked to one vertex and will be linked to another vertex. (This method is quite standard as recursive counting).

\begin{tabular}{||c|c|c|c|c|c|c||}
Vertex & Color 1 & Color 2 & Color 3 & Color 4 & Color 5 & Color 6 
A & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 
B & 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 
C & 5 & 4 & 4 & 4 & 4 & 4 
D & 20 & 21 & 21 & 21 & 21 & 21 
E & 105 & 104 & 104 & 104 & 104 & 104 
\end{tabular}

We need  $E$  to be a different color than Vertex 1, so there are  $104 \cdot 5 = 520$  ways to color given that  $A$  is Color 1. However,  $A$  can be any color; therefore there are  $520 \cdot 6 = 3120$  total ways.</details>

However, this naïve count allows for the possibility that vertices  $1$  and  $5$  have the same color, so we must subtract those cases off:


- If vertex  $3$  has the same color as vertices  $1$  and  $5$ , then there are  $5$  ways to color vertices  $2$  and  $4$ ;
- If not, then there are  $5$  ways to choose this extra color, and then  $4$  ways to color vertices  $2$  and  $4$ .

stem_md:
Seven students count from  $1$  to  $1000$  as follows:


- Alice says all the numbers, except she skips the middle number in each consecutive group of three numbers. That is, Alice says  $1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, \cdots, 997, 999, 1000.$
- Barbara says all of the numbers that Alice doesn't say, except she also skips the middle number in each consecutive group of three numbers.
- Candice says all of the numbers that neither Alice nor Barbara says, except she also skips the middle number in each consecutive group of three numbers.
- Debbie, Eliza, and Fatima say all of the numbers that none of the students with the first names beginning before theirs in the alphabet say, except each also skips the middle number in each of her consecutive groups of three numbers.
- Finally, George says the only number that no one else says.

What number does George say? $ \textbf{(A)}\ 37\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 242\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 365\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ 728\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 998 $
solution_md:
First look at the numbers Alice says. 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9 ... skipping every number that is congruent to 2 mod 3. Thus, Barbara says those numbers EXCEPT every second - being  $2 + 3^1 = 5$  mod  $3^2=9$ . So Barbara skips every number congruent to 5 mod 9. We continue on and see: (see this for yourself)

Alice skips 2 mod 3, Barbara skips 5 mod 9, Candice skips 14 mod 27, Debbie skips 41 mod 81, Eliza skips 122 mod 423, and Fatima skips 365 mod 729.

Since the only number congruent to 365 mod 729 and less than 1,000 is 365, the correct answer is '''(C)'''.

see http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Wiki/index.php/2011_AMC_10A_Problems/Problem_23

Barbara doesn't say the numbers that end in 12 (XXXXXX12), since the numbers that are left after Alice speaks are cyclic, in the form XXXX02, XXXX12, XXXX22.

stem_md: Two distinct regular tetrahedra have all their vertices among the vertices of the same unit cube. What is the volume of the region formed by the intersection of the tetrahedra? $ \textbf{(A)}\ \frac{1}{12}\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{12}\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{12}\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ \frac{1}{6}\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{6} $
solution_md:
The two tetrahedra look somewhat like this.[[File:CubeAndStel.gif]] A regular unit tetrahedron can be split into eight tetrahedra that have lengths of $\frac{1}{2}$ . The volume of a regular tetrahedron can be found using base are and height: For a tetrahedron of side length 1, its base area is $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$ , and its height can be found using Pythagoras' Theorem. Its height is $\sqrt{1^2-\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\right)^2}=\frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt3}$ . Its volume is $\frac13\times\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\times\frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt3}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{12}$ . The tetrahedron actually has side length $\sqrt2$ , so the actual volume is $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{12}\times\sqrt2^3=\frac13$ . On the eight small tetrahedra, the four tetrahedra on the corners of the large tetrahedra are not inside the other large tetrahedra. Thus, $\frac{4}{8}=\frac{1}{2}$ of the large tetrahedra will not be inside the other large tetrahedra. The intersection of the two tetrahedra is thus $\frac12\times\frac13=\frac{1}{6}=\boxed{D}$ . see http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Wiki/index.php/2011_AMC_10A_Problems/Problem_24

stem_md: Let  $R$  be a square region and  $n\ge4$  an integer.  A point  $X$  in the interior of  $R$  is called  $n\text{-}ray$  partitional if there are  $n$  rays emanating from  $X$  that divide  $R$  into  $n$  triangles of equal area.  How many points are 100-ray partitional but not 60-ray partitional? $\textbf{(A)}\,1500 \qquad\textbf{(B)}\,1560 \qquad\textbf{(C)}\,2320 \qquad\textbf{(D)}\,2480 \qquad\textbf{(E)}\,2500$
solution_md:
We assume WLOG that the area of the square is  $1.$ Now, note that the problem states that the square must be divided into *triangles*. This means that rays must emanate from  $X$  to all four corners of the square, since otherwise, we would end up with one or more quadrilaterals. Now, we easily see that the four rays from  $X$  to the corners of the square divide the square into four triangles. If  $X$  is 100-ray partitional, it follows that each of these four triangles must be able to be divided into smaller triangles with area  $\frac{1}{100}.$  Equivalently, the area of each of these four *larger*triangles must be a multiple of  $\frac{1}{100}.$  
Now, let the length of the altitude from  $X$  to the bottom side of the square be  $h.$  It follows that the area of the bottom triangle is  $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(1\right)\left(h\right) = \frac{h}{2}$   $\quad$  by the one half base times height area formula. Similarly, the area of the top triangle is  $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(1\right)\left(1 - h\right) = \frac{1 - h}{2}.$ We need both of these areas to be a multiple of  $\frac{1}{100}.$  In other words, there must exist positive integers  $m, n$  such that \[\frac{m}{100} = \frac{h}{2}; \quad \frac{n}{100} = \frac{1 - h}{2}\]\[\iff m = 50h; \quad n = 50 - 50h.\] It is clear that these conditions are met iff  $h \le 1$  is a multiple of  $\frac{1}{50}$  and  $h \ne 0, 1.$  Therefore, all possible values of  $h$  are  $h = \frac{i}{50}$  where  $i \in \{1, 2, ..., 49\}.$  It follows that there are  $49$  possible values of  $h.$  
Similarly, if we let  $h'$  be the length of the altitude from  $X$  to the right side of the square, we see that there are  $49$  possible values of  $h'.$  Since the point  $X$  is uniquely determined by the two values  $h, h'$ , it follows that there are  $49^2$  points in the square that are 100-ray partional.
Now, we need to count how many of these points are also 60-ray partional.
If  $h$  denotes the length of the altitude from  $X$  to the bottom side, we see, by an identical argument as earlier, that  $X$  is 60-ray partitional iff  $h = \frac{i}{30}$  where  $i \in \{1, 2, ..., 29\}.$  It follows that for a point to be both 100-ray partitional and 60-ray partitional, there must exist positive integers  $k \in \{1, 2, ..., 29\}, l \in \{1, 2, ..., 49\}$ , such that \[\frac{k}{30} = \frac{l}{50} \iff \frac{k}{3} = \frac{l}{5}.\] We easily see, from the domains of  $k, l$ , that there are  $9$  such pairs  $(k, l)$  for which this equality holds. Therefore there are  $9$  possible lengths  $h$ , where  $h$  is the length of the altitude from a point  $X$  to the bottom side, such that  $X$  can be both 100-ray partitional and 60-ray partitional. 
Similarly, if we let  $h'$  be the length of the altitude from  $X$  to the right side of the square, we see that there are  $9$  possible values of  $h'$  for which  $X$  can be both 100-ray partitional and 60-ray partitional. It follows that there are  $9^2$  points  $X$  that are both 100-ray partitional and 60-ray partitional. 
Our final answer is then  $49^2 - 9^2 = \left(49 + 9\right)\left(49 - 9\right) = 58 \cdot 40 = \boxed{2320}$

Depending on the location of  $X$ , the number of rays distributed among these four triangular sectors will vary. We start by finding the corner-most point that is  $100$ -ray partitional (let this point be the bottom-left-most point). We first draw the four rays that intersect the vertices. At this point, the triangular sectors with bases as the sides of the square that the point is closest to both do not have rays dividing their areas. Therefore, their heights are equivalent since their areas are equal. The remaining  $96$  rays are divided among the other two triangular sectors, each sector with  $48$  rays, thus dividing these two sectors into  $49$  triangles of equal areas. Let the distance from this corner point to the closest side be  $a$  and the side of the square be  $s$ . From this, we get the equation  $\frac{a\times s}{2}=\frac{(s-a)\times s}{2}\times\frac1{49}$ . Solve for  $a$  to get  $a=\frac s{50}$ . Therefore, point  $X$  is  $\frac1{50}$  of the side length away from the two sides it is closest to. By moving  $X$   $\frac s{50}$  to the right, we also move one ray from the right sector to the left sector, which determines another  $100$ -ray partitional point. We can continue moving  $X$  right and up to derive the set of points that are  $100$ -ray partitional. In the end, we get a square grid of points each  $\frac s{50}$  apart from one another. To find the overlap from the  $60$ -ray partitional, we must find the distance from the corner-most  $60$ -ray partitional point to the sides closest to it. Since the  $100$ -ray partitional points form a  $49\times49$  grid, each point  $\frac s{50}$  apart from each other, we can deduce that the  $60$ -ray partitional points form a  $29\times29$  grid, each point  $\frac s{30}$  apart from each other. To find the overlap points, we must find the common divisors of  $30$  and  $50$  which are  $1, 2, 5,$  and  $10$ . The total overlapping set of points is a  $9\times9$  grid, which has  $81$  points. Subtract  $81$  from  $2401$  to get  $2401-81=\boxed{\textbf{(C)}\ 2320}$ .

solution_md:
Margie bought $3$ apples at a cost of $50$ cents each. She paid with a $5$ -dollar bill. How much change did Margie receive? $ \textbf{(A)}\$ 1.50\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ $2.00\qquad\textbf{(C)}\$ 2.50\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ $3.00\qquad\textbf{(E)}\$ 3.50 $

SolutionThere are $351$ adults in the town. $45$ of them own motorcycles. Therefore, $351-46=306$ people don't own motorcycles.
