*Proof:* Suppose we have a collision involving two ants which have only been walking on the lines up to now. Any ant which has only been walking along the lines is at a single-colored point at times  $k$  and a double-colored point at times  $k + \tfrac{1}{2}$  for integers  $k$ . So if we reverse to the last time that one of these two ants was on a gridpoint, the other ant must have been as well, and these gridpoints must have been either both single-colored or both double-colored on the same line. So then the ants meet at the midpoint of these two points, which is a double-colored or single-colored gridpoint respectively. Then since they meet at a gridpoint and turn  $90^\circ$ , they continue to be walking along the lines.

In particular, this means collisions can only occur at times  $\tfrac{k}{2}$  for integers  $k$ . So this means we can analyze the process only by looking at times  $\tfrac{k}{2}$  - at each such time, we draw an arrow from each ant in the direction it will be pointing right after that time (so after any collisions at that half-second have happened). Then the ant must walk in that direction for that half-second, which sends it to another gridpoint.

Call an ant outward-facing if it is strictly closer to the wall it is facing than the wall on the opposite side, and inward-facing otherwise. Also, we use the taxicab distance to mean the sum of the  $x$  and  $y$  distances. **Claim:** At time  $t$  (such that  $2t$  is an integer), all gridpoints with taxicab distance at most  $t$  from some corner cannot have any inward-facing ants (so they can only have outward-facing ants).

Now at time  $t$ , consider any gridpoint at distance at most  $t$  from some corner. Any gridpoint from which an inward-facing ant could have come there is distance at most  $t - \tfrac{1}{2}$  from a corner, and if it came to this gridpoint, then it would have been inward-facing at time  $t - \tfrac{1}{2}$ . So this is impossible, which means any ant that came to this corner is outward-facing before any collisions. But then no collisions can happen at that gridpoint, because we cannot have two ants facing in opposite directions meet at that point. So then any ant at that point will be outward-facing.

Now this means that at time  $\tfrac{2n - 1}{2}$ , all gridpoints except the center can only have outward-facing ants. Additionally, at this time no ants can be at the center (because the ant must be at a double-colored gridpoint, and the center is single-colored). Then no ants are facing each other, which will mean no more collisions can occur. Additionally, every ant is facing in a direction from which it is at most  $\tfrac{n - 1}{2}$  from the wall, so it can travel for at most  $\tfrac{n - 1}{2}$  more seconds. So then all ants must fall off the board by  $\tfrac{2n - 1}{2} + \tfrac{n - 1}{2} = \tfrac{3n - 2}{2}$  seconds.</details>

Then create a co-ordinate system, with the bottom left square of the board being  $(0,0)$ . We claim that if the game is at  $T_x$ , then if an ant is in square  $(a,b)$ ,
with  $a+b < x$ , then the ant is either pointing down or to the right. We will prove this by induction.

For the base case, note that the only way to get to the bottom left square after phase  $T_1$  is to move into it from the square immediately above it or the square immediately to the left of it. However, this means that no two ants can collide on this square moving in opposite directions, so if the ant moves onto this square in phase  $T_k$ , then in phase  $T_{k+1}$  it will have fallen off of the board, and so will not be moving in the opposite direction, establishing the base case.
For the step, note that if it is phase  $T_{a+b+1}$  or later there will not be an ant moving from a square to the right of or below  $(a,b)$  onto  $(a,b)$ . This means that if an ant moves onto this square, it will be from above or to the left, and since by the inductive hypothesis afterwards there will be no ant to collide with it to change its direction, as it would have had to be pointing either to the right or up, so it would have had to move in such a direction on the previous turn, which is impossible. 

Now, we will split into cases based on the parity of  $n$ .

stem_md:
Let  $n$  be a positive integer, and let  $W = \ldots x_{-1}x_0x_1x_2 \ldots$  be an infinite periodic word, consisting of just letters  $a$  and/or  $b$ . Suppose that the minimal period  $N$  of  $W$  is greater than  $2^n$ .

A finite nonempty word  $U$  is said to *appear* in  $W$  if there exist indices  $k \leq \ell$  such that  $U=x_k x_{k+1} \ldots x_{\ell}$ . A finite word  $U$  is called *ubiquitous* if the four words  $Ua$ ,  $Ub$ ,  $aU$ , and  $bU$  all appear in  $W$ . Prove that there are at least  $n$  ubiquitous finite nonempty words.

*Proposed by Grigory Chelnokov, Russia*
solution_md:
<details><summary>Hint</summary>Note that there is always a word of length  $n$  which appears twice in  $W$  ( $K$ , say). Use this to prove that there must be a word containing  $K$  which is ubiquitous.</details>
<details><summary>Badly written solution</summary>First, note that by the pigeonhole principle since there are  $N > 2^n$  strings of length  $k$  in  $W$  up to periodicity, since there are  $2^k$  different possible strings of length  $k$ , by the pigeonhole principle there exists a string of length  $k$  appearing in  $W$  at least  $2^{n-k} + 1$  times. Now, we claim that if a string appears twice (not in different periods), there exists a superset of that string which is ubiquitous.

Note that if a string  $K$  appears twice and is not ubiquitous, then either  $aK$ ,  $Ka$ ,  $bK$  or  $Kb$  appears twice. Therefore, we have two equal strings of a length one larger. Assuming that there is no superset of  $K$  which is ubiquitous, we can keep doing this process until we get two equal strings of length  $N$ . Note that these will overlap, so say that the string which they overlap on is  $Y$ , and the remaining string is  $X$ . Then we need that  $XY = YX$ . We claim that there exists a period  $V$  of  $Y$  such that  $X$  is periodic in  $V$ , implying that  $XY$  is periodic in  $V$ , a contradiction; we will prove this by induction. $Base$ :  $Y$  has length  $1$ .
This forces  $Y = a$  or  $Y = b$ , WLOG  $Y = a$ . Then note that  $aX = Xa$ , so  $X$  must both start and end in  $a$ . If  $X$  has length smaller than or equal to  $2$ , then we are done, as this forces that  $X$  contains only  $a$ , and so is periodic in  $a$ . Otherwise, let  $X = aZa$ . Then we need that  $aaZa = aZaa$ .
This implies that  $aZ = Za$ , so if we keep doing this we will eventually arrive at something with length  $2$  or less, so  $X$  is made up of only  $a$ s, as required. $Step$ :  $Y$  has length  $y$  (let  $X$  have length  $x$ )
Note that we need that the first  $y$  letters of  $X$  are  $Y$ , as otherwise  $XY$  wouldn't start with  $Y$  but  $YX$  would, which is impossible. Likewise, the last  $y$  letters of  $X$  must be  $Y$ . Now, if  $x \leq 2y$ , we have that either  $X = YY$ , so both  $X$  and  $Y$  are periodic in  $Y$ ,  or the two  $Y$ s overlap. If we let the overlap be  $Z$ , and the non-overlap be  $W$ , then we need that  $ZW = WZ$ . Therefore, by the inductive hypothesis (since  $ZW = Y$  both  $Z$  and  $W$  are shorter than  $Y$ ) there exists a  $w$  such that  $W$  is periodic in  $w$  and  $Z$  is periodic in  $w$ . Therefore,  $Y$  is periodic in  $w$ , and  $X$  is periodic in  $w$ , as required. On the other hand, if  $x > 2y$ , then we can let  $X = YZY$  as before, and then we need that  $YYZY = YZYY \implies YZ = ZY$ . We can keep doing this until eventually we get that  $X = Y...YCY...Y$ , where  $C$  has length shorter than  $2y$ . Hence, there exists a  $w$  such that  $Y$  and  $C$  are periodic in  $w$ , so  $X$  and  $Y$  are periodic in  $w$ , as required, completing the induction.

Now, let  $K$  have length  $k$ , and assume that  $E$  is the smallest superset of  $K$  which is ubiquitous, and that  $K$  appears at least  $2^{n-k}+1$  times. Then, note that if  $E$  has length larger than  $k+1$ , then for all  $K_i$  appearing in  $W$  (up to periodicity), either  $aK_i$ ,  $K_ia$ ,  $bK_i$  or  $K_ib$  appears in  $W$ , say that  $aK_i$  appears in  $W$  for all  $i$ . Then  $aK$  appears in  $W$   $2^{n-k}+1$  times. Therefore, we can keep doing this to get that if  $E$  has length  $e$ , then there are  $2^{n-k}+1$  equal subsets of  $E$  with  $e-1$  letters appearing in  $W$  (say that this subset is  $F$ ). Therefore, either there are  $2^{n-k-1} + 1$  appearances of  $aF$  in  $W$  or  $2^{n-k-1} + 1$  appearences of  $bF$  in  $W$ . Then, we can do the same thing to get a new ubiquitous word  $G$  with  $2^{n-k-1}+1$  equal subsets  $H$  with one less letter than  $H$ , and then keep doing this method until we get only two equal strings, in which case we do the method one last time to get one more ubiquitous word. If we start this at  $k=0$ , then this method will generate  $n$  ubiquitous words, as required (we go up to  $k = n-1$ , and get a new ubiquitous word for each  $k$ , but there are  $n$   $k$ s in total, as required).</details>

Combining these two claims, note that in  $\{s_i\}$ , we must have at least  $\left\lceil\log_2\left(\frac{n_0}{n_k}\right)\right\rceil\ge n$  ubiquitous words, as desired.

Here is one important observation. Let  $T$  be the period of  $W$ . Suppose  $X_iX_{i+1}\cdots X_{i+d} = X_jX_{j+1}\cdots X_{j+d}$ , and this word is NOT ubitquitous. Say it always has a prefix a, then we add  $a$  to it, and consider that string instead. Eventually, we can form a ubiquitous string.

Now, the  $2^n$  suggests a divide and conquer algorithm, so here is a solution.

WLOG, there are more than  $2^{n-1}$  a's in the period. Call this number  $A$ . Obviously  $a$  is an ubiquitous string. We consider this algorithm to construct  $c_i$  from  $c_{i-1}$  where  $c_i$  are strings with  $c_1=1$ .

Append a prefix to our current string. 

Case 1: Preceding all occurences of  $c_i$ , there is all a (or all b). Then we simply add this letter to the left of our current string  $c_i$ .

Case 2: Preceding occurences of  $c_i$ , some start with  $a$ , and some start with  $b$ . Take the one with more letters. By pigeonhole, there are more than  $2^{n-i}$  of them. If suffixes turn out to be a problem, i.e. they all end with the same letter, I can append that letter until that is no longer a problem. If this goes on long enough, we can also conclude our string is periodic.

This indeed produces  $\lceil \log_2(A) \rceil$  ubiquitous substrings.

Example: N=aabaabab

Our string is aabaabaabab|aabaabab...

First of all, a work. Let  $c_1=a$ .

There are 3 occurences of  $ba$  and 2 occurrences of  $aa$  (we can see  $X_1=X_2=X_4=X_5=X_7=a, X_3=X_6=X_8=b$  here,  $X_{8+i}=X_i$ , and this counts  $1\le i\le 8$  as our leftmost character of the string), so we take ba.

There are 3 occurrences of  $aba$ . Do nothing

There are 2 occurences of  $aaba$  and one occurence of  $baba$ , so  $aba$  is ubiquitous.

If there happens to all stop in case 1 before there is one occurence of something, then  $X_i=X_j \rightarrow X_{i-1}=X_{j-1} \rightarrow \cdots$ , we can easily see that there is a smaller period.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Without loss of generality, suppose  $x_1x_2\ldots x_N$  contains at least as many  $a$ 's as  $b$ 's. Initially, let  $S$  be the set of indices  $1 \leq i \leq N$  for which  $x_i = a$ , so  $|S| > 2^{n - 1}$ . 

At each step, suppose  $|S| \geq 2$ , and we have some  $k$ ,  $\ell \geq 0$  such that  $x_{i - k}\ldots x_{i + \ell}$  is the same word for all  $i \in S$ . (At the start,  $k$  and  $\ell$  are  $0$ , and this common word is  $a$ .) Then let  $m$  be the smallest positive integer such that  $x_{i - m}$  is not the same for all  $i \in S$  (in particular  $m > k$ ) -- this must exist because otherwise the word would be periodic with period dividing the difference of two elements of  $S$ . Similarly, let  $n$  be the smallest positive integer such that  $x_{i + n}$  is not the same for all  $i \in S$  (so  $n > \ell$ ). 

Then  $x_{i - m + 1}\ldots x_{i + n - 1}$  is the same word for all  $i \in S$ , and over all  $i \in S$ ,  $x_{i - m}$  takes on both  $a$  and  $b$ , as does  $x_{i + n}$ . So the word  $x_{i - m + 1}\ldots x_{i + n - 1}$  is ubiquitous. 

Now consider the more common value of  $x_{i - m}$  over all  $i \in S$ . Let  $k = m$ ,  $\ell = n - 1$ , and restrict  $S$  to only the indices  $i$  with  $x_{i - m}$  equal to the more common value. Repeat this process until we end up with  $|S| = 1$ . 

Then each step gives us an ubiquitous word -- and these words must be distinct, since their length is strictly increasing. But each step multiplies  $|S|$  by at least  $\tfrac{1}{2}$ . So since  $|S| > 2^{n - 1}$  at the start, we can perform at least  $n$  steps before it reaches  $1$ , giving us at least  $n$  ubiquitous words.</details>

If we have a word  $w$  that works and occurs more than  $k$  times in any minimal period, we can have a word  $w'$  that works and occurs more than  $\frac{k}{2}$  times in any minimal period, for any  $k > 2.$  

By Pigeonhole more than  $\frac{k}{2}$  of the  $w$ -words are preceded by a common letter, say an  $a.$  Append this to  $w.$  Extend this new word in both directions until we find differing characters in the preceding and following positions. This exists since there occur multiple instances of our word within each period, but there is not a smaller period.

One of  $a$  or  $b$  occurs more than  $2^{n-1}$  times in each minimal period and works, so we're done.

Let  $x_1x_2 \cdots x_p$  be the repeating part of the word  $W$ , with  $p > 2^n$ . Define the *value* of a word  $X = w_1w_2 \cdots w_k$  (denoted by  $f(X)$ ) as the number of  $i$  with  $1 \le i \le p$  such that  $w_i w_{i+1} \cdots w_{i+k-1}$  coincides with  $X$ . Note that since this is succeeded by an  $a$  or a  $b$  in all occurences, we have  $f(Xa) + f(Xb) = f(X)$ . 

Suppose  $U$  is a ubiquitous word with  $f(U) = m \geqslant 2$ . Construct two binary trees from  $U$ , one going forward, where  $X$  points to  $Xa$  and  $Xb$  and one going backward, with  $X$  pointing backward to  $aX$  and  $bX$ . Move forward on the tree until we have a word  $X$  such that  $f(Xa), f(Xb) > 0$ . Similarly move backward until we have a word  $Y$  such that  $f(aY), f(bY) > 0$ . Such a point must exist since otherwise we get a word of length  $> p$  which has value at least  $2$ , which would contradict the fact that  $p$  was its minimal period. 

Now, the new word  $YUX$  is ubiquitous too. Note that if each time, we go along the branch with higher value, we can ensure that he new word satisfies that  $f(YUX) \geqslant \frac{m}{2}$ . To finish, see that one of  $a,b$  whichever appears more times, must be ubiquitous. Since such a word must appear  $> 2^{n-1}$  times and each time,  $f(U)$  at most halves, we can ensure that by this procedure, we obtain at least  $n$  ubiquitous finite nonempty words, as desired.  $\blacksquare$

When we refer to *words*, we consider two such words to be the same as long as the characters in the words are the same. When we refer to *substrings*, we only consider them to be the same if their positions differ by a multiple of the period of  $W$ .

For a set  $S$  of substrings, let the *shared ancestor* of  $S$  be the longest word that appears right before every substring in  $S$ ; let the *shared successor* be the longest word that appears right after every substring in  $S$ . These could possibly be empty. As long as  $S$  contains at least two distinct substrings, the shared ancestor/successor *must* be finite, due to the period conditon of  $W$ .**Claim:** If a ubiquitous word  $w$  appears  $k \geq 2$  times in  $W$ , there is a longer word  $w'$  (in fact, containing  $w$ ) which appears at least  $\lceil \tfrac{k}{2} \rceil$  times in  $W$ .**Proof:** WLOG assume at least half of the instances of  $w$  are followed by the letter  $a$ . Let  $S$  be this set of substrings. We can add the shared ancestor and shared successor to the front and back of each substring in  $S$ , extending each substring by at least one character (since the shared successor contains at least an  $a$ ). The word formed by this new extension is ubiquitous (since shared ancestors and successors are maximal).

Clearly, at least one of the words  $a$  or  $b$  is ubiquitous and appears  $2^{n-1}+1$  times, so we are done by the claim.

stem_md:
On a square table of  $2011$  by  $2011$  cells we place a finite number of napkins that each cover a square of  $52$  by  $52$  cells. In each cell we write the number of napkins covering it, and we record the maximal number  $k$  of cells that all contain the same nonzero number. Considering all possible napkin configurations, what is the largest value of  $k$ ?

*Proposed by Ilya Bogdanov and Rustem Zhenodarov, Russia*
solution_md:
The answer is a flashy
\[ \boxed{2011^2 - [(17 \cdot 157) + 37 \cdot (52^2-35^2)] = 3986729} \]
Another (more illuminating) way to say this is
\[ \boxed{2011^2 - [39 \cdot 2 \cdot (17 \cdot 35) + 38 \cdot 17^2]} \]
However, the nicest way I've found to showcase the answer is
\[ \boxed{1994^2 + 37 \cdot (17^2)} \]
as this shows the improvement from the unoptimized  $1994^2$ , a  $k$  one may have come up first.

<details><summary>A trashy description of the config.</summary>Divide the  $2011 \times 2011$  grid into  $39$   $\textbf{layers}$ : name the top-left  $35 \times 35$  grid the first layer, and for each  $2 \leq i \leq 39$ , name the top-left
\[ (52i-17) \times (52i-17) \]
grid, minus the union of all the previous layers to be the  $i^{\text{th}}$  layer. 

Next, on the first layer, place a napkin exactly on the top-left  $52 \times 52$  grid. 

On the subsequent layers, place  $i-1$  napkins filling the  $\textit{vertical}$  part of the layer (so they cover  $52(i-1)$  rows in some  $52$  consecutive columns, in each respective layer); place  $i-1$  napkins analogously for the  $\textit{horizontal}$  part of the layer, and put one napkin on the bottom-right of the layer. 

(This is just a reflection of the official config with respect to the  $x$ -axis.)

Then, count the squares covered by exactly one napkin.</details>
The major illusion in this problem is the existence of  $2011$  and  $52$  --- I didn't realize their significance and function(s) until 3-4 hours in. 

<details><summary>What the problem hides from you. BIG SPOILER!</summary>We will extensively use the fact that 
\[ 2011 \equiv 35 \pmod{52} \]
and
\[ \text{If} \ 35 = c, 52-35 = 17 = m \Rightarrow c > 2m \]

The problem would've swung a different way if this identity isn't true.</details>
--------
First we introduce some relatively basic notations. Let the cells that contain the same nonzero number is covered by  $A$  napkins. We alter  $k$ 's definition to be  $52$  and  $n$  to be  $2011$ . We also differentiate between  $\textbf{compliant}$ ,  $\textbf{positive}$  and  $\textbf{negative}$  cells; compliant if it is covered by  $A$  napkins, and positive/negative if its number is strictly more/less than  $A$ . 

Also, name the rows/columns to be  $r_i,c_j$ , with  $r_1$  to  $r_{2011}$  sorted from top-to-bottom and  $c_1$  to  $c_{2011}$  from left-to-right. (Too lazy to follow standard Cartesian Coordinates, sorry for that)

Our main ingredient in proving the bound will not be  $\textbf{entire napkins}$ ; but the relative covering of the napkins  $\textbf{projected}$  into each row  $\textbf{and}$  column.  $\color{yellow} \rule{7.5cm}{2pt}$   $\color{magenta} \clubsuit$   $ \boxed{\textbf{The Convoluted Grouping of Strips.}}$   $\color{magenta} \clubsuit$   $\color{yellow} \rule{7.5cm}{2pt}$  
Following the configuration mentioned above (we omit the definitons of the layers and opt for a clearer one), define  $c = 35$  and  $m = 17$  ( $c$  stands for corner,  $m$  stands for middle). 

In each row (and column), call the first  $c$  cells to be corner cells, next  $m$  to be middle cells, next  $c$  to be corner cells, and et cetera, until we have  $39$  sets of corner cells and  $38$  of middles. 

We Claim that each row (and column) to have either  $m$  positive cells among its (set of) middle cells, or  $c$  negative cells among its (set of) corner cells.    $\color{green} \rule{25cm}{0.2pt}$   $\color{green} \spadesuit$   $\boxed{\textbf{Proof.}}$   $\color{green} \spadesuit$  

<details><summary>Unused Main Idea, which helps see the point clearer.</summary>This is actually much easier proven than conjured: call an  $\textit{index}$   $i$  ( $1 \leq i \leq 52$ )  $\color{green} \textbf{\textit{tarnished}}$  with respect to a row if not all cells having position  $i \pmod{52}$  are compliant. 

Observe that we cannot have un-tarnished indexes  $i$  and  $j$  so that  $1 \leq i \leq 35$  and  $36 \leq j \leq 52$ . This is because if it is so, there are both  $39A$  and  $38A$  napkins covering that row --- since each napkin covers one cell of each index. 
(And there are  $39$  cells congruent  $i \pmod{52}$ , and  $38$  cells congruent  $j \pmod{52}$ ) 

This means that somehow all-indices  $i$  or all-indices  $j$  are tarnished --- and we can use ineq-summing to infer the positivity/negativity of the aforementioned tarnished cells.</details>

If each index  $36 \leq j \leq 52$  has a positive cell with position  $j \pmod{52}$ , there are at least  $17$  positive cells. Otherwise, there is an index  $j$  where all its  $38$  cells having a number of at most  $A$ . In turn, there are at most  $38A$  napkins covering that row, and so all  $39$  cells from each index  $i, 1 \leq i \leq 35$  cannot all be compliant or positive. 

So, there are at least one negative cell from each index, implying the result.  $\blacksquare$  
-------- $\color{blue} \rule{5.2cm}{2pt}$   $\color{blue} \clubsuit$   $\color{blue} \boxed{\textbf{Computing in Regions.}}$   $\color{blue} \clubsuit$   $\color{blue} \rule{5.2cm}{2pt}$  
Here we prove that the total number of noncompliant cells is at least
\[ 39 \cdot 2 \cdot (17 \cdot 35) + 38 \cdot 17^2 \]
a.k.a. the number being substracted in the answer's second form. 

We take this a bit further: define a cell to be type  $CC,CM,MC$  or  $MM$  if it belongs to a  $c$ -row and  $c$ -column, and so on. Define  $P_X$  and  $N_X$  where 
\[ X \in \{CC,CM,MC,MM\} \]
to be the set of positive and negative cells in type- $X$  cells. We prove that
\[ |P_{MM}| +   |P_{MC}| + |N_{MC}| + |P_{CM}| + |N_{CM}| + |N_{CC}| \]
is at least the number mentioned earlier.  $\blacksquare$   $\blacksquare$  
-------- $\color{blue} \spadesuit$   $\color{blue} \boxed{\textbf{Proof.}}$   $\color{blue}\spadesuit$  
The computation is also easier than it may seem (on the first official Shortlist Solution, or at the post above.) Variable Spam Incoming! 

Call the rows having  $m$  positive cells among its middle cells to be a  $\textit{positive-centered}$  row, and rows having  $c$  negative cells among its corner cells to be a  $\textit{negatively-cornered}$  row. Also, call a row to be a  $\textit{middle}$  or  $\textit{corner}$  row by a similar procedure (to its cell counterpart).

First, we bound the sum of the  $\color{blue} \text{first, third and fifth term}$ . Let there are  $a_m,b_m$  positive-centered rows and columns among the middle rows and columns, respectively. So, there are at least  $38m-a_m$  and  $38m-b_m$  negative-corned rows and columns (among the same rows/columns). 

By easy position-tracking we get that all the  $m$  positive cells/ $c$  negative cells obtained from  $\color{magenta} \clubsuit$   $ \boxed{\textbf{The Convoluted Grouping of Strips}}$   $\color{magenta} \clubsuit$  must lie on  $P_{MM}$  or  $N_{MC} \cup N_{CM}$ . Moreover, each positive cell in  $P_{MM}$  may be counted twice (a.k.a. belonging to some positive-centered row and column, simultaneously) while each negative cell in the latter union-set may only contribute once. 

Summing, their total cardinality must be at least
\[ \dfrac{m \cdot a_m + m \cdot b_m}{2} + c \cdot (38m-a_m) + c \cdot (38m-b_m)  \]
which attains minimality if  $a_m, b_m$  maximum (they equalling  $38m$ ); as  $-c + \dfrac{m}{2} \leq 0$ . 

The same reasoning can be applied to bound the total of the  $\color{blue} \text{second, fourth and sixth}$  term. Letting  $a_c$  and  $b_c$  as the counterparts of  $a_m,b_m$ , we get that their sum is at least
\[ \dfrac{c \cdot (39c-a_c) + c \cdot (39c-b_c)}{2} + m \cdot a_c + m \cdot b_c \]
which attains minimality if  $a_c,b_c$  maximum; as  $-\dfrac{c}{2}+m \leq 0$ . 

When these all are satisfied, the sum of  $\color{blue} \text{all six terms}$  is
\[ m \cdot 38m + 2 \cdot c \cdot (0) + c \cdot 0 + 2 \cdot m \cdot 39c \]
as claimed. We are done.  $\blacksquare$   $\blacksquare$   $\blacksquare$  
--------

<details><summary>Motivation: Clever Region-Counting and Role-Assigning.</summary>If it's not apparent by now, I'll be using left-to-right and up-to-down coordinates. I'll also be replacing  $2011$  and  $52$  with  $n$  and  $k$ , and I'll identify a  $k \times k$   $\textit{napkin}$  by the coordinate of its upper left corner. 

For example, when  $n = 4$ , a  $3 \times 3$  napkin covering  $r_1,r_2,r_3$  and  $c_2,c_3,c_4$  will synonymously be called a  $(1,0)$  napkin (with its identity being 1 unit to the right and 0 unit below the  $\textit{origin}$ .)  $\color{green} \rule{25cm}{2pt}$   $\color{red} \text{Sec 1: Lower Configs.}$  When  $(n,k) = (3,2)$ , it may be tempting to call out that the maxima occurs when placing four napkins of different identities. This is not the case, as two napkins  $(0,0)$  and  $(1,1)$  will yield six compliant squares. This is also (obviously) true when  $(n,k) = (4,3)$  yielding ten compliant squares, but I wasn't so sure about  $(n,k) = (5,3)$ . 

While I was searching for how to surely prove the existence of a noncompliant square for each row of  $(n,k) = (5,3)$ , I also wondered how to construct the config for  $(n,k) = (2011,52)$ . Emulating the obvious nonintersecting placement when  $k \mid n$ , I noted that
\[ 52 \mid 2011-35 \]
and I knew that sooner or later, the numbers  $35$  and  $52-35 = 17$  would appear a lot. The easiest options would be to simply place  $38^2$  nonintersecting napkins, but we could easily do better by placing  $39^2$  napkins covering  $\textbf{the final layer}$  of squares of width  $35$  to yield a config with
\[ 1996^2 \ \text{compliant squares} \]
as  $2011-38 \cdot 52 = 35$  and  $39 \cdot 52 - 2011 = 17$ ; and  $35 > 17$ . 

Still going off with  $k = 3$ , for  $n = 8$  and  $n = 7$  I could  $\text{try the easy way out}$  and single out 3 corner rows and columns  and use the config for  $n-3$  to cover the rest. This yields a relatively beautiful config of 
\[ \text{napkins of identity} \ (4,0); (4,3); (0,4); (3,4) \]
and either  $(0,0); (1,1)$  or  $(0,1); (1,0)$  to yield an almost symmetric config. Doing this for  $n = 8$  begs the question: why does there seem to exist multiple configs producing sixteen compliant squares? (A non-obvious example would be  $(0,0); (2,0); (2,2)$  or  $(0,0); (0,2); (2,1)$ .) 

Since this is a question which has no clear answer for me, I turned to solving  $k = 4$  (and supposing that the problem is easy for  $n = 2k-1$ ) and  $n = 7$ , but the existence of a big  $3 \times 3$  square at the two corners bothered me. Putting this aside for a bit, I was sure that an easy config exists for  $k = 2$ . Here, for size reasons I picked  $n$  much larger than  $2$  ---  $n = 7$  was my first choice.

Indeed, I marked the  $3 \times 3$  squares with identity
\[ (0,0); (2,2); (4,4) \]
I noted that I could copy the config of  $(n,k) = (7,3)$  with three layers instead of two. Namely, I could make six compliant squares out of 8-9 for each  $3 \times 3$  box, and fill out the rest evenly. This config's maximality is easy to verify, since there is exactly one noncompliant square in each row; and it's easy to prove that there must exist one for each row. 

Next came the idea of making  $38$   $(35+17+35) \times (35+17+35)$  squares and fill out each of them with two  $52 \times 52$ ; and this makes for a better constant than  $1994^2$ !  $\color{cyan} \rule{25cm}{2pt}$   $\color{blue} \text{Sec 1.1: Optimizing A Little More.}$  Not much happened here --- I considered what happens to a particular napkin config's corners. I made a mental note to always let  $A$  (the number in each compliant square) to be  $1$ ; as if we factor in the corners, they can only be covered by napkins of one type --- and it's reasonable to expect that the centers needed to adapt to the corners, not vice versa. 

Next was the crucial doubting of a  $35^2$  noncompliant block in the corners. If there isn't a surefire way to make out  $35$  squares from a lot of rows (which there isn't, but we can indeed guarantee 35 minuses if the row is not positive ... but this is also a complicated and loaded condition) then what's holding us to make  $17$  appear more often? 

Here I tried to separate the  $\textit{tarnished}$  cells, as I still thought of this as a coloring problem, akin to the second (and harder) official Solution. Conveniently, positively-tarnished cells are usually better placed in the middle cells; but to make a bundle of the positive cells turn into compliant cells, I would need their neighbors to make some sort of sacrifice. 

Finally, it came to me that  $35 > 2 \cdot 17$ ; and I could replace the large  $35 \times 35$  block by two  $17 \times 35$ ; but this process is not a clean one: the  $35 \times 35$  area with identity  $(35,35)$  can protrude to its up-left or down-right; it may even go two other ways (even if they don't produce optimal results.) 

<details><summary>Skippable Notes.</summary>$\rule{25cm}{2pt}$   $\color{magenta} \text{Detour: The Garden of Dreams.}$  Since the case  $(n,k) = (2011,52)$  was very overwhelming (and I also didn't see how I could make that appear with inequalities), I knew that I had to answer the question for simpler  $(n,k)$  first before being sure to tackle  $\textbf{general and extended}$  cases. 

First, I acknowledged how  $k$  relates to  $n$  is central to the answer. For example, both the cases
\[ (n,k) = (7,4) \ \text{and} (5,3) \]
are very distinct --- it seems that  $(7,4)$  has only the config with four napkins; but  $(5,3)$  has a variety of them. Possibly, this is because the center-of-impact has different sizes in them. While both has a  $MM$  area of  $1 \times 1$ , the  $MC$  and  $CC$  area are significantly bigger in  $(7,4)$  --- bringing a larger incentive to push more squares towards the corner cells. 

While this observation doesn't bring much help, I was able to isolate the four regions with each other. That so, when  $(n,k) = (8,3)$ , I made the pathway rows and colums 
\[ r_3,r_6,c_3,c_6 \]
disappear completely, and made it so that their existence is secondary to the larger  $6 \times 6$  body remaining. I think this is the closest I've gotten to Solution 2 --- but I missed the important part of categorizing all cells into  $c_{vv}$  and removing  $\textbf{all}$  vicious cells, instead of independently considering positives/negatives. 

For example, considering the artificially made  $6 \times 6$  earlier, I made a  $\textit{Town Plaza grid}$  with 9 blocks of  $2 \times 2$  buildings surrounded by a fence, and the remaining cells colored differently as pathways. 

Here, even if I only considered the  $3 \times 3$  which cover one  $2 \times 2$  block (saying nothing about the napkins with identity  $(1,0)$ , for example), I noted the difficulty of determining whether an individual block is compliant or not. 

You can try this with the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, seventh, eighth block completely covered (for example) --- where the paveway squares heavily depends on their neighbors' fences (on whether they choose to extend towards that particular pavement.) Here the  $2 \times 2$  block with identity  $(0,3)$  functions as the fourth block, and  $(6,3)$  as the sixth block. 

(Too lazy to draw tikz here)</details> $\color{green} \rule{25cm}{2pt}$   $\color{red} \text{Sec 2: Actually Pure Algebra.}$  Aside from considering two-dimensional neighbors and individual inclusions (as in the  $\color{magenta} \text{Detour}$ ) I realized that the config just relies mostly on the rows  $\textbf{having squares}$  from  $MM$  having seventeen plusses in the  $37m$  center cells. While they could (and oftentimes, must) have positives on  $CM$  and  $MC$ , that's a problem for later. 

This approach brought me more confidence, as in the case of  $3 \times 7$  grid (the only time I'll consider something different from  $n \times n$ ), we could place  $2 \times 2$  napkins on
\[ (0,0); (0,1); (2,0); (2,1); (4,0); (4,1); (5,0) \]
and note that for  $c_1$  up to  $c_4$ , they all have one positive cell (in the middle) and  $c_5$  to  $c_7$  only having four. One of the four lies in  $MM$ , two tanking a positive from  $r_1$  and  $c_5$ , and the remaining taking a negative from  $r_3$  and  $c_7$ . 

Not only does this made me consider that the bound is tighter than what I envisioned, but this can be reached by  $\textsf{simply double-counting the right way.}$  

By this, I was almost stumbling on the correct idea --- but there is still one pickle: what  $\textbf{really}$  happens on regions  $CM$  and  $MC$ ? 

While it's true that the  $c$ -columns are at a loss if one of them are a negative row (meaning they would require a support of  $35$  negatives in  $CC$ , each of which has value  $\frac{1}{2}$   --- or one strawberry, in the words of the first official Solution) a non-positive  $m$ -column may contribute compliant cells to  $CM$ .

The answer is  $2011^2 - 39 \cdot (35 \cdot 34) - 38 \cdot 17^2$ . Call the number that appears most frequently in the grid  $N$ . In each cell with a number less than  $N$  we write a minus, and in each cell with a number greater than  $N$  we write a plus. Let  $S$  be the number of cells with a plus or minus; we wish to show that  $S \geq 39 \cdot (35 \cdot 34) + 38 \cdot 17^2$ .

We first consider an individual row or column of the table, which is effectively the same as a  $1 \times 2011$  table having napkins of size  $1 \times 52$ . Notice that  $2011 = 39 \cdot 35 + 38 \cdot 17$ . Number the squares of the table  $0, 1, 2, \ldots, 2010$ , and consider each number's remainder when divided by 52. There are 39 squares for each remainder  $0$  to  $34$ ; color these white. Similarly there are 38 for each remainder  $35$  to  $51$ ; color these black. Each napkin covers exactly one square with each residue. Then if there are less than  $39N$  napkins, there are at least 35 white squares with a minus; call such a row *deficient*. Similarly if there are more than  $38N$  napkins, there are at least 17 black squares with a plus; call such a row or column *dense*. Clearly each row or column is either deficient or dense, possibly both.

In the original table, color all squares white which are white for both the row and column, and likewise black for those which are black for both the row and column. If a square is white for the row and black for the column, color it red, and color the remaining squares blue. Thus, each row either has red and white squares or blue and black squares. Likewise, each column has blue and white squares or red and black squares.

Let  $A$  be the number of rows with white squares; note there are also  $A$  such columns and that  $A = 39 \cdot 35$ . Define  $B = 2011 - A$ , the number of rows (or columns) with black squares. Consider all deficient rows or columns containing white squares, and suppose there are  $a$  such rows and  $b$  such columns. WLOG  $a \geq b$ . Then there are at least  $35a$  minuses in the white squares. The other  $A - a$  rows with white squares are dense, so they have at least 17 plusses in red squares. Similarly the other  $A - b$  columns are dense, with at least 17 plusses in blue squares. Finally, consider the  $B$  columns with black squares. Each has either 35 minuses in red squares or 17 plusses in red squares, neither of which we have counted yet. So there are at least 17 marked squares in each of these columns. Summing all of this up,
\[ S \geq 35a + 17(A - a) + 17(A - b) + 17B = 18a - 17b + 17 (2A + B) \geq 17(2A+B). \]
The last inequality follows from  $a \geq b \geq 0$ . It can be checked that  $17(2A+B)$  is equal to the bound we need, so we are done.

Let  $ABC$  be an acute triangle. Let  $\omega$  be a circle whose centre  $L$  lies on the side  $BC$ . Suppose that  $\omega$  is tangent to  $AB$  at  $B'$  and  $AC$  at  $C'$ . Suppose also that the circumcentre  $O$  of triangle  $ABC$  lies on the shorter arc  $B'C'$  of  $\omega$ . Prove that the circumcircle of  $ABC$  and  $\omega$  meet at two points.

*Proposed by Härmel Nestra, Estonia*
solution_md:
I liked this a lot! Few years ago, I bashed it out to get a nasty inequality which somehow worked. I will post a synthetic solution now :

Let  $D$  be the midpoint of  $BC$  and  $R$  be the circumradius of  $\triangle ABC$ . Note that  $AL$  bisects angle  $BAC$  and  $O$  lies inside  $\triangle ABC$  so   $$ \angle B'OC'>\angle BOC \Longrightarrow 90^{\circ}+\frac{A}{2}>2A \Longrightarrow A<60^{\circ}. $$   Extend ray  $OL$  beyond  $L$  to meet the circumcircle  $\gamma$  of  $\triangle ABC$  at  $X$ . Evidently,   $$ OL \ge OD=R\cos A>\frac{R}{2} \Longrightarrow OL>LX, $$   so  $\omega$  contains point both in the interior and the exterior of  $\gamma$ . It follows that  $\omega$  and  $\gamma$  have two points in common.  $\square$

Let $A_1A_2A_3A_4$ be a non-cyclic quadrilateral. Let $O_1$ and $r_1$ be the circumcentre and the circumradius of the triangle $A_2A_3A_4$ . Define $O_2,O_3,O_4$ and $r_2,r_3,r_4$ in a similar way. Prove that \[\frac{1}{O_1A_1^2-r_1^2}+\frac{1}{O_2A_2^2-r_2^2}+\frac{1}{O_3A_3^2-r_3^2}+\frac{1}{O_4A_4^2-r_4^2}=0.\] *Proposed by Alexey Gladkich, Israel*
Consider the following result.**Claim:** Let $ABC$ be a triangle and $\ell$ be a line. Point $P$ varies uniformly over line $\ell$ , say, at distance $p \in \mathbb{R}$ from a fixed point; then the power of point $A$ in circle $(BPC)$ is given by a rational function $\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ in $p$ with $\text{deg} \, f \le 2$ and $\text{deg} \, g \le 1$ . (Proof) Notice that the equation of $(BPC)$ is $$ ux(x+y+z)-a^2yz-b^2zx-c^2xy=0. $$ Plug $A=(1,0,0)$ to see that it has power equal to $u$ . Plug $P=(x', y', z')$ to see that $u$ has the desired form since $x', y', z'$ are linear functions of $p$ with $x'+y'+z'=1$ . $\blacksquare$ Fix $\triangle A_1A_2A_3$ and vary $A_4$ uniformly along a fixed line $\ell$ intersecting $(A_1A_2A_3)$ twice, with parameter $z$ . Consider $$ \frac{f_i(z)}{g_i(z)} \overset{\text{def}}{:=} O_iA_i^2-R_i^2, $$ for all $i$ ; then we wish to show that $$ \sum_{1 \le i \le 4} \frac{g_i(z)}{f_i(z)}=0. $$ Here, $g$ 's are linear (or constant) and $f$ 's are quadratic (or lower degree). Notice that when $A_4$ is on $(A_1A_2A_3)$ , all these rational functions vanish. Consequently, there exists a quadratic polynomial $h(z)$ which is a factor of $f_i(z)$ for all $1 \le i \le 4$ . Hence, the desired equation is a linear equation in $z$ . Notice that $\ell$ intersects at least two of the sides of $\triangle A_1A_2A_3$ . For $A_4$ on line $A_2A_3$ , we see that $$ \sum_{i} \frac{1}{O_iA_i^2-R_i^2}=\frac{1}{\overline{A_2A_4} \cdot \overline{A_2A_3}}+\frac{1}{\overline{A_3A_4} \cdot \overline{A_3A_2}}+\frac{1}{\overline{A_4A_2} \cdot \overline{A_4A_3}}, $$ which is clearly zero. Hence, for all points on a line $\ell$ meeting $(A_1A_2A_3)$ twice, the result is true. It is clear now that it is true for every point $A_4$ on the plane. $\blacksquare$

Plugging in  $A_1$  gives  $u=-\frac{C}{m}$ .Then, the power of  $A_2$  wrt  $(A_1A_3A_4)$  is simply  $u=-\frac{C}{m}$ Similarly, the equation of  $(A_1A_2A_4)$  is  $C+(x+y+z)(-\frac{C}{n}x)=0$ , so the power of  $A_3$  wrt that circle is  $-\frac{C}{n}$ . The equation of  $(A_1A_2A_3)$  is  $C+(x+y+z)(-\frac{C}{p}x)=0$ , so the power of  $A_4$  wrt that circle is  $-\frac{C}{p}$ . The sum reduces to:  $$ \frac{1}{C}-\frac{m}{C}-\frac{n}{C}-\frac{p}{C}=\frac{1-(m+n+p)}{C}=0 $$  as required.

Let  $A$  be the intersection of the diagonals of  $A_1A_2A_3A_4$ , and let  $a_i$  be the distance  $AA_i$  for  $1\le i\le 4$ . We will only compute  $\frac{1}{A_1O_1^2-r_1^2}$ , as the other three fractions will simply be cyclic expressions. Notice that the expression  $O_1A_1^2-r^2$  simply denotes the power of  $A_1$  with respect to circle  $O_1$ . Therefore, if we let  $B$  be the second intersection of circle  $O_1$  with line  $A_1A_3$ , then we have  $O_1A_1^2-r_1^2=A_1B\cdot A_1A_3$ . Notice that  $AB\cdot a_3=a_2\cdot a_4 \Rightarrow AB=\frac{a_2a_4}{a_3}$  by power of a point, so  $A_1B=A_1A-AB=a_1-\frac{a_2a_4}{a_3}$ . Since  $A_1A_3=a_1+a_3$ , we get that   $$ O_1A_1^2-r_1^2=(a_1+a_3)\left(a_1-\frac{a_2a_4}{a_3}\right) \Rightarrow \frac{1}{A_1O_1^2-r_1^2}=\frac{1}{(a_1+a_3)\left(a_1-\frac{a_2a_4}{a_3}\right)}=\frac{a_3}{(a_1+a_3)(a_1a_3-a_2a_4)}. $$  Similarly,   $$ \frac{1}{A_3O_3^2-r_3^2}=\frac{a_1}{(a_1+a_3)(a_1a_3-a_2a_4)}. $$   Therefore, adding these two together cancels out the  $a_1+a_3$  term in the denominator and gives  $\frac{1}{a_1a_3-a_2a_4}$ . Similarly,   $$ \frac{1}{A_2O_2^2-r_2^2}+\frac{1}{A_4O_4^2-r_4^2}=\frac{1}{a_2a_4-a_1a_3}. $$   Since these expressions are negations of each other, they sum to zero, and we are done.

Let  $B=\overline{A_1A_3}\cap\overline{A_2A_4},$   $C=\overline{A_1A_3}\cap(A_2A_3A_4),$  and  $x_i=BA_i.$  By PoP,  $A_2B\cdot BA_4=CB\cdot BA_3$  so   $$ A_1C=A_1C-CB=A_1B-\frac{A_2B\cdot BA_4}{BA_3}=\frac{x_1x_3-x_2x_4}{x_3}. $$   Thus, \begin{align*}O_1A_1^2-r_1^2&=A_1C\cdot A_1A_3=A_1C\cdot(x_1+x_3)=\frac{(x_1+x_3)(x_1x_3-x_2x_4)}{x_3}&\implies \frac{1}{O_1A_1^2-r_1^2}=\frac{x_3}{(x_1+x_3)(x_1x_3-x_2x_4)}.\end{align*} Hence,   $$ \sum_{i=1}^{4}{\frac{1}{O_iA_i^2-r_i^2}}=\sum_{\text{cyc}}{\frac{x_3}{(x_1+x_3)(x_1x_3-x_2x_4)}}=\sum_{\text{cyc}}{\frac{x_1+x_3}{(x_1+x_3)(x_1x_3-x_2x_4)}}=0. $$    $\square$

$A_1A_3$  and  $A_2A_4$  intersection  $X$  $A_1X = a,A_2X=b,A_3X=c,A_4X=d$   $$ \frac{1}{O_1A_1^2-r_1^2} = \frac{c}{(a+c)(ac-bd)} $$  the expression is 0 if all these sums are calculated by connecting them to  $a, b, c, d$ .
I think it’s easier than the G1.

Note the equation is equivalent to  $$ \sum_\text{cyc} \frac1{\text{Pow}_{(A_2A_3A_4)}(A_1)}=0. $$  Let  $X$  be the intersection of  $A_1A_3$  and  $A_2A_4$ . Let  $P_i$  be the intersection of  $A_iA_{i+2}$  and  $(A_{i+1}A_{i+2}A_{i+3})$  besides  $A_{i+2}$  with indices taken mod 4. Let  $x_i=A_iX$ .

We have  $\text{Pow}_{(A_2A_3A_4)}(A_1)=A_1P_1\cdot A_1A_2$  using signed lengths. By power of a point on circle  $(A_2A_3A_4)$ ,  $P_1X=\frac{x_2x_4}{x_3}$ . So, using signed lengths,  $$ \text{Pow}_{(A_2A_3A_4)}(A_1)=A_1P_1\cdot A_1A_2=(x_1-\frac{x_2x_4}{x_3})(x_1+x_2)=\frac1{x_3}(x_1x_3-x_2x_4)(x_1+x_3) $$  So, using similar logic on the other points, the whole expression is  $$ \frac{x_3}{(x_1x_3-x_2x_4)(x_1+x_3)}+\frac{x_4}{(x_2x_4-x_1x_3)(x_2+x_4)}+\frac{x_1}{(x_1x_3-x_2x_4)(x_1+x_3)}+\frac{x_2}{(x_2x_4-x_1x_3)(x_2+x_4)} $$    $$ =\frac{1}{x_1x_3-x_2x_4}+\frac{1}{x_2x_4-x_1x_3}=0.\qquad\square $$

Note that the equation is equivalent to   $$ \sum_{cyc}\frac{1}{\text{pow}_{(A_2A_3A_4)}(A_1)} =0. $$   We use barycentric coordinates with respect to  $A_1A_2A_3$ . Let  $A_4=(d,e,f)$ . We have that   $$ \frac{1}{\text{pow}_{(A_2A_3A_4)}(A_1)} = \frac{1}{-a^2ef-b^2df-c^2de}. $$   Note that the circumcircle of  $A_1A_2A_4$  is of the form  $-a^2yz-b^2xz-c^2xy+(x+y+z)(wz)=0$ . Plugging in  $a_4$ , we have  $w=\frac{a^2ef+b^2df+c^2de}{f}$ . We thus get that  $\frac{1}{\text{pow}_{(A_1A_2A_4)}(A_3)} = \frac{f}{a^2ef+b^2df+c^2de}$ . Symmetrically applying this argument, we have   $$ \sum_{cyc}\frac{1}{\text{pow}_{(A_2A_3A_4)}(A_1)} = \frac{1}{a^2ef+b^2df+c^2de}(-1+d+e+f)=0 $$   as desired so we are done.

From here every length mentioned is directed. Denote by  $\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4$  the circumcircles of  $\triangle A_2A_3A_4,\triangle A_3A_4,A_1,\triangle A_4A_1A_2,\triangle A_1A_2A_3$  respectively. Let  $A_1A_3$  and  $A_2A_4$  intersect at a point  $P$ , and let  $A_iO_i$  intersect  $\omega_i$  at  $B_i$  for  $i=1,2,3,4.$  Let  $x_1$  be the directed length  $PA_i.$ Note that \[\text{pow}_{w_1}(A_1)=A_1B_1\cdot A_1A_3=(PB_1-PA_1)(PA_3+PA_1)=(x_3+x_1)(\frac{x_2x_4}{x_3}-x_1).\] Now use this advanced method called "adding" to get  $0.$

Note that the equation of a circle,  $-a^2yz-b^2zx-c^2xy+(x+y+z)(ux+vy+wz)$ ), gives the power of the point  $(x,y,z)$  where  $x+y+z=1$ . 

The equation of  $(\triangle A_2A_3A_4)$  is \[-a^2yz-b^2zx-c^2xy=0.\] Thus  $O_1A_1^2-r_1^2=-a^2y_1z_1-b^2z_1x_1-c^2x_1y_1=-K$ .

The equation of  $(\triangle A_3A_4A_1)$  is of the form  $-a^2yz-b^2zx-c^2xy+(x+y+z)(ux+vy+wz)=0.$  Plugging in  $A_3=(0,1,0)$  gives  $v=0$ , and plugging in  $A_4=(0,0,1)$  gives  $w=0$ . Finally, plugging in  $A_1=(x_1,y_1,z_1)$  gives  $u=\frac{a^2y_1z_1+b^2z_1x_1+c^2x_1y_1}{x_1}=\frac{K}{x_1}$ , so the equation of the circle is \[-a^2yz-b^2zx-c^2xy+(x+y+z)\left(\frac{K}{x_1}x\right).\]
Therefore  $O_2A_2^2-r_2^2=\frac{K}{x_1}$ .

The equation of  $(\triangle A_4A_1A_2)$  is of the form  $-a^2yz-b^2zx-c^2xy+(x+y+z)(ux+vy+wz)=0.$  Plugging in  $A_4=(0,0,1)$  gives  $w=0$ , and plugging in  $A_2=(1,0,0)$  gives  $u=0$ . Finally, plugging in  $A_1=(x_1,y_1,z_1)$  gives  $v=\frac{a^2y_1z_1+b^2z_1x_1+c^2x_1y_1}{y_1}=\frac{K}{y_1}$ , so the equation of the circle is \[-a^2yz-b^2zx-c^2xy+(x+y+z)\left(\frac{K}{y_1}y\right).\]
Therefore  $O_3A_3^2-r_3^2=\frac{K}{y_1}$ .

The equation of  $(\triangle A_1A_2A_3)$  is of the form  $-a^2yz-b^2zx-c^2xy+(x+y+z)(ux+vy+wz)=0.$  Plugging in  $A_2=(1,0,0)$  gives  $u=0$ , and plugging in  $A_3=(0,1,0)$  gives  $v=0$ . Finally, plugging in  $A_1=(x_1,y_1,z_1)$  gives  $w=\frac{a^2y_1z_1+b^2z_1x_1+c^2x_1y_1}{z_1}=\frac{K}{z_1}$ , so the equation of the circle is \[-a^2yz-b^2zx-c^2xy+(x+y+z)\left(\frac{K}{z_1}z\right).\]
Therefore  $O_4A_4^2-r_4^2=\frac{K}{z_1}$ .

Thus 
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{O_1A_1^2-r_1^2}+\frac{1}{O_2A_2^2-r_2^2}+\frac{1}{O_3A_3^2-r_3^2}+\frac{1}{O_4A_4^2-r_4^2}
&=-\frac{1}{K}+\frac{x_1}{K}+\frac{y_1}{K}+\frac{z_1}{K}
&=\frac{1}{a^2y_1z_1+b^2z_1x_1+c^2x_1y_1}(-1+x_1+y_1+z_1)
&=0,
\end{align*}
as desired.  $\blacksquare$</details>

(In this solution, consider all lengths in the directed sense, and take all indices modulo  $4$ .) First of all, notice that the desired result is equivalent to \[ \sum_{i=1}^4 \frac{1}{\text{Pow}(A_i, (A_{i+1}A_{i+2}A_{i+3}))} = 0. \] Let  $P=\overline{A_1A_3} \cap \overline{A_2A_4}$  and  $X=\overline{A_1A_3} \cap (A_2A_3A_4)$ . Furthermore, let  $PA_i=x_i$  for  $1 \le i \le 4$ . By PoP on  $X$  with respect to  $(A_2A_3A_4)$ ,  $PX=\frac{x_2x_4}{x_3}$ . Thus, 
\[ \frac{1}{\text{Pow}(A_1, (A_2A_3A_4))} = \frac{1}{(A_1P+PA_3)(PX-PA_1)} = \frac{1}{(x_3-x_1)(\frac{x_2x_4}{x_3}-x_1)} = \frac{x_3}{(x_3-x_1)(x_2x_4-x_1x_3)}. \]
Replacing  $A_1$  with  $A_i$  and summing over  $1 \le i \le 4$ , we have \[ \frac{1}{O_1A_1^2-r_1^2}+\frac{1}{O_2A_2^2-r_2^2}+\frac{1}{O_3A_3^2-r_3^2}+\frac{1}{O_4A_4^2-r_4^2} = \sum_{i=1}^4 \frac{x_{i+2}}{(x_{i+2}-x_i)(x_{i+1}x_{i+3}-x_ix_{i+2})} = 0, \]
which completes the proof.

Let  $\alpha_i=\angle A_{i-1}A_iA_{i+1}$ , with indices taken modulo  $4$ . We also let  $\gamma_1$  be the circumcircle of  $A_2A_3A_4$  and define  $\gamma_2,\gamma_3,\gamma_4$  in a similar way.
We need to prove that 
\[\sum_i \frac{1}{\mathcal P_{\gamma_i}(A_i)}=0\]
We now examine each term individually :**Claim :** We have  $\mathcal P_{\gamma_1}(A_1)=-\sin (\alpha_4+\alpha_2)\frac{A_1A_2\cdot A_1A_4}{\sin \alpha_3}$ , and similarly for the other  $A_i$ 's.
*Proof :* Suppose circle  $\gamma_1$  intersects line  $(A_1A_2)$  again at a point  $X$ . An angle chase gives  $\angle A_1A_4X=\alpha_4+\alpha_2-180$ , as well as  $\angle A_1XA_4=\alpha_3$ .
Sine law in triangle  $A_1A_2A_4$  then gives 
\[A_1X=-\sin (\alpha_4+\alpha_2)\frac{A_1A_4}{\sin \alpha_3},\]
and the conclusion follows since  $\mathcal P_{\gamma_1}(A_1)=A_1X\cdot A_1A_2$ .  $\square$ We're actually done now. Indeed, pair up the  $A_1$  and  $A_3$  terms to get 
\begin{eqnarray*}
    \frac{1}{\mathcal P_{\gamma_1}(A_1)}+\frac{1}{\mathcal P_{\gamma_3}(A_3)}&=&-\frac{1}{\sin(\alpha_4+\alpha_2)}\cdot \left(\frac{\sin \alpha_3}{A_1A_2\cdot A_1A_4}+\frac{\sin \alpha_1}{A_3A_2\cdot A_3A_4}\right)
    &=& -\frac{1}{\sin(\alpha_4+\alpha_2)}\cdot \left(\frac{2S_1+2S_3}{A_1A_2\cdot A_2A_3\cdot A_3A_4\cdot A_4A_1}\right)
    &=& -\frac{1}{\sin(\alpha_4+\alpha_2)}\cdot \underbrace{\left(\frac{2S}{A_1A_2\cdot A_2A_3\cdot A_3A_4\cdot A_4A_1}\right)}_{:\overset{def}{=} T},
\end{eqnarray*}
where we let  $S$  be the area of  $A_1A_2A_3A_4$  and  $S_i$  be the area of the triangle  $A_{i+1}A_{i+2}A_{i+3}$ . 
By symmetry, we also have 
\[\frac{1}{\mathcal P_{\gamma_2}(A_2)}+\frac{1}{\mathcal P_{\gamma_4}(A_4)}=-\frac{1}{\sin(\alpha_3+\alpha_1)}\cdot T\]
Thus summing up we'll get the desired result, since  $\sin(\alpha_3+\alpha_1)=-\sin(\alpha_4+\alpha_2)$ . $\blacksquare$

<details><summary>Storage</summary>Consider directed lengths from  $M$  to  $A_1, A_2, A_3, A_4$  to have lengths  $x, y, z, w$  respectively. Let  $B_1 = AM \cap \omega_1$  where  $\omega_1$  is the circle with center  $O_1$  with radius  $r_1$ . 
Note that:  $\overline{MB_1} = \frac{yw}{z}$ . Thus:  $A_1 B_1 = \frac{yw}{z}-x$ . Summing up with power of point we are done.</details>

Proof:Let \( M \) be the point of intersection of the diagonals \( A_1A_3 \) and \( A_2A_4 \). On each diagonal, choose a direction and let \( x, y, z, w \) be the signed distances from \( M \) to the points \( A_1, A_2, A_3, A_4 \), respectively. Let \( \omega_1 \) be the circumcircle of triangle \( A_2A_3A_4 \), and let \( B_1 \) be the second intersection of \( \omega_1 \) and \( A_1A_3 \) (thus, \( B_1 = A_3 \) if and only if \( A_1A_3 \) is tangent to \( \omega_1 \)). Since the expression \( O_1A_1^2 - r_1^2 \) is the power of the point \( A_1 \) with respect to \( \omega_1 \), we get
\[
O_1A_1^2 - r_1^2 = A_1B_1 \cdot A_1A_3.
\]

On the other hand, from the equality \( MB_1 \cdot MA_3 = MA_2 \cdot MA_4 \), we obtain
\[
MB_1 = \frac{yw}{z}.
\]

Hence, it follows that
\[
O_1A_1^2 - r_1^2 = \left( \frac{yw}{z} - x \right)(z - x) = \frac{z - x}{z}(yw - xz).
\]

Doing the same thing for the other three expressions, we then get that
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{4} \frac{1}{O_iA_i^2 - r_i^2} 
= \frac{1}{yw - xz} \left( \frac{z}{x - z} - \frac{w}{w - y} + \frac{x}{x - z} - \frac{y}{y - w} \right) = 0.
\]

Let  $B  =A_1A_3 \cap A_2A_4$ , let  $A_{i + 4} = BA_i\cap (A_{(i + 1) \mod 4} A_{(i + 2) \mod 4} A_{(i + 3) \mod 4})$  for  $1 \le i \le 4$ . The expression on the left side is the negative of the power of  $A_i$  with respect to the circle with center  $O_i$  and radius  $r_i$ , so we can write the expression as  $\sum \frac{1}{(A_iA_{i + 4}) (A_iA_{(i + 2) \mod 4})} = \frac{1}{A_1A_3}(\frac{1}{BA_1 - BA_5} + \frac{1}{BA_3 -BA_7})+ \frac{1}{A_2A_4}(\frac{1}{BA_2 - BA_6} + \frac{1}{BA_4 -BA_8}) $ . We expand inner part of the first term. We have  $\frac{BA_1 + BA_3-BA_5 - BA_7}{(BA_1)(BA_3) - (BA_1)(BA_7)- (BA_3)(BA_5) + (BA_7)(BA_5) }$ . By power of point,  $(BA_1)(BA_7) = (BA_3)(BA_5) = (BA_2)(BA_4) $ . Thus we can rewrite  $(BA_7)(BA_5) = \frac{(BA_2)^2 (BA_4)^2}{(BA_1)(BA_3)}$ , and we can rewrite the inner part as  $\frac{(BA_1)(BA_3)(A_1A_3  - \frac{(BA_2)(BA_4)}{BA_1} - \frac{(BA_2)(BA_4)}{BA_3})}{(BA_1)^2(BA_3)^2 + (BA_2)^2(BA_4)^2 - 2(BA_1)(BA_2)(BA_3)(BA_4)}$ . Multiplying by  $A_1A_3$  and considering the symmetric variant for even indices, we can toss out the denominators, it is sufficient to show  $\frac{(A_1A_3) (BA_1) (BA_3) - \frac{(BA_2) (BA_4) (A_1A_3) (BA_1) (BA_3)}{(BA_1) (BA_3)}}{A_1A_3}$  plus its symmetric sum with indice parity switched is equal to zero, which is obvious when you simplify it to  $(BA_1)(BA_3) - (BA_2)(BA_4)$

Let  $ABCD$  be a convex quadrilateral whose sides  $AD$  and  $BC$  are not parallel. Suppose that the circles with diameters  $AB$  and  $CD$  meet at points  $E$  and  $F$  inside the quadrilateral. Let  $\omega_E$  be the circle through the feet of the perpendiculars from  $E$  to the lines  $AB,BC$  and  $CD$ . Let  $\omega_F$  be the circle through  the feet of the perpendiculars from  $F$  to the lines  $CD,DA$  and  $AB$ . Prove that the midpoint of the segment  $EF$  lies on the line through the two intersections of  $\omega_E$  and  $\omega_F$ .

*Proposed by Carlos Yuzo Shine, Brazil*

I have some changes in the notations.Let the circles with  diameters  $AD,BC$  meet at  $X,Y$  inside the quadrilateral  $ABCD$ .
So  $\angle AXD=\angle AYD=\angle BXD=\angle BYD=90^{\circ}$ .
Let  $X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4$  be the foot of perpendiculars from  $X$  to  $BC,CD,DA,AB$  respectivley.
Let  $Y_1,Y_2,Y_3,Y_4$  be the foot of perpendiculars from  $Y$  to  $BC,CD,DA,AB$  respectively.
Observation:From the perpendiculars we get  $(X,X_3,A,X_4);(X,X_4,B,X_1);(X,X_1C,X_2);(X,D,X_2,X_3)$  are cyclic.The similar cases with  $Y$ .
Note that these properties are independent of the positions of the foot of perpendiculars meaning the properties are valid even if some the foots lie on the extensions of sides  $AB,BC,CD,DA$ .

<details><summary>Motivation</summary>For this problem it is very difficult to draw a good diagram, but it should be clear from what is asked of you, to prove that something bisects another thing, that a parallelogram of some kind could be involved. Indeed, many parallel lines exist extensively in this problem, which makes finding some parallelogram that contains  $E$  and  $F$  a doable task. 

The only really parallel lines that exist with  $E$  and  $F$  in them in this configuration are  $FF_3$  and  $EE_1$ ,  $FF_1$  and  $EE_3$ ,  $FF_2$  and  $EE_2$ , and  $FF_4$  and  $EE_4$ . That's not many things to look through, and  $FPEQ$  being a parallelogram should be obvious. 

The only task left is to relate  $PQ$  and  $MN$ . In fact, proving  $PNQM$  is a parallelogram suffices, but we can do much better from a semi-decent diagram by saying that  $PQ$  is a subsegment of  $MN$ . What remains is to show the concurrency conditions, and that's where the circles come in handy. Extend a few necessary segments and prove some cyclics, and then everything falls into place.</details>

A few remarks: the most difficult part of the problem is making sense of the diagram. It's physically impossible to draw the circumcircles too far apart, so it's difficult to distinguish main claims just by staring at what's going on. It helps immensely to draw two separate diagrams (one for $E$ and one for $F$ ). We spend most of the solution defining points. Let $E_{BC}$ be the perpendicular from $E$ to $\overline{BC}$ , and define all $7$ other points similarly. Let $I$ and $K$ be the second intersections of $\omega_E$ with $\overline{BC}$ and $\overline{AD}$ , respectively, and define $J$ and $L$ similarly for $\omega_F$ . Let $\overline{PQ}$ be the endpoints of the radical axis, $O$ to be the midpoint of $\overline{EF}$ , $X = \overline{E_{BC}E} \cap \overline{F_{DA}F}$ , and $Y = \overline{E_{DA}E} \cap \overline{F_{BC}F}$ . Note first that $\omega_E$ contains all four feet from $E$ ; this is by [USAMO 1993/2.](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h58206p356408) A similar result holds for $\omega_F$ .**Claim.** [Main Claim] $I$ lies on $\overline{EE_{DA}}$ , and the three other cyclic permutations follow similarly. *Proof.* Angle chase. Redefine $I$ as $\overline{EE_{DA}} \cap \overline{BC}$ instead, and show it lies on the circle. This is fairly easy: \begin{align*} \angle E_{BC}IE &= \angle E_{BC}EE_{CD} + \angle E_{CD}EE_{DA} - 90^\circ &= 270^\circ - \angle E_{BC}CE - \angle ECE_{CD} - \angle EDE_{CD} - \angle EDE_{DA} &= 180^\circ - \angle E_{BC}E_{CD}E_{DA}. \ \blacksquare \end{align*} Note that this implies $\angle LE_{BC}K = 90^\circ$ and similar permutations. Now I claim $\overline{XY} = \overline{PQ}$ . Suffices to show $Y$ lies on the radical axis, but this is true by radical center theorem as $(LE_{BC}KF_{DA})$ is cyclic by the previous observation. Then note $EYFX$ is a parallelogram, so the midpoint $O$ of $\overline{EF}$ lies on $\overline{XY}$ or the radical axis.

Begin with a bunch of point definitions. Let the feet of the altitudes from  $E$  to  $AB$ ,  $BC$ ,  $CD$  and  $DA$  be  $W_e$ ,  $X_e$ ,  $Y_e$  and  $Z_e$ . Also let  $M$  be the midpoint of  $EF$ Claim:  $W_e$ ,  $X_e$ ,  $Y_e$  and  $Z_e$  are concylic.
Proof: This is just a simple angle chase. Note that 
    \begin{align*}
        \angle W_eZ_eY_e &= 180 - \angle W_eZ_eD - \angle Y_eZ_eB
        &= 180 - \angle W_eED - \angle Y_eEC 
        &= 180 - \angle EAW_e - \angle EBY_e
        &= 180 - \angle W_eX_eY_e
    \end{align*}

We can find a similar conclusion for  $F$ . Now extend  $X_eE$  past  $E$  to meet  $AD$  at a point  $P_e$ . 

Claim:  $P_e \in (W_eX_eY_eZ_e)$ . 
Proof: Note that,
\begin{align*}
    \angle EP_eZ_e &= 90 - \angle P_eEZ_e
    &= \angle X_eEY_e + \angle Y_eEZ_e - 90
    &= \angle X_eEC + \angle Z_eED
    &= \angle 180 - X_eY_eZ_e
\end{align*}
as desired. 

Now define  $Q_e$  to be the intersection of  $Z_eE$  and  $BC$  and define  $P_f$  and  $Q_f$ , noting that similar results hold. Finally let  $R$  be the intersection of  $P_eE$  and  $Q_fF$  and let  $S$  be the intersection of  $P_fF$  and  $Q_eE$ . Then we can easily find that  $ERSF$  is a parallelogram from which we get that  $R$ ,  $M$ ,  $S$  collinear. Also noting that  $R$  and  $S$  lie on the radical axis  $PQ$  we are done.

Let the feet from $E$ to $AB$ , $BC$ , $CD$ , $DA$ be $E_1$ through $E_4$ in order, and the feet from $F$ to $CD$ , $DA$ , $AB$ , $BC$ be $F_i$ .**Claim:** $F_4$ and $E_4$ lie on $\omega_E$ and $\omega_F$ . *Proof.* This is just angle chasing. From the cyclic quads formed by feet we have \[\measuredangle E_2E_1E_4 =\measuredangle E_2E_1E+\measuredangle EE_1E_4=\measuredangle CBE+\measuredangle EAD= \measuredangle ECB+\measuredangle ADE=\measuredangle E_2E_3E_4.\] Some steps use the fact that $\angle BEC+\angle AED=180^{\circ}$ which is true from $\angle BEA=\angle CED=90^{\circ}.$ $\blacksquare$ **Claim:** We have $O=E_4E\cap BC$ , $E_2E\cap DA$ lie on $\omega_E$ and $R=FF_4\cap DA$ and $FF_2\cap BC$ lie on $\omega_F$ . *Proof.* We show $O$ lies on $\omega_E$ and the rest follow by symmetry. To do so, observe that \begin{align*} & \measuredangle E_2E_1E_4=\measuredangle E_2E_1E+\measuredangle EE_1E_4=\measuredangle E_2BE+\measuredangle EAE_4 & =90^{\circ} + \measuredangle E_2EB+\measuredangle BEA=\measuredangle =90+\measuredangle E_2EO & =\measuredangle E_2OE=\measuredangle E_2OE_4 \end{align*} as desired. During this proof we make use of the many right angels, and some cycic quads formed by them yet again. $\blacksquare$ Now define $P=EE_4\cap FF_4$ and $Q=EE_2\cap FF_2$ . First, note that $EP\perp AD$ and $QF\perp AD$ so $QF\parallel EP$ and $QE\parallel PF$ so $EPFQ$ is a parallelogram. To finish, we present the final claim.**Claim:** Line $PQ$ is the radical axis of $\omega_E$ and $\omega_F$ . *Proof.* We prove that $P$ lies on the radical axis and it follows that $Q$ does as well by symmetry. To do so, note that by right angles $OF_4E_4R$ is cyclic and hence $OP\cdot PE_4=PR\cdot PF_4$ . But we have that \[\operatorname{pow}_{\omega_E}(P)=PO\cdot PE_4 =PR\cdot PF_4=\operatorname{pow}_{\omega_{F}}(P)\] Implying the result. $\blacksquare$ Then, we have that the diagonals of $EPFQ$ bisect each other so $PQ$ , the radical axis of $\omega_E$ and $\omega_F$ bisects $EF$ as desired.

Define the feet to  $AB$ ,  $BC$ ,  $CD$ , and  $DA$  from  $E$  be  $E_{1,2,3,4}$  and  $F$  be  $F_{1,2,3,4}$ , respectively. These induce several cyclic quadrilaterals.

Note that  $E_1E_2E_3E_4$  is cyclic, as
\[\angle E_4E_1E_2 + \angle E_2E_3E_4 = 360 - \angle BEC + \angle DEC = 180,\]

and analogously for  $F$ . Letting  $E_2E \cap AD = E_2'$ , and similarily for other even indexed points, we have that this point also lies on  $\omega_C$ , as
\[\angle E_2E_2'E_4 = \angle E_2EE_3 + \angle E_3EE_4 - 90 = 180 - \angle E_2CE - \angle E_4DE = 180 - \angle E_2E_3E_4,\]

and analogously for the other altitudes from  $E$ ,  $F$  to  $BC$  and  $DA$ . Consider points  $K = EE_2 \cap FF_4$  and  $L = EE_4 \cap FF_2$ :


- Cyclic quadrilateral  $E_2E_2'F_4F_4'$  tells us  $K$  lies on the radical axis of  $\omega_E$  and  $\omega_F$ , and similarily for  $L$ .
- $EKFL$  is a parallelogram, so  $LK$  bisects  $EF$ , and hence the midpoint of  $EF$  lies on the radical axis, as desired.  $\blacksquare$

**2011 G3** 

Here is a **Sketch** of the solution.


Let  $P_1,P_2,P_3,P_4$  denote the perpendiculars from  $E$  to  $AB,BC,CD,AD$ . Define  $Q_1,Q_2,Q_3,Q_4$  similarly wrt to  $F$ .


Let  $M$  and  $N$  denote midpoints of  $AB$  and  $CD$ ,let  $R$  denote the midpoint of  $EF$ , we show that  $R$  lies on radicle axis of these two circles.

Let  $RP_3 \cap \omega_E=K$  and  $RQ_3 \cap \omega_F=L$ **Claim:**  $RP_i=RQ_i$  for  $i=1,2,3,4$ .

After that we can easily show that  $RMEP_1$  and  $RNFQ_1$  are cyclic. 

Now for the main claim.**Claim:**  $RK=RP_1$  and  $RL=RQ_1$ .

After proving the claim above, we would be done by POP.

Let  $P,Q$  be the isogonal conjugates of  $E,F$ , and let the reflections of  $E,F$  over  $AB$  be  $W,X$  and over  $CD$  be  $Y,Z$ . Let  $M$  be the midpoint of  $EF$ .

First note that under inversion at  $E$ ,  $P$  inverts to a Miquel point, and  $W,Y$  invert to midpoints, so by gliding principle  $WFPY$  is cyclic. Similarly  $XEQZ$  is cyclic. Next by properties of isogonal conjugates,  $PW=PY$  and  $QX=QZ$  so  $FP$  bisects  $\angle WFY$  and  $EQ$  bisects  $\angle XEZ$ . Thus  $\angle AFD=\tfrac12\angle WFY=\angle WFP-90^\circ$  and similarly  $\angle BEC=\angle XEQ-90^\circ$ .

Now we have \[\frac{FP}{EQ}=\frac{\frac{FP}{\sin\angle FBP}}{\frac{EQ}{\sin\angle EBQ}}=\frac{\frac{BC}{\sin\angle BFC}}{\frac{BC}{\sin\angle BEC}}=\frac{\sin\angle BEC}{\sin\angle AFD}=\frac{-\cos\angle XEQ}{-\cos\angle WFP}\] so \[-4\operatorname{pow}_{\omega_E}(M)=WP^2-FP^2=WF^2-2WF\cdot FP\cos\angle WFP=XE^2-2XE\cdot EQ\cos\angle XEQ=XQ^2-EQ^2=-4\operatorname{pow}_{\omega_F}(M)\] as desired.

Let the midpoints of  $EF,AB,CD$  be  $M,M_1,M_2$ . Let the feet from  $F$  to  $AB,DA,CD$  be  $A',K,D'\implies FKAA'$  cyclic. (Similarly define  $B',C'$ .)  $M_1M_2\perp EF\implies FA'M_1M$  cyclic.

Let  $\angle FKA'=\alpha,\angle D'KF=\beta$ . Then  $\angle FAM_1=\alpha\implies\angle A'MF=\angle A'M_1F=180^\circ-2\alpha$ . Similarly,  $\angle FMD'=180^\circ-2\beta\implies\angle A'MD'=360^\circ-2\alpha-2\beta$ .

Let  $P$  be on  $MD'$  such that  $AKD'P$  is cyclic. Then  $\angle A'PM=180^\circ-\alpha-\beta=\frac{\angle A'MD}{2}\implies \angle APM=\angle MA'P\implies MP=MA'$ . Therefore the power of  $M$  with respect to  $(A'KD')$  (which is  $\omega_F$ ) is  $MA'\cdot MD'$ . Analogously, the power of  $M$  with respect to  $\omega_E$  is  $MB'\cdot MC'$ . However,  $ME=MF\implies MA'=MB',MC'=MD'\implies$  the powers are equal, hence  $M$  lies on the radical axis, so we're done.

Let  $ABC$  be an acute triangle with circumcircle  $\Omega$ . Let  $B_0$  be the midpoint of  $AC$  and let  $C_0$  be the midpoint of  $AB$ . Let  $D$  be the foot of the altitude from  $A$  and let  $G$  be the centroid of the triangle  $ABC$ . Let  $\omega$  be a circle through  $B_0$  and  $C_0$  that is tangent to the circle  $\Omega$  at a point  $X\not= A$ . Prove that the points  $D,G$  and  $X$  are collinear.

*Proposed by Ismail Isaev and Mikhail Isaev, Russia*
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2011 Contests/2011 IMO Shortlist/488829.json

candidates: Let  $\Gamma,O$  be the circumcircle and circumcenter of  $\triangle ABC$ , and let  $A_0$  be the midpoint of  $BC$ . Let  $XB_0,XC_0$  meet  $\Gamma$  again at  $B',C'$ , and let  $E=BB' \cap CC'$ . Pascal's Theorem on hexagon  $ABB'XC'C$  gives  $E \in B_0C_0$ . Since the dilation carrying  $\omega$  to  $\Gamma$  carries  $B_OC_0$  to  $B'C'$ ,  $B'C' \parallel B_0C_0 \parallel BC$ . Then  $B'C'BC$  is an isosceles trapezium, so  $E$  is the foot of the perpendicular of  $A_0$  on  $B_0C_0$ . The dilation centered at  $G$  taking  $\triangle ABC$  to  $\triangle A_0B_0C_0$  takes  $D$  to  $E$ , so  $D,G,E$  are collinear. It suffices to show  $B'B_0, C'C_0, ED$  are concurrent. Since lines  $BB_0, CC_0, ED$  concur at  $G$ ,  $\triangle BCE$  and  $\triangle B_0C_0D$  are perspective. Let  $U=BE \cap B_0D$  and  $V=CE \cap C_0D$ .  Desargue's Theorem implies  $UV \parallel B_0C_0$ . By Desargue's Theorem again, this implies  $\triangle B'C'E$  and  $\triangle B_0C_0D$  are perspective, so  $B'B_0, C'C_0, ED$  are concurrent as desired.

Alternative solution:

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>If  $ABC$  is isosceles at  $A$ , then  $DG$  is a symmetry axis of  $\Omega$ , of  $ABC$ , and of  $B_0C_0$ . Hence  $X$  is clearly on this axis of symmetry ( $X$  is actually the second point  $\neq A$  where the perpendicular bisector  $AD$  of  $BC$  meets  $\Omega$ ). Assume henceforth wlog that  $\angle B>\angle C$ , since they may be exchanged without altering the problem.

Triangle  $AB_0C_0$  is clearly the result of applying a homothety  $\tau$  with center  $A$  and scale factor  $\frac{1}{2}$  to triangle  $ACB$ .  Let  $\omega'$  be the result of applying  $\tau$  to  $\Omega$ , clearly the circumcircle of  $AB_0C_0$ , and  $\omega',\Omega$  are tangent at  $A$ .  Since  $B_0C_0$  is a common chord of $\omega,\omega'$ , then  $B_0C_0$  is their radical axis.  Let  $P$  be the point where  $B_0C_0$  meets the common tangent to  $\omega',\Omega$  at  $A$ , clearly the radical center of  $\Omega,\omega,\omega'$ , hence  $PX$  is the common tangent to  $\Omega,\omega$  at  $X$ , and  $P$  is the center of a circle through $A,X$ .

Since  $P$  is on the perpendicular bisector  $B_0C_0$  of  $AD$ , the circle with center  $P$  through  $A,X$  also passes through  $D$ , and  $\angle AXD=\frac{1}{2}\angle APD=\angle APB_0$ .  Since  $AO\perp AP$  forms angles  $90^\circ-\angle C$  and  $90^\circ-\angle B$  respectively with lines  $AB,AC$ , it follows that  $AO$  and  $B_0C_0$  form an angle of  $90^\circ-(\angle B-\angle C)$ , or  $\angle AXD=\angle APB_0=\angle B-\angle C$ .  Therefore,  $XD$  meets  $\Omega$  again at a point  $Y\neq X$  such that  $\angle ACY=\angle AXD=\angle B-\angle C$ , or  $\angle BCY=\angle B$ , hence  $Y$  is the symmetric of  $A$  with respect to the perpendicular bisector of  $BC$ .

Let  $A_0$  be the midpoint of  $BC$ .  Clearly  $A_0B_0C_0D$  is an isosceles trapezoid, and so is  $ABCY$ .  Moreover,  $A_0B_0C_0$  is the result of applying a homothety  $\tau'$  with center  $G$  and scale factor  $-\frac{1}{2}$  to triangle  $ABC$ , or  $Y$  is the result of applying  $\tau'$  to  $D$ , and  $D,G,Y$  are collinear.  Since  $D,X,Y$  are also collinear, we are done.</details>

<details><summary>solution by inversion</summary>Let us perform an inversion centered at  $A$  and of arbitrary power. We will denote the image  $P'$  of any point again by  $P$  to simplify notation. It will be enough to show that  $A$ ,  $D$ ,  $G$ ,  $X$  are concyclic.
Under this inversion  $\Omega$  maps to  $BC$ (i.e  $B'C'$ ) and  $\omega$  maps to a circle via  $B_0, C_0$  touching  $BC$  at  $X$  (See figure).  $B$ , $C$  now become the midpoints of  $AC_0$ ,  $AB_0$  respectively.
Moreover,  $D$  maps to the circumcenter of  $\triangle AC_0B_0$  and  $G$  is the second intersection of  $\odot (ACC_0)$  and  $\odot (ABB_0)$ .  $AG$  also becomes a symmedian. 
Let the tangents at  $C_0$ ,  $B_0$  to  $\odot(AB_0C_0)$  intersect at  $K$ . It is well known that  $AK$  is a symmedian and hence  $A$ ,  $G$ ,  $K$  are collinear. Let  $E=KB_0 \cap BC$ . Then  $\angle B_0EC=\angle A \Longrightarrow E$  lies on  $\odot(ABB_0)$ . Now,  $XDB_0E$  is cyclic implies  $KB_0 \cdot KE=KD \cdot KX=KG \cdot KA$   $\Longrightarrow$   $A$ ,  $G$ ,  $D$ ,  $X$  are concyclic  $\text{    } \square$ [asy]

Let  $T$  be on  $BC$  such that  $AT$  tangents cirumcircle of  $ABC$ . Now by radical axis theorem on  $ABC, AB_0C_0, B_0C_0X$ , their radical centre is midpoint of  $AT$ , call it as  $S$ . Let  $\gamma$  be circle  $TAD$  with centre  $S$ . Since  $SA\perp AO$  where  $O$  is cirumcentre of  $ABC$ ,  $\omega$  and  $\gamma$  are orthogonal. Also,  $SX$  is tangent to  $\omega$  and so,  $\gamma$  passes through  $X$ . Now by Reim's theorem on circles  $\gamma, \omega$  with lines  $XD$  and  $AP$ , we have that if  $XD$  intersects  $\omega$  at  $U$ , then  $AU\parallel BC$ . The foot of the altitude on the antimedial triangle from vertex corresponding to  $A$  lies on the nine point circle  $\omega$  and is also the image of the point  $D$  under a homothety with centre  $G$  and so, we see that that point is  $U$ . This proves the result.

This very short solution is from Evan o'Dorney:

Let  $R$  be intersection of  $B_0C_0$  and tangents at  $A$  and  $X$ .  Take  $E$  s.t.  $AEBC$  is an isosceles trapezoid; well-known  $D$ ,  $G$  and  $E$  are collinear.    $RA = RD = RX \implies \angle AXD = \frac 12 \angle ARD = \angle ARB_0 = \pi - \angle RAE = \angle AXE$ , done.

Here are some facts I want to say about this problems and these will also lead to the solution.....**1.**  $A_0, B_0, C_0$  are the midpoints of the sides  $BC, CA, AB$ . Now we define the points  $Y,Z$  such that  $\odot YA_0C_0$  us tangent to  $\odot ABC$  at  $Y$  and similar for  $Z$ . Then the lines  $AX, BY, CZ$  concur at the isogonal conjugate of the isotomic conjugate of orthocente rof  $\triangle ABC$ .**2.** Let  $D'$  be the isotomic point of  $D$  wrt  $BC$ . Then  $GD$  bisects  $AD'$ .**Proof of (1):-** Inverting with respect to  $A$  with some power,  $B_0', C_0'$  becomes the reflection of  $A$  wrt  $B', C'$  respectively. The point  $X'$  is such that the line  $B'C'$  is tangent to  $\odot X'B_0'C_0'$  at  $X'$  Hence  $X'$  is the midpoint of the arc  $B_0'C_0'$ . So  $X'$  lies on the perpendicular bisector of  $B_0'C_0'$ . Hence  $X'$  is the reflection of the foot of A-altitude of the triangle  $\triangle AB'C'$  wrt the midpoint of  $B'C'$ . So  $AX, BY, CZ$  concur at the isogonal conjugate of isotomic conjugate of the orthocenter of  $\triangle ABC$ .**Proof of (2):-** Reflect  $G$  wrt the midpoint of  $BC$ . Let it be  $G'$ .Then clearly  $G'D'\parallel GD$ . Now  $G$  is the midpoint of  $AG'$ . So  $GD$  bisects  $AD'$ .**Main Proof:-** Suppose the isogonal ray of  $AD'$  cuts  $\odot ABC$  at  $D_2$ . And  $AD'$  cuts the circumcircle at  $D_1$ . Then clearly  $D_1D_2\parallel BC$ .So the perpendicular bisector of  $D_1D_2$  passes through the midpoint of  $BC$  which again passes through the midpoint of  $AD'$  (easy to see). So  $D_2, D, \text{midpoint of} AD'$  are collinear. So  $D_1, D, G$  are collinear. Hence proven.

Let  $\odot AB_0C_0=\alpha,\odot XB_0C_0=\omega,M=AD \cap B_0C_0$ .
Let  $AD' \bot B_0C_0,D' \in B_0C_0$ , $O$  be the centre of  $\Omega$ .
Let  $K$  be the intersection of the tangents to  $\Omega$  from  $A,X$ . $AK$  is the radical axis of  $\Omega,\alpha$ ; $KX$  is the radical axis of  $\Omega,\omega$  and  $B_0,C_0$  is the radical axis of  $\alpha,\omega$ .
So  $K \in B_0C_0$ . $\angle OAK+\angle OXK=90^{\circ}+90^{\circ}=180^{\circ} \rightarrow AKXO$  are cyclic.
A homothety of ratio  $-2$  and centre  $G$  sends  $O$  to  $H$ ,the orthocentre of   $ABC$  and  $\triangle A_0B_0C_0$  to  $\triangle ABC$ .
So  $O$  is the orthocentre of  $\triangle A_0B_0C_0$ . $\angle OD'K=\angle OAK=90^{\circ} \rightarrow AKXOD'$  is cyclic. $AB_0C_0 \cong A_0B_0C_0 \rightarrow AM=A_0D'$  $AM \bot B_0C_0,A_0D' \bot B_0C_0 \rightarrow AM \parallel A_0D'$ which implies  $AMA_0D'$  is a parallelogram.
Note that a homothety of ratio  $-2$  and centre  $G$  sends  $D'$  to  $D$ .
Hence  $D,G,D'$  are collinear.
So it suffices to prove that  $X,D,D'$  are collinear. $\angle KD'X=\angle KAX=\angle KXA=\angle KD'A=\angle AD'M$  $=\angle A_0MD'=\angle MA_0D=\angle MD'D$ [The last arguement comes from the fact that  $MDA_0D'$  is a rectangle.]
which implies  $X,D,D'$  are collinear.

**Lemma: If  $DG$  intersects the circumcircle at  $E$ , then  $ABCE$  is an isosceles trapezoid.**

<details><summary>Proof</summary>Consider the  reverse homthety centered at  $G$  taking the nine-point circle to the circumcircle. We see that if  $D$  is taken to  $E$ , then  $GE/GD=GC/GC_0=GB/GB_0=2$ , and we obtain  $\triangle BEC\sim\triangle DC_0B_0\sim\triangle ABC$ , and we have desired.</details>

Let  $ABC$  be a triangle with incentre  $I$  and circumcircle  $\omega$ . Let  $D$  and  $E$  be the second intersection points of  $\omega$  with  $AI$  and  $BI$ , respectively. The chord  $DE$  meets  $AC$  at a point  $F$ , and  $BC$  at a point  $G$ . Let  $P$  be the intersection point of the line through  $F$  parallel to  $AD$  and the line through  $G$  parallel to  $BE$ . Suppose that the tangents to  $\omega$  at  $A$  and  $B$  meet at a point  $K$ . Prove that the three lines  $AE,BD$  and  $KP$  are either parallel or concurrent.

*Proposed by Irena Majcen and Kris Stopar, Slovenia*

*Lemma 1. The quaderilaterals*  $BIGD$  *and*  $AIFE$  *are cyclic.*
*Proof.* Easy angle chasing gives  $\angle GPF = 90 - \frac{C}{2}$  and  $\angle FGP = \frac{A}{2}.$  Also  $\angle FGC= \angle GFC$  by angle chasing. Now note that  $\angle BGD = \angle BID = 90 - \frac{C}{2}$  to finish.

*Lemma 2. If*  $PG,PF$  *meet*  $\odot (AIFE),\odot (BIGD)$  *at*  $M,N$  *then*  $M,I,N$  *are collinear.* 
*Proof.* Easy angle chase again, with cyclic quads and angle sum property.

*Lemma 3.*  $P$  *lies on the radical axis of*  $\odot (BIGD),\odot (AIFE).$ *Proof.* Since  $MNGF$  is cyclic (trivial angle chase again) by power of point we have  $PG \cdot PN= PF \cdot PM.$  The result follows.

*Lemma 4.*  $K$  *lies on the radical axis of* $\odot (BIGD), \odot (AIFE).$ *Proof.* First note that  $\angle MAF = \angle MAE + \angle CAE = \angle MFE + \angle CBE = \frac{B}{2} + \frac{B}{2} = B.$  Thus  $MA$  and similarly     $BN$  are tangent to  $\odot (ABC).$  Hence  $K = NB \cap MA.$    But also  $\angle AMI = \angle AEB = \angle ACB = C,$  and  $\angle NBA = A +B = 180 - C$  so  $BAMN$  is cyclic. By power of point we have  $KB \cdot KN = KA \cdot KM.$ Now we are ready to finish off. Note that  $AE,BD,KP$  are the radical axes of the circles  $ \odot (AIFEM), \odot (ABDCE), \odot  (BIGDN)$  taken pairwise. Hence the required result follows by radical axes theorem.

*A note, and some motivation. See the way the problem is worded? The lines are concurrent **or parallel**. When the solution just involves, say, like Ceva, Menelaus, Desargues, Pappus etc. we don't usually have that bold part. The only way this can enter is by virtue of radical axes. Hence we wish to interpret the lines as the radical axes of three circles. Hence the construction of the two new points and two new circles.*

I found this one to be easier than G1 :P. Anyhow, here's my solution (maybe different): We start off with the following lemma:- Lemma Let $\triangle ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB=AC$ . Let $D$ be a point inside $\triangle ABC$ , and let $E$ be its reflection about $BC$ . Suppose the lines through $D$ parallel to $AC$ and $AB$ meet $BC$ at $X$ and $Y$ . Let $AX \cap BE=P,AY \cap CE=Q$ . Then $PQ$ is parallel to $XY$ .**PROOF:** (There also exists an easy bary bash for this Lemma, something which I had discovered before this proof which evaded me for a long time) Note that $\angle DXY=\angle ACB=\angle ABC=\angle DYX$ , and so $DX=DY$ . This gives that $EX=EY$ and $EX \parallel AB,EY \parallel AC$ , as $E$ is the reflection of $D$ about $XY$ . Thus, $$ \frac{PX}{PA}=\frac{EX}{BA}=\frac{EY}{CA}=\frac{QY}{QA} \Rightarrow PQ \parallel XY \text{ } \Box $$ Return to the problem at hand. Let the tangents to $\omega$ at $D$ and $E$ meet at $T$ . Let $TF \cap AD=U,TG \cap BE=V$ . Then $$ \angle CFG=\angle CEF+\angle FCE=\angle CAD+\angle ABE=\frac{A}{2}+\frac{B}{2}=90^{\circ}-\frac{C}{2} $$ Similarly, we get that $\angle CGF=90^{\circ}-\frac{C}{2}$ , giving that $\triangle CFG$ is isosceles with $CF=CG$ . Also, Using Fact 5, we have that $DE$ is the perpendicular bisector of $CI$ . As $TD \parallel CG$ and $TE \parallel CF$ , and because $\triangle TDE$ is isosceles, applying our Lemma to $\triangle TDE$ , we get that $UV$ is parallel to $FG$ . Now, Let $\infty_{AD}$ and $\infty_{BE}$ be the point at infinity on the lines $AD$ and $BE$ . Then, by the above result, $\triangle FTG$ and $\triangle \infty_{AD} I \infty_{BE}$ are perspective from a line. By Desargues' Theorem of Two Triangles, we get that these two triangles must also be perspective from a point, and so we get that $P$ lies on $TI$ . But, By Pascal Theorem on the degenerate hexagons $DDAEEB$ and $AADBBE$ , we have that $K,T,I$ are collinear, and that $AE,BD,TI$ concur. Thus, $AE,BD,KP$ are concurrent. $\blacksquare$
